evidence.text: The article says there is no ground fighting in Iran and that major North Carolina-based Army and Marine units have not been tapped for the war. Fort Bragg’s 82nd Airborne Division could deploy quickly if the Trump administration decided to send ground troops, but a spokesperson for the 18th Airborne Corps, which includes the 82nd, said the division had received no Pentagon orders regarding the war. President Trump told reporters that weekend there would “have to be a very good reason” to send ground troops into Iran. The article also notes that a smaller special-operations mission in Iran could potentially draw on units based at Fort Bragg.

evidence.title: Iran war: Tuesday to be 'most intense day' of US strikes - dw.com
evidence.text: The Trump administration is reportedly considering sending special forces into Iran to secure its 440kg stockpile of highly enriched uranium, which experts say could be used to make at least 10 nuclear warheads. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told Congress that “people are going to have to go and get it,” and US and Israeli reports describe discussions of a mission involving special forces from either or both countries. No deployment is reported. On Saturday, Trump said US troops would not be sent until Iranian ground defenses were greatly weakened: “We wouldn’t do it now. Maybe we will do it later.” Experts described an extraction as risky and complex, potentially requiring major ground operations at sites near Isfahan and Natanz, deep inside Iran. One analyst said the US and Israel appeared to be monitoring the material while deciding what to do longer-term.

evidence.title: Hawley doesn’t see Trump asking for U.S. ground troops to enter war against Iran - stlpr.org
evidence.text: A March 8, 2026, social-media post claimed that a failed U.S. air operation in Tehran ended with Iran capturing 173 U.S. Delta Force soldiers and officers. The article found no official reports or credible news accounts supporting the claim. One purported photo was rated 100% likely AI-generated, and another bore a Google Gemini AI watermark. This does not provide evidence that U.S. ground forces entered Iran; it does not establish what will happen by December 31.

evidence.title: Will US send troops to Iran for ground operation, and will Trump seize enriched uranium in Tehran with the - The Economic Times
evidence.text: The United States is reviewing options for sending forces into Iran, but no ground operation has been approved or announced. President Trump has not ruled out ground troops, saying they would be deployed only for a strong reason. Analysts say a full invasion would require around 500,000 troops and would be difficult to launch quickly. Officials are also considering a smaller special-forces mission to secure Iran’s enriched uranium, but it remains a contingency plan. US air operations continue while other options are reviewed. The article gives no timetable for US forces to enter Iran by December 31.

evidence.title: Saudi Arabia Opens King Fahd Air Base to US Forces as Iran War Shifts West - houseofsaud.com
evidence.text: The article says thousands of additional US ground troops are en route from East Asia to the Gulf region, citing Turkiye Today and Western military officials. It also reports that President Trump had earlier ordered additional Marines to the Gulf. Saudi Arabia has agreed to open King Fahd Air Base in Taif to US forces for operations against Iran, while US forces are already operating from Prince Sultan Air Base and other Gulf bases. These are reports of deployments and basing around Iran; the article does not say US forces have entered Iranian territory or announce plans for them to do so by December 31.

evidence.title: Iranian Kurdish fighters find themselves in the middle of U.S.-Iran war as they wait in Iraq - CBC
evidence.text: The article says the US is deploying additional warships and troops to the Middle East, not that US forces have entered Iran. It reports a US-Israeli attack on Iran’s Natanz nuclear enrichment facility and says the war is entering its fourth week. President Donald Trump gave mixed signals, suggesting he was considering “winding down” regional military operations while also threatening an attack on Iran’s Kharg Island; he said he might have a plan but would not disclose it. The article reports no decision or plan for US troops to enter Iran by December 31.

evidence.title: Middle East Travel, Immigration & Corporate Mobility: FAQs for Employers - Newland Chase
evidence.text: The article says the United States and Israel launched a coordinated military operation against Iran on February 28, 2026, killing Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei and much of Iran’s political and military leadership. It says Iran retaliated against US military installations and other targets across 11 regional countries. The article does not say US ground forces entered Iran or report plans for them to do so by December 31.

evidence.title: The mission that could end the Iran war? What’s really going on behind the scenes - The Economic Times
evidence.text: As of March 19, 2026, the article says President Donald Trump had launched Operation Epic Fury against Iran on February 28. It describes the operation as America-led and coordinated with Israel, aimed at Iran’s leadership, naval and air power, manufacturing capabilities, and nuclear infrastructure. It reports no U.S. forces entering Iran and gives no plan or forecast for such an entry by December 31.

evidence.title: The overlooked resilience of Iraqi militias and Houthi forces in the Iran war - The Times of Israel
evidence.text: On the conflict’s 20th day, the article says reports indicated that US President Donald Trump was planning to send soldiers—potentially thousands of troops—to clear a blockade in the Strait of Hormuz and restart global energy supplies. It does not say US forces have entered Iran, that the reported plan calls for entering Iranian territory, or when any deployment would occur. The article cautions that past invasions of Iran have been difficult and says Iran has prepared for a prolonged fight against a larger adversary such as the US.

evidence.title: Iran Update Special Report, March 18, 2026 - Institute for the Study of War
evidence.source: Institute for the Study of War
evidence.text: The article says President Trump is seeking regime change in Iran without committing U.S. ground troops. Its author argues that airstrikes alone cannot achieve regime change in a country of 90 million people, four times the size of Iraq, but that Trump’s MAGA base and the U.S. public have little appetite for a prolonged Middle Eastern ground war. The author frames Trump’s choice as accepting failure to achieve regime change or breaking his promise of “no more forever wars,” and suggests he may instead declare victory. The article reports no U.S. ground-force entry into Iran or decision to undertake one by December 31.

evidence.title: Reports of large US invasion to get Iran 60% nuke uranium likely overblown - The Jerusalem Post
evidence.text: The article describes a proposed Kurdish ground offensive, not a confirmed plan for U.S. forces to enter Iran. It says Trump called Iranian Kurdish politician Mustafa Hijri on March 3, 2026, the fourth day of the war, and reportedly offered Kurdish leaders in Iran and Iraq weapons, intelligence and U.S. air support. The proposed uprising would seek to take Iran’s predominantly Kurdish northwestern provinces and inspire broader opposition to the regime. U.S. personnel crossing into Iran are not part of the plan as described. The article says Iranian Kurdish commanders in Iraq expressed readiness to attack targets in Iran, but Iraqi Kurdistan officials denied reports that armed Kurds had already crossed the border. It also cites obstacles to the offensive: Iranian Kurdish groups have an estimated 4,000–8,500 fighters, versus 250,000–300,000 personnel in Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps alone, and Iraqi Kurdish forces are politically divided.

evidence.title: Will Trump Deploy Ground Troops to Iran? Here’s What to Know - The National Interest
evidence.text: Two weeks after U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran began in mid-March 2026, online posts claimed U.S. soldiers were openly refusing orders to deploy to Iran. The article says those claims remain unverified: searches and social-media reviews found no reputable video or other evidence that active-duty or reserve service members had rejected official orders. Organizations assisting conscientious objectors reported increased requests from service members, but the article says this does not establish that anyone refused a deployment order. It reports no U.S. ground forces entering Iran and provides no confirmed deployment orders to do so.

evidence.title: Seizing Iran’s uranium could take ‘largest special forces operation in history’ – WSJ - The Times of Israel
evidence.text: The article says the United States and Israel began an ongoing military operation against Iran on February 28, 2026, and that an airstrike on Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei’s compound in Tehran killed him. Iran responded with drone and missile strikes on U.S. and allied targets across the Middle East. The article reports no evidence for a viral claim that large numbers of U.S. soldiers were refusing orders to deploy to Iran. It does not say U.S. forces have entered Iran or that a ground deployment is planned by December 31.

evidence.title: Next US move on Iran: Seize Kharg Island, secure uranium or risk ground war escalation - Fox News
evidence.text: A March 18, 2026 article says the US Defence Department sent a unit operating LUCAS attack drones to the Middle East before Operation Epic Fury against Iran began. It says US forces have deployed the drones in the current war, which began with US and Israeli airstrikes. It does not say the unit entered Iran or report plans for US ground forces to do so.

evidence.title: How realistic is a US ground operation in Iran? - The New Arab
evidence.text:
The article says analysts consider a full US ground invasion of Iran the most extreme and least plausible option because of the country’s size, mountains, deserts and history of resisting invasion. Bahraini analyst Abdullah Aljunaid notes that the 1991 liberation of Kuwait required more than 500,000 troops and says a war inside Iran would be far more complicated. Despite sustained US-Israeli strikes, Iran’s regime remains intact, the article reports.

That does not rule out a smaller US entry. The article discusses a possible operation to seize Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub, or a targeted operation to secure or disable nuclear material that airstrikes may not reach. Retired Gen. Jack Keane says the US could take Kharg but has so far chosen not to. Former Iraq adviser Rick Clay says he does not expect troops on Iran’s mainland; if troops are used, he expects only an island operation. The article reports no decision to send ground forces and no ground entry, and gives no forecast specifically for December 31.

evidence.title: In Choosing ‘Epic Fury,’ Trump Names a War and Defines His Presidency - The New York Times
evidence.text: The article says the United States and Israel launched attacks on Iran at the end of February, after which Tehran closed the Strait of Hormuz. It describes the US–Iran war as entering its third week despite President Donald Trump’s March 10 statement that it was “very complete, pretty much.” It mentions US missiles and naval assets being deployed against Iran, but does not report US forces entering Iranian territory or predict that they will do so by December 31.

evidence.title: 'Worse than Afghanistan' task facing US troops as Trump invades Iran - Daily Mail
evidence.text: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni told the Italian Senate that Italy “does not take part and does not intend to take part” in the U.S.-Israeli strikes against Iran. The article describes an ongoing war involving the United States, Israel, and Iran, but does not report U.S. forces entering Iran or give a date for any such move. Despite the headline’s reference to an invasion, the body provides no evidence of a U.S. ground entry.

evidence.title: U.S. military bombs Iran's main oil export hub, as Mideast war toll mounts - npr.org
evidence.text: On March 13, 2026, the article says approximately 5,000 U.S. sailors and Marines were deploying to the Middle East to support the war in Iran. It describes a deployment to the region, not U.S. forces entering Iran. It also reports that the Trump administration downplayed concerns about Iran blocking the Strait of Hormuz as gas and oil prices rose.

evidence.title: Trump Wants to Secure Hormuz. Here’s What It Would Take. - WSJ
evidence.text: The article says the conflict began Feb. 28, when U.S. forces joined Israel in targeting senior leaders and military sites in Iran. It reports that 12 active U.S. service members have been killed since then, including six aboard a refueling plane that crashed in Iraq during Iran-war operations; a 13th died of a medical issue. The article establishes U.S. military action against targets in Iran but does not say U.S. personnel have entered Iran.

evidence.title: Marine Expeditionary Unit Deploying To The Middle East: Report (Updated) - TWZ
evidence.text: The article says President Donald Trump’s administration is considering “boots on the ground” during the war with Iran. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the US should reserve options both with and without ground troops. It describes a full-scale invasion as highly unlikely, but discusses possible missions inside Iran: securing enriched uranium, which it calls unlikely in the near term; taking Kharg Island with special operators and conventional forces, which it calls achievable but troop-intensive; and sending small teams to work with Iranian opposition groups, which it calls high-risk. These are potential operations, not reported entries by US forces into Iran. The article gives no timetable for a ground operation or December 31 forecast.

evidence.title: Could the US deploy troops to Iran, and how could that play out? - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: The article says the United States has threatened ground operations inside Iran, and President Donald Trump has said he does not want to rule out any options. It describes limited special-operations raids as the most viable form of ground deployment. Larger incursions or a full-scale invasion are described as unlikely without a major shift in regional and U.S. domestic support because of severe logistical, political and strategic risks. The article does not report that U.S. forces have entered Iran or give a deployment date.

evidence.title: What You Need to Know About Hezbollah: The Anti-Israel Terror Group With More Firepower Than Most NATO Militaries - American Jewish Committee (AJC)
evidence.text: Since President Trump chose to strike Iran, U.S. military operations have primarily been an air campaign. Sen. Josh Hawley said Thursday that he did not foresee Trump asking Congress for ground troops to invade Iran and had “absolutely no indication” he would do so; Hawley cited two occasions earlier that week when Trump dismissed the need for ground troops. Hawley said he might reconsider his opposition to a War Powers resolution restricting force in Iran if Trump sought to send ground troops. Some military analysts questioned whether U.S. goals could be achieved without them. The article reports no U.S. forces entering Iran and gives no December 31 forecast.

evidence.title: Iran war rages as Pentagon says about 140 U.S. service members wounded overall - CBS News
evidence.text: In a March 11, 2026 video, Adm. Brad Cooper, head of U.S. Central Command, said American forces had hit more than 5,500 targets inside Iran during Operation Epic Fury, which began February 28. He said about 50,000 U.S. service members were deployed in and around the Middle East. The article describes strikes on Iranian targets but does not report U.S. forces entering Iran or plans to do so.

evidence.title: Epic Fury: How the UK and its allies have been involved in the Middle East conflict so far - forcesnews.com
evidence.text: In a Sunday interview about Operation Epic Fury, Fox News’ Maria Bartiromo asked White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt about a possible military draft and President Trump’s plans for “troops on the ground.” Leavitt said it was “not part of the current plan right now,” but that the president was keeping his options open while assessing the operation. The article says it was unclear whether she meant ground combat troops in Iran or a draft. Operation Epic Fury began February 28, and the U.S. military had struck more than 5,000 Iranian targets as of Tuesday. The article does not report a decision to send U.S. ground forces into Iran.

evidence.title: In Iran fight, US scrambles to adapt in its 1st major drone war - ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
evidence.source: ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
evidence.text: Operation Epic Fury is described as ongoing US-Israeli strikes across Iran, while the UK, other NATO countries and allies are increasing their presence in the Gulf and Mediterranean. The article says the UK agreed to let US forces use British bases for defensive airstrikes on Iranian missile sites, and France offered US forces use of Istres Air Base for operational support. It does not report US ground forces entering Iran or announce plans for them to do so by December 31.

evidence.title: Democratic senator: ‘We seem to be’ on path toward deploying US troops on the ground in Iran - The Hill
evidence.text: U.S. Central Command said U.S. forces destroyed multiple Iranian naval vessels on March 10, including at least 16 minelayers near the Strait of Hormuz, and posted aerial videos of the strikes. President Trump had earlier put the tally at 10. U.S. officials said Iran might be preparing to lay mines in the strait. The article also says U.S.-Israeli strikes on Iran began February 28, but it does not report U.S. forces entering Iran or a decision to deploy ground troops there.

evidence.title: What We Know About the Thirteen U.S. Service Members Killed in the Iran War - Time Magazine
evidence.text: On Tuesday, March 10, U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the U.S. would send its largest number of fighter jets and bombers to attack Iran since the war began 10 days earlier, calling it the “most intense day of strikes inside Iran.” He said the strikes targeted Iran’s missiles and defense industrial base. The article describes airstrikes inside Iran but does not report U.S. ground forces entering the country or announce plans for them to do so by December 31.

evidence.title: The Kurdish Attack on Iran That Never Happened - bylinesupplement.com
evidence.text: U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began on February 28, 2026, and reported strikes have targeted facilities in northwest Iran. The article does not report U.S. forces entering Iran. It says the Trump Administration may be considering material support for Iranian Kurdish groups, but has not confirmed any such support. The outcome of a possible partnership would depend partly on the groups’ capabilities and support within Iran, and on whether assistance included training, continued airstrikes, no-fly zones, or direct military support involving ground operations. One source estimates that Kurdish factions based in Iraq have about 2,500 fighters; another says they may have sent hundreds into Iran in recent weeks. Those reports concern Kurdish fighters, not U.S. forces.

market.question: US forces enter Iran by December 31?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if active US military personnel physically enter Iran at any point by the listed date (ET). Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

Military special operation forces will qualify, however intelligence operatives will not count.

US military personnel must physically enter the terrestrial territory of Iran to qualify. Entering Iran's maritime or aerial territory will not count.

Military contractors, military advisors, or high-ranking US service members entering Iran for diplomatic purposes (and their accompanying entourage) will not qualify.

The resolution source will be a consensus of credible reporting.

evidence.title: How seriously wounded US airman climbed mountain, hid in crevice and dodged Iranian bounty hunters for 36 hours - New York Post
evidence.text: The article reports that U.S. special operations forces extracted an F-15E crew member from mountainous terrain in southwestern Iran after Iranian fire struck the aircraft on a Friday. The colonel was injured during ejection and evaded capture for more than 36 hours with only a pistol. The reported rescue involved hundreds of commandos, dozens of aircraft, CIA intelligence support, and airstrikes against approaching Iranian forces. President Trump said the earlier rescue of the pilot involved U.S. forces operating over Iranian territory for seven hours in daylight. The article announces an April 6 press conference but does not state a year for these events.

evidence.title: Iran’s Revolutionary Guard would fiercely resist a US ground invasion. History proves it - The Conversation
evidence.text: The article reports that US forces operated deep inside Iran to rescue the weapons systems officer of an F-15E shot down over southwestern Iran on a Friday. Citing the New York Times, it says Navy SEAL Team 6 rescued him Saturday night in an operation involving hundreds of special-operations troops and other military personnel in enemy territory. US commandos fired to keep Iranian forces away from the rescue site but did not engage them in a firefight. The article does not give a calendar date for the rescue.

evidence.title: Downed US pilot hid in mountain crevice, hiked 7,000 feet to evade Iranians for 48 hours - Rediff
evidence.text: The article reports claims that U.S. personnel were on the ground in Iran during a mission to recover the second crew member of a downed F-15. On Sunday, Iran’s IRGC said two U.S. C-130 aircraft and two Black Hawk helicopters were destroyed in Isfahan. Iran’s Defa Press Agency separately claimed that Iranian units continued fighting on the ground with surviving or supporting U.S. personnel after initial clashes. Fox News reported several U.S. service members were injured. The article says the U.S. had issued no official statement on the Iranian claims, so the reported ground fighting remains unconfirmed.

evidence.title: US special forces enter Iran to rescue downed airman - The Telegraph - armenpress.am
evidence.text: The article reports that, in an update dated 5 April 2026, U.S. Special Operations forces rescued a U.S. Air Force weapons officer whose F-15E had been shot down over Iran. It says the night mission involved U.S. military forces operating deep inside Iran. This is a reported instance of U.S. forces entering Iran before December 31, 2026.

evidence.title: Three Generals Ousted as Pentagon Shakeup Hits War Command - Military.com
evidence.text: The article says a U.S. F-15E Strike Eagle was shot down over Iran’s Khuzestan province. Of its two crew members, one was rescued by U.S. Combat Search and Rescue (CSAR), while the other remained missing inside Iran. It says U.S. search-and-rescue operations were ongoing under hostile conditions, with Iranian forces and local actors mobilized to find the missing pilot. The response included rescue helicopters and close-air-support aircraft, and the article describes the mission as taking place over Iran. It does not explicitly say U.S. personnel entered Iran on the ground or give a date establishing whether this occurred by December 31.

evidence.title: Scenarios and risks: Will the US invade Iran? - Anadolu Ajansı
evidence.text: US troops and warships are moving into the Middle East, but the article reports no decision to send US forces into Iran. The USS Tripoli has arrived with an amphibious group of more than 3,000 soldiers and sailors, including marines; the USS Boxer is en route with another marine unit, and the 82nd Airborne Division has been committed. Jennifer Parker estimated that these units, together with a further 10,000 troops under discussion, would add about 17,000 personnel to the region. She said the deployments give the US options to escalate through coastal raids, brief seizures of territory or Iranian islands, or seizures of Iranian ships at sea—not a large-scale invasion. US media has also reported options involving an Iranian uranium stockpile or troops opening the Strait of Hormuz. Trump said on April 1 that the US would hit Iran hard over the next two to three weeks, while also saying the operation was near completion. Analysts described island assaults as possible but high-risk.

evidence.title: Iran War: What a Marine Expeditionary Unit is – and other US military terms - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: As of April 2, 2026, the Pentagon had sent ships carrying thousands of Marines and elements of the 82nd Airborne Division to the Middle East for operations against Iran, but had not placed American service members on Iranian territory. Hundreds of 82nd soldiers had deployed to undisclosed locations in the region. President Trump did not say whether those troops might be assigned ground combat operations inside Iran; he said strikes would continue for the next two to three weeks. The article therefore reports no US entry into Iran to date and leaves any entry by December 31 unresolved.

evidence.title: WATCH: Hegseth won't say if U.S. will send ground troops into Iran - PBS
evidence.text: US Central Command confirmed that 2,200 Marines from the 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit arrived in Middle Eastern waters after being ordered on March 13 to leave their usual station in Sasebo, Japan. A second unit, the 11th MEU, was inbound with roughly 2,500 Marines after leaving San Diego on March 18. The Pentagon also ordered about 2,000 soldiers from the 82nd Airborne Division to begin moving to the Middle East, adding to 50,000 US troops already in the region. The article says Marine units can conduct sea-to-land assaults and that their amphibious ships are designed to put troops ashore. It reports no US ground forces entering Iran.

evidence.title: Soldiers supporting Iran war approved for combat patches as casualty numbers rise - stripes.com
evidence.text: As of April 1, 2026, the article says the U.S. was preparing for *potential* ground operations in Iran, not that U.S. forces had entered the country. Thousands of Marines and paratroopers were arriving in the region, and the Pentagon was reportedly considering sending 10,000 more ground troops there. A March 26 memo from Army Chief of Staff Gen. Randy A. George authorized combat patches for soldiers supporting military operations while deployed to the Middle East and Africa, beginning Feb. 28; the authorization does not establish deployment inside Iran. U.S. strikes had hit more than 11,000 targets inside Iran. The number of U.S. service members wounded had risen from 303 the previous Friday to 348 as of Tuesday. Trump said Tuesday that he expected the operation against Iran to end in ‘maybe two weeks, maybe three.’

evidence.title: Iran: US ground troops would be ‘set on fire’ - The Hill
evidence.text: The article says thousands of U.S. special operations personnel—including Navy SEALs, Army Rangers and Marines—are in the region, but does not say they have entered Iran or received orders to do so. It describes a prolonged ground campaign as a possible worst-case scenario, while also reporting signs of de-escalation: Trump suggested allies should handle the Strait of Hormuz, and the White House said reopening it is not a core objective. At the same time, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said U.S. strikes would intensify if no deal with Iran is reached soon. The article reports no decision or timetable for U.S. forces to enter Iran by December 31.

evidence.title: Five Scenarios for a U.S. Ground War on Iran - foreignpolicy.com
evidence.text: According to the article, reports say the Pentagon is poised to move thousands of ground troops into the Middle East and is preparing for “weeks” of possible ground operations after about a month of war with Iran. The article says the US is signaling that it may send ground troops into Iran, but it does not report that they have entered. It puts the US force in the Middle East at about 50,000 troops, roughly 10,000 above the usual level, and says possible missions being discussed include occupying Iranian territory, removing stockpiled uranium, and seizing key islands. It gives no confirmed deployment into Iran or date for one.

evidence.title: Limited missions, big risks: What a US ground fight in Iran could become - Military Times
evidence.text: Thousands of U.S. troops are deploying to the Middle East while the Pentagon weighs possible ground operations in Iran; the article does not report that U.S. forces have entered Iran or that an operation has been ordered. The USS Tripoli and its 31st Marine Expeditionary Unit arrived in regional waters last Friday, and elements of the 82nd Airborne Division are deploying, according to the Pentagon. Analysts describe possible missions including seizing Iranian islands or coastal positions to help reopen the Strait of Hormuz and raiding a nuclear site at Isfahan to retrieve enriched uranium. President Donald Trump threatened Kharg Island, Iran’s primary oil export hub, in a Monday post. Analysts warn that even limited missions could face Iranian fire and expand into a longer conflict. The article gives no timetable for a ground operation.

evidence.title: US Ground Forces Arrive in Middle East as Iran Conflict Escalates - Military.com
evidence.text: The article says the U.S. is building up forces in the Middle East during the second month of Operation Epic Fury against Iran. President Donald Trump has not ruled out sending ground troops to secure the mission’s objectives. Thousands of soldiers are arriving at staging grounds, and thousands more have been told to prepare for deployment. The article does not report that U.S. forces have entered Iran or that a ground deployment there has been ordered.

evidence.title: US-Iran: 'Boots on the ground is a very different matter' - CGTN
evidence.text: Washington says it has been preparing a series of ground incursions into Iran to seize strategic islands on its southern shores. The article says the islands are important for oil and gas processing and control of the Strait of Hormuz. It reports no US ground entry. It also says the US and Israel have considered using Iraq-based Kurdish armed groups to open a ground front in Iran, but Israel’s Channel 12 reported that the Trump administration considered that plan unfeasible for now. The forces the article reports entering Iran were Iraqi PMF fighters accompanying a convoy, not US forces.

evidence.title: ‘Loyalty campaign’: Iraqi armed groups in Iran as US talks of ground war - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: A Wall Street Journal report cited in the article says the Pentagon is considering sending another 10,000 soldiers to the Middle East, in addition to 7,000 ground troops already heading to the region. Retired air vice-marshal Sean Bell said the initial 5,000–7,000 Marines are equipped for amphibious landings, while the additional troops could reinforce an established position. He cautioned that the force is small compared with the 300,000 troops used in the US invasion of Iraq and Iran’s more than one million personnel under arms. Bell described a major operation along Iran’s shore to secure the Strait of Hormuz as highly unlikely. He considered a move against Iran’s Kharg Island more plausible, but said troops there would be vulnerable. He also suggested the deployments may be intended as negotiating leverage rather than a plan for a ground offensive. The article reports no US forces entering Iran and gives no date for such an operation.

evidence.title: How could US forcibly reopen strait of Hormuz and what are the risks? - The Guardian
evidence.text: The article says half of a 5,000-person US Marine contingent trained for amphibious landings arrived in the Middle East on Saturday, with about 2,000 paratroopers also due to arrive. It does not report US forces entering Iran. It says Trump is considering options including seizing an Iranian island such as Kharg or sending special operations forces onto the mainland to seize enriched uranium. Trump said taking Kharg was one option, but made no commitment. Experts said the deployed force would be spread thin, and Iran has threatened severe attacks on US troops on its soil. One expert said the deployment might instead be a show of force for negotiations.

evidence.title: Trump wants to invade Iran to seize oil, calls US objectors ‘stupid people’ - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: As the US-Israel war on Iran entered its fifth week, the Trump administration deployed US Marines to the Middle East and was planning to send thousands of soldiers from the Army’s 82nd Airborne to the region. US Central Command said about 3,500 additional personnel arrived in the Middle East on Saturday aboard the USS Tripoli. Trump said he wanted to take Iran’s oil by seizing Kharg Island, but said, “Maybe we take Kharg Island, maybe we don’t.” US officials said the administration had discussed a possible seizure over the past month. Iran’s parliament speaker threatened US troops if they invaded. The article reports deployments to the Middle East and discussion of entering Iran, not that US forces had entered Iran.

evidence.title: Army approves combat patches for soldiers in Iran war zone - Task & Purpose
evidence.text: The article reports that at least 2,500 Marines and sailors aboard the USS Tripoli have entered the Middle East region with aviation assets, equipment and rapid-response ground units. Elements of the 82nd Airborne Division have also deployed to the region. These ground-capable forces could support limited operations, and the article says planning for missions inside Iran is reportedly underway, but remains contingent and has not been publicly approved. Entering the region is not the same as entering Iran: the article says there has been no official announcement that U.S. ground troops have entered Iranian territory or that a ground invasion has been ordered.

evidence.title: Thousands of US Army paratroopers arrive in Middle East as buildup intensifies - The Times of Israel
evidence.text: Hundreds of US special operations troops, including Army Rangers and Navy SEALs, have deployed to the Middle East as President Donald Trump weighs a ground mission inside Iran. More than 50,000 US troops are now in the region, roughly 10,000 above normal levels; earlier deployments included about 2,500 Marines, 2,500 sailors and 2,000 troops from the 82nd Airborne Division. The special operations troops have not been assigned specific missions. Options under discussion include operations along the Strait of Hormuz, seizing Kharg Island and entering Iran to extract roughly 400 kilograms of enriched uranium. Planners say a uranium-extraction mission could take days or weeks. Trump has not made a final decision, and officials say diplomacy remains an option. The article reports preparations and possible operations, not that US forces have entered Iran.

evidence.title: The number of conscientious objectors is on the rise: Here is how U.S. soldiers can apply to avoid being deplo - Diario AS
evidence.text: The article says the US has expanded its forces by deploying troops and special operations teams, including members of the 82nd Airborne Division. Iran warned of severe consequences if American troops crossed its borders. Trump suggested the US could take control of Iran’s oil “very easily,” but the article says such an operation would require ground troops and an extended military campaign. market.question: Will there be between 6 and 9 US strikes on Somalia in March 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve according to the number of independent incidents of US-initiated drone, missile, or air strikes on the soil of Somalia that occur between March 1 and March 31, 2026, and are announced by the United States Africa Command (AFRICOM) by April 4, 2026, 12:00 PM ET.

For the purposes of this market, a qualifying "strike" is defined as the use of aerial bombs, drones, or missiles (including FPV and ATGM strikes as well as cruise or ballistic missiles) launched by any United States operatives, including military forces, intelligence agencies, or other U.S. government operatives, that physically impact ground territory within the listed country.

A strike on any area within the terrestrial territory (including rivers, lakes, ports, but excluding territorial sea) of the listed country counts.

Missiles or drones that are intercepted and surface-to-air missile strikes will not count, regardless of whether they land in the listed country’s territory or cause damage.

Actions such as artillery fire, small arms fire, ground incursions, naval shelling, or cyberattacks will not qualify.

An incident of a US-initiated drone, missile, or air strike refers to any strike or series of strikes described by AFRICOM as a contiguous incident in a single region. Each AFRICOM press release describing a strike or series of strikes will count as one incident, unless AFRICOM explicitly distinguishes incidents as separate strike events. For example, the strikes on January 25-26, 2026 (https://www.africom.mil/pressrelease/36183/us-forces-conduct-strikes-targeting-al-shabaab) and January 12, 2026 (https://www.africom.mil/pressrelease/36174/us-forces-conduct-strikes-targeting-al-shabaab) would have counted as single incidents, even though they included multiple individual strikes.

The date of a qualifying strike incident will be determined by the date provided by AFRICOM. Any strike incident announced by AFRICOM to have occurred at least partially in the listed period will count (e.g. a strike incident announced to have occurred from February 28-March 1, 2026, would count). If the date of an announced strike is not released by AFRICOM, a consensus of credible reporting may be used to determine the timing of a strike incident. In this case, a strike will be considered to have occurred in the specified period if it is determined that it occurred in that period, in Eastern Time (timeframes partially, but not fully, in this period will count). Any strike incident announced by AFRICOM after April 4, 2026, 12:00 PM ET will not count, regardless of the timing of the strike.

This market will remain open until April 4, 2026, 12:00 PM ET. If the date/time of a qualifying strike cannot be confirmed by that time, it will not count, regardless of whether a strike was later confirmed to have taken place.

The primary resolution source for this market will be the United States Africa Command (AFRICOM) (https://www.africom.mil/media-gallery/press-releases); however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used to determine the timing of an announced strike incident.

evidence.text: AFRICOM said it carried out an airstrike on a Tuesday targeting ISIS fighters about 70 kilometers southeast of Bosaso, in northeastern Somalia’s Togga Baallade and Al-Miskaad mountain areas. It said the strike was coordinated with the Somali federal government and security forces. The article reports one strike but gives no calendar date or March 2026 strike total, so it does not establish whether there will be 6–9 U.S. strikes that month.

evidence.title: BOK senior official hints at rate hike pivot amid inflation fears - The Korea Herald
evidence.text: Bank of Korea Senior Deputy Gov. Ryoo Sang-dai said it was time to consider pausing rate cuts and potentially raising rates. Asked whether the Monetary Policy Board’s May 28 meeting could signal a hike, he said “the possibility remains open,” but that officials would monitor conditions through the end of May before deciding because uncertainty remained high. The base rate has been held at 2.50 percent for seven consecutive meetings. Ryoo cited resilient growth and inflation that he said was increasingly likely to exceed March’s 2.2 percent. Some economists expect hikes to begin in the third quarter, possibly two totaling 0.5 percentage points this year; others expect a more gradual path into next year. The article reports no decision to raise the rate.

evidence.title: BOK senior deputy gov. says time to consider rate hike on solid growth - The Korea Times
evidence.text: Bank of Korea senior deputy governor and monetary policy board member Ryoo Sangdai said it was time to consider ending rate cuts and thinking about increases. Asked whether the BOK might signal possible rate hikes this year at its May 28 meeting, he said “the possibility is open,” but policymakers would assess incoming data before deciding. The BOK has held its benchmark rate unchanged since July last year. Ryoo cited stronger-than-expected growth, including a 1.7% first-quarter rebound and robust semiconductor shipments, alongside rising inflation pressure. The bank’s February forecasts for this year were 2% growth and 2.2% inflation; Ryoo said growth now appeared unlikely to fall much below that forecast, while inflation was likely to exceed it. The article does not report a decision to raise rates after the May meeting.

evidence.title: F&R Union Minister virtually joins 29th ASEAN+3 Finance Ministers’ and Central Bank Governors’ Meeting (AFMGM+3) - Global New Light Of Myanmar
evidence.text: On May 4, Bank of Korea monetary policy board member and senior deputy governor Ryoo Sang-dai said the bank’s guidance would become more hawkish at its May 28 meeting. He said growth was unlikely to be much below 2.0% and inflation would be above 2.2%, making it time to stop cutting rates and consider hikes. He also said inflation pressure remained high despite government price-control measures. The bank had held rates steady the previous month while assessing Middle East-related uncertainty. His remarks signal a shift toward hikes, but do not say the bank will raise its base rate at or after the May meeting.

evidence.title: US Fed official says rate hikes may be needed if inflation surges - Digital Journal
evidence.text: Local analysts expect the Bank of Korea to hold its benchmark rate at 2.5% at its May 28 meeting, its first under Gov. Shin Hyun-song, after the U.S. Federal Reserve held its rate at 3.50%–3.75%. They see possible BOK increases after May: a Hyundai Research Institute economist expects gradual hikes in the second half of the year; a Korea Investment & Securities analyst forecasts 0.25-percentage-point hikes in August and November, taking the rate to 3%; and a Citibank economist sees 0.25-point hikes in July and October. They cite stronger-than-expected first-quarter GDP growth of 1.7% versus the BOK’s 0.9% forecast, rising oil prices, inflation and import-price pressure from a weaker won. These are forecasts, not announced BOK decisions.

evidence.title: Statement on Monetary Policy – May 2026 2. Economic Conditions - rba.gov.au
evidence.text: Markets do not expect the Bank of Korea to raise its base rate at the Monetary Policy Board meeting on May 28, but analysts expect a strong hawkish message that could point to a later hike. Senior Deputy Governor Ryoo Sang-dai said it was time to “stop cutting rates and consider raising them.” April inflation reached 2.6% year on year, its highest since July 2024, driven in part by a 21.9% rise in petroleum prices; 12-month public inflation expectations rose to 2.9%. A BOK committee expects inflation to rise further in May. Hana Securities strategist Park Jun-oo said the May meeting’s dot plot could clarify timing: around 11 projections favoring a hike would suggest a fourth-quarter increase, around 14 a pre-emptive third-quarter increase, and seven or fewer a prolonged hold.

evidence.title: Bank of Korea's new chief says monetary policy has to be cautious and flexible - NST Online
evidence.text: Earlier this month, the Bank of Korea kept its policy interest rate steady, warned that the path ahead was highly uncertain, and flagged upward revisions to its inflation forecasts and a downgrade to growth projections. New governor Shin Hyun-song said higher oil prices linked to the Iran war were increasing inflation pressure while weighing on growth, calling for cautious and flexible monetary policy. He will chair his first policy meeting on May 28. The article does not say whether the base rate will rise after that meeting.

evidence.text: Bank of Korea governor nominee Shin Hyun Song said the 2.5% benchmark rate is around the midpoint of South Korea’s estimated neutral-rate range, according to studies inside and outside the bank. In a written response to lawmaker Chun Haram, he cautioned that those estimates are uncertain and should be weighed against broader financial conditions and policy effects. The BoK kept rates unchanged last Friday for a seventh straight meeting, saying it was premature to adjust policy amid uncertainty over the war in Iran. It said a temporary shock would not prompt a rate change, but a persistent one could warrant a response. The article does not report a decision for the May meeting or a commitment to raise rates afterward.

market.question: UK Cabinet Minister resigns by June 30, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if any sitting Cabinet Minister of the United Kingdom as of February 4, 2026 ET, resigns from their position in the cabinet by June 30, 2026 ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No."

Only an actual resignation will qualify toward a "Yes" resolution. If the Prime Minister accepts a letter of resignation from a cabinet minister, or a cabinet minister otherwise formally resigns, this market will resolve to "Yes" immediately, even if the cabinet minister in question agrees to stay for a period of time for any reason (e.g., until a replacement is ready, etc.). If a minister submits a letter of resignation and it is refused, or they otherwise withdraw that letter, it will not qualify toward this market's resolution.

If a minister submits a letter of resignation and is subsequently fired from their position, it will still qualify toward a "Yes" resolution.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the government of the United Kingdom; however, a consensus of credible reporting will also be used.

evidence.text: Prime Minister Keir Starmer faced calls to resign after a report that Peter Mandelson was initially denied security clearance to become UK ambassador to the United States, but the Foreign Office overruled the vetting process. The government said Starmer learned of that decision only “earlier this week”; he had previously told Parliament that the appointment followed the necessary vetting rules. Opposition lawmakers said he should resign if he misled Parliament. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called him “definitely in resigning territory,” while Liberal Democrat leader Ed Davey said he “must go” if he misled Parliament and lied to the public. Starmer appointed Mandelson in late 2024 and fired him in September 2025 over revelations about his links to Jeffrey Epstein. The article reports calls for Starmer’s resignation, not that he or another Cabinet minister has resigned.

evidence.title: Starmer faces calls to resign as UK government admits ambassador to US failed vetting process - CityNews Halifax
evidence.text: Downing Street faced calls for Prime Minister Keir Starmer to resign over Peter Mandelson’s appointment as UK ambassador to the US. UK Security Vetting denied Mandelson clearance on 28 January 2025, but Foreign Office officials overrode that recommendation before he took up the post in February. No 10 said neither Starmer nor any government minister knew of the override until earlier in the week. Sir Olly Robbins, the Foreign Office’s top civil servant, was forced to resign after Starmer and Foreign Secretary Yvette Cooper lost confidence in him. The article reports demands for Starmer’s resignation, not his resignation; it does not report a Cabinet minister resigning over this vetting disclosure.

evidence.title: Keir Starmer tries to move on from his Morgan McSweeney era - politico.eu
evidence.text: Dozens of Keir Starmer’s aides and ministers are due to have private messages with former U.K. ambassador Peter Mandelson published as early as mid-April, with potentially embarrassing consequences for Starmer’s allies across government. The release follows controversy over Mandelson’s appointment: Morgan McSweeney resigned as No. 10 chief of staff on Feb. 8 after pushing Starmer to appoint him. McSweeney’s phone was stolen last October, so many of his messages are expected to be missing from the release. The article does not say that any Cabinet minister plans to resign, but identifies the messages as a potential source of pressure before June 30, 2026.

market.question: UK Cabinet Minister resigns by June 30, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if any sitting Cabinet Minister of the United Kingdom as of February 4, 2026 ET, resigns from their position in the cabinet by June 30, 2026 ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No."

Only an actual resignation will qualify toward a "Yes" resolution. If the Prime Minister accepts a letter of resignation from a cabinet minister, or a cabinet minister otherwise formally resigns, this market will resolve to "Yes" immediately, even if the cabinet minister in question agrees to stay for a period of time for any reason (e.g., until a replacement is ready, etc.). If a minister submits a letter of resignation and it is refused, or they otherwise withdraw that letter, it will not qualify toward this market's resolution.

If a minister submits a letter of resignation and is subsequently fired from their position, it will still qualify toward a "Yes" resolution.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the government of the United Kingdom; however, a consensus of credible reporting will also be used.

It also reports a 20-point Tisza advantage among decided voters in several recent surveys. Tisza won around 30% of the vote and 7 of Hungary’s 21 seats in the 2024 European Parliament election. The article judges a Tisza defeat of Fidesz and formation of a new government highly likely, but these are polling figures and a forecast, not a 2026 national-list result; the reported leads differ, and it does not establish that the final margin will be 6–9 points.

evidence.title: Hungary election 2026: A rare poll breaks the trend, showing Orbán’s Fidesz with a clear lead - Daily News Hungary
evidence.text: Ahead of Hungary’s 12 April 2026 parliamentary election, a pro-government Nézőpont Institute phone survey of 1,000 adults conducted 16–17 March projected Fidesz–KDNP at 46% of the national party-list vote and Péter Magyar’s Tisza at 40% if the election were held “this Sunday.” That is a six-point lead for Fidesz–KDNP, not a 6–9-point lead for Tisza. Nézőpont attributed a slight increase in Fidesz–KDNP’s advantage to mobilisation after 15 March, reporting intended turnout of 92% among Fidesz supporters, up from 86%, versus 98% among Tisza supporters. The article also says other recent polls have placed Tisza ahead, sometimes by a wide margin, depending on methodology and the voters measured.

evidence.title: Are the Fake Tisza Polls Setting Up a ‘Stolen Election’ Narrative? - Hungarian Conservative
evidence.text: A Medián poll cited in the article puts the opposition Tisza Party 20 points ahead of incumbent Fidesz among likely voters, well above the 6–9-point margin in the question. An earlier Medián survey had Tisza ahead by 12 points. The article disputes the plausibility of the newer poll: Fidesz beat Tisza by 15.5 points in the June 2024 European Parliamentary election, so a Tisza lead of 20 would imply a 35.5-point reversal in less than two years. It says the largest previous shift between a Hungarian European Parliamentary election and a parliamentary election was 16 points, from 2019 to 2022; the margin moved 4.5 points toward the opposition between 2022 and 2024. It also reports that Medián head Endre Hann said on 30 January 2026 that a Fidesz landslide defeat was unlikely. The article offers no poll specifically placing Tisza’s national-list lead at 6–9 points; its author suggests a 2–3-point popular-vote win would be nearer the edge of possibility. It distinguishes the national-list vote from the overall seat outcome: 93 seats are allocated proportionally to parties clearing 5%, while 106 are decided in regional contests.

evidence.title: 45 days to election: Poll shows a significant Tisza lead, Orbán puts soldiers on the streets - EUobserver
evidence.text: Polling cited in the article does not establish a 6–9-point Tisza win in the national list vote for Hungary’s 12 April 2026 election. Median’s results, published on 25 February, put opposition Tisza 11 percentage points ahead of ruling Fidesz among all voting-age people and 20 points ahead among decided voters certain to vote (55%–35%). Median said that, if the election matched its survey, Tisza would receive about 800,000 more votes; its lead had widened by eight points since its previous survey. By contrast, the Fidesz-aligned Nézőpont Institute projected a *list* result of 45% for Fidesz and 40% for Tisza if an election were held that Sunday—a five-point Fidesz lead. The article says major nationally representative polls have generally shown Tisza ahead for over a year, but cautions against firm conclusions from the divergent surveys.

evidence.title: OSW update. Hungary election, no. 2 - OSW Ośrodek Studiów Wschodnich
evidence.text: OSW says Hungary’s 2026 election uses separate votes for constituency candidates and national party lists. The article describes TISZA as Fidesz’s main challenger and notes that smaller parties polling around the 5% list threshold could affect how opposition votes are distributed. market.question: Israeli forces cross the Litani River by June 30?

evidence.title: Israel bombs five bridges over Litani river in Lebanon - Punch Newspapers

Israeli army chief Eyal Zamir said the operation against Hezbollah, which resumed on March 2, “has only begun,” would be “prolonged,” and that forces were preparing to advance targeted ground operations and strikes. The article reports two Israeli soldiers killed in fighting in southern Lebanon, but does not say Israeli forces have crossed the Litani River.

evidence.title: Hezbollah attack kills one in north Israel as assault on Lebanon continues - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: Israel has sent more troops into southern Lebanon for its ground invasion. Hezbollah said it targeted Israeli soldiers and vehicles near Taybeh and Khiam. The article does not report Israeli forces crossing the Litani River or give a date for any planned crossing.

Hezbollah said on Wednesday that more than half its attacks targeted IDF soldiers in Lebanon. The article does not say Israeli forces have crossed the Litani River or give a plan to do so by June 30.

The article reports no Israeli forces crossing the Litani or stated plan to cross it by June 30.
