evidence.title: Ukraine rejects Russia's 'Victory Day' truce after Moscow violates Kyiv's ceasefire - The Kyiv Independent
evidence.text: Ukraine and Russia had proposed different ceasefire windows: Russia announced a two-day “Victory Day truce” for May 8–9, while Ukraine proposed a pause starting at midnight on May 6 to test whether fighting could stop. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia had responded to Kyiv’s proposal “only with new strikes and new attacks.” He claimed Russian forces violated Ukraine’s proposed truce 1,820 times in its first 10 hours, including attacks on civilian infrastructure and drone strikes. The article also reports a Russian strike on a kindergarten in the Sumy region that killed two people; no children were present. Zelenskyy said Moscow knew how to contact Ukraine or its partners to agree on ceasefire details, and warned Kyiv would decide how to respond based on subsequent events.

evidence.title: Russia declares a truce in Ukraine to mark Victory Day - NPR
evidence.text: Moscow had not agreed to Kyiv’s proposed ceasefire starting at midnight on May 6. Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky proposed it after Russian President Vladimir Putin announced a separate, temporary Victory Day ceasefire for May 8–9. Zelensky said Russian forces violated Kyiv’s ceasefire 1,820 times by 10 a.m. on May 6, including attacks on civilian infrastructure, attempted assaults and drone strikes. Moscow, in turn, accused Kyiv of attacks, and a Ukrainian official said Ukraine saw no reason to observe Russia’s Victory Day ceasefire. The article says earlier ceasefires in the war had not held. It does not report a mutually agreed ceasefire extending to May 31, 2026.

evidence.title: Putin, Zelenskiy proclaim rival ceasefires around Russia's Victory day commemorations - Reuters
evidence.text: Ukraine declared an open-ended ceasefire starting at midnight on 6 May, saying it would not attack unless Russia did first. Russia did not accept the proposal before it began, and Moscow officials gave no sign they had suspended operations. Kyiv said Russia launched more than 100 drones and three missiles after midnight; President Volodymyr Zelensky alleged 1,820 ceasefire violations by late Wednesday morning and said Ukraine would respond in kind to continued attacks. Russia had instead proposed a pause for 8–9 May around its Victory Day commemorations. The article says US-backed peace talks remained stalled and Russia continued operations in eastern Ukraine.

evidence.title: U.S.-Iran ceasefire holding for now, Hegseth says, as Trump looks to finalize deal - CBS News
evidence.text: Russia and Ukraine announced rival unilateral ceasefires earlier in the week, but had not agreed on their terms, duration or monitoring. Moscow called for a truce on 8–9 May for Victory Day; Kyiv announced an open-ended ceasefire from midnight Tuesday and said it would respond “symmetrically.” Zelensky accused Russia of continuing attacks after Kyiv’s announcement, including drone and missile strikes; local authorities said two people were killed when a kindergarten in the Sumy border region was hit Wednesday. Moscow had not addressed Ukraine’s ceasefire demand and threatened a major strike on central Kyiv if Ukraine violated Russia’s proposed truce. The article does not establish a mutually agreed Russia–Ukraine ceasefire.

evidence.title: Ukraine war latest: Kyiv rejects Russia's 'Victory Day' truce after Moscow violates ceasefire - The Kyiv Independent
evidence.text: On May 4, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine would implement a ceasefire starting May 6. He argued it would test whether a genuine pause in fighting could take hold, but Moscow had not agreed to it. Zelensky said Russia had violated the Ukrainian-proposed ceasefire 1,820 times by 10 a.m. on May 6, hours after it took effect. Russia separately proposed a May 8–9 ceasefire for its Victory Day celebrations; a senior Ukrainian official said Kyiv saw no reason to observe it solely for the parade. Ukrainian officials said they wanted an unconditional ceasefire rather than a brief pause. The article reports that earlier ceasefires had not held, citing Ukraine’s General Staff claim of 10,721 Russian violations during a 32-hour Easter truce in April. Moscow, in turn, accused Kyiv of attacks during the May ceasefire; Kyiv had not responded to that accusation at publication.

evidence.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of breaking Kyiv ceasefire - helsinkitimes.fi
evidence.text: Ukraine declared a ceasefire beginning at midnight on May 6, after Russian President Vladimir Putin announced a separate two-day “Victory Day ceasefire” for May 8–9. Moscow had not agreed to Kyiv’s proposed ceasefire. By 10 a.m. on May 6, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Russia had violated it 1,820 times, including through attacks on civilian infrastructure, attempted assaults and drone strikes. Moscow, in turn, accused Kyiv of attacks on Russian-occupied Crimea and Russia’s Bryansk Oblast. Kyiv had not responded to that accusation at publication, and Zelensky had not said whether Ukraine had withheld its own attacks.

evidence.title: ’Ukraine will respond in kind’, Zelenskyy says after Russia breaks Kyiv’s ceasefire - Euronews.com
evidence.text: Ukraine said Russia violated Kyiv’s unilateral ceasefire by striking Ukrainian cities with 108 combat drones and three missiles on Wednesday. Ukraine had proposed a ceasefire starting 6 May, ahead of the 8–9 May pause Moscow announced around its 9 May victory parade. Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha called the strikes evidence that Russia rejected peace and said its parade-related ceasefire call was not genuine diplomacy. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged Russian leaders to take real steps to end the war and warned that Kyiv would “act reciprocally.” The article describes Russia’s apparent rejection of Ukraine’s proposal, not a mutually agreed ceasefire, and gives no evidence of one extending to 31 May 2026.

evidence.title: Trump Administration Foreign Policy Tracker: May - Foundation for Defense of Democracies
evidence.text: Russia and Ukraine separately announced limited pauses in fighting tied to Russia’s 81st Victory Day commemorations of the Soviet Union’s defeat of Nazi Germany in 1945. Russia’s defence ministry announced a truce for May 8–9, 2026, and asked Ukraine to do the same. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine would observe a pause starting at midnight on May 5, but gave no end date, saying Ukraine would act symmetrically. He said Ukraine had received no official appeal about how the Russian-claimed cessation would work and criticized Russia for ignoring calls for a lasting end to the fighting. An Orthodox Easter ceasefire the previous month had collapsed, with each side alleging violations. The article reports proposed short-term pauses, not an agreed ceasefire lasting through May 31.

evidence.title: Russia, Ukraine announce separate ceasefire windows ahead of May 9 Victory Day commemorations - ANI News
evidence.text: Russia’s Defense Ministry said on May 4 that Putin had ordered a Victory Day ceasefire for May 8–9 and expected Ukraine to follow it. Shortly afterward, Zelensky announced a Ukrainian “silence regime” beginning at midnight on May 6, saying Ukraine had received no official communication about the format of the ceasefire discussed on Russian social media. The article therefore describes separate announcements, not a confirmed agreement. It also reports attacks by both sides within hours of the announcements, including a Russian strike in Ukraine’s Poltava Region that killed four people and wounded more than 30. Neither announced pause was said to extend to May 31, 2026.

evidence.title: Ukraine Announces Ceasefire First as Russia Strips Tanks From Victory Day Parade - The SOFX Report
evidence.text: Russia and Ukraine announced separate, apparently unilateral ceasefires: Russia said it would pause fighting on May 8–9, while Ukraine said it would observe an open-ended ceasefire from midnight on May 6 and respond “symmetrically.” The article says the sides had not agreed on the ceasefires’ terms, length or monitoring. Ukrainian official Kyrylo Budanov said Ukraine would continue observing its ceasefire if Russia reciprocated. Fighting was still reported on Tuesday ahead of the proposed pauses, including Russian attacks that killed more than 20 people across Ukraine.

evidence.title: Russia offers Ukraine May 8-9 WWII anniversary ceasefire - DW.com
evidence.text: The article reports competing unilateral ceasefire proposals, not an agreed pause in fighting. Moscow announced a Victory Day truce for May 8–9 and said Ukraine was expected to observe it, threatening a “massive missile strike on the center of Kyiv” if it did not. Rather than reject that ultimatum, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy proposed a ceasefire starting at midnight on May 5, saying Ukraine would “act reciprocally” from then. The article says this could theoretically extend the pause to four days, but reports no Russian acceptance or ceasefire taking effect.

evidence.title: Ukraine declares a ceasefire starting May 6 - Zelenskyy - RBC-Ukraine
evidence.text: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine would begin a ceasefire at 00:00 on the night of May 5–6, in response to Russia’s proposed Victory Day truce. He said Ukraine had received no official request specifying the modalities of Russia’s announced ceasefire and would act in a “mirror response.” On May 4, Russia’s Ministry of Defense said Vladimir Putin had ordered a ceasefire for May 8–9; it also threatened a massive missile strike on central Kyiv if Ukraine did not agree. The article reports competing ceasefire announcements, not a confirmed, mutually implemented ceasefire.

evidence.title: Ukraine and Russia Declare Separate Temporary Ceasefires - The Moscow Times
evidence.text: Putin declared a unilateral two-day ceasefire for May 8–9, and Russia’s Defense Ministry said it expected Ukraine to follow suit. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had received no official Russian appeal and instead announced a ceasefire starting at midnight on May 5–6, saying Ukraine would act “in a mirror fashion.” The article says it was unclear whether Ukraine’s offer would extend through May 8–9. Russia threatened a massive missile attack on central Kyiv if Ukraine declined and attacked Moscow’s May 9 commemorations. The article reports separate proposals, not an agreed or implemented ceasefire; it does not specify the year of those May dates.

evidence.title: Putin and Zelensky both unilaterally declare conflicting 2-day truces - France 24
evidence.text: Russia’s defence ministry said that, on President Vladimir Putin’s decision, it had declared a unilateral ceasefire for May 8–9, 2026, and hoped Ukraine would follow suit. It threatened a massive missile strike on central Kyiv if Ukraine disrupted Russia’s Victory Day celebrations. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy separately announced a ceasefire starting at midnight on May 5–6, saying Ukraine would act reciprocally; he said Russia’s proposal had not been officially communicated to Kyiv. The article reports competing unilateral declarations, not an agreed ceasefire, and says deadly attacks were continuing.

evidence.title: Russian attacks kill more than 20 ahead of rival ceasefires proposed by Kyiv and Moscow - bbc.com
evidence.text: Putin announced a unilateral ceasefire around Russia’s Friday commemoration of the Soviet Union’s victory over Nazi Germany. Zelenskyy accused Moscow of seeking a truce for its military parade while continuing daily missile and drone strikes. The article reports 23 people killed in attacks on Ukraine, including at least 12 in Zaporizhzhia and five in Kramatorsk. It describes rival ceasefire proposals, not an agreed or sustained Russia–Ukraine ceasefire.

President Vladimir Putin ordered Russian forces to cease hostilities in all directions; the Kremlin called it a “humanitarian” pause and said it assumed Ukraine would follow Russia’s example. President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had proposed an Easter ceasefire and would reciprocate. The Kremlin said the pause had not been discussed with Ukraine or the United States beforehand. The article reports an announced, short truce—not that it had taken effect or held. It also says Russia has rejected a longer-term unconditional ceasefire, previous truces drew accusations of hundreds of violations, and US-brokered peace talks have been effectively frozen since late February amid unresolved territorial disputes.

evidence.title: Fact-checking Trump and Hegseth's claims of U.S. 'victory' in the Iran war - PBS
evidence.text: President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine was ready to mirror ceasefire steps after Russian President Vladimir Putin announced a temporary Easter truce. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had proposed a ceasefire for the Easter holidays and urged Russia not to resume strikes afterward. Putin ordered Russian forces to halt hostilities for 32 hours, from 4 p.m. Saturday through Sunday. The article says previous ceasefire attempts had little impact, with both sides alleging violations. It also says U.S.-led talks had made no progress on key issues, Russian and Ukrainian forces remained in combat, and Moscow continued to insist on longstanding demands that have blocked an agreement.

evidence.title: Russia and Ukraine Agree to Easter Ceasefire - themoscowtimes.com
evidence.text: Russian President Vladimir Putin announced a 32-hour ceasefire for Orthodox Easter, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine would honour it. The Kremlin said the pause would run from 4 p.m. Moscow time on Saturday until midnight Sunday; Russia’s defence minister instructed forces to halt operations, while remaining ready to respond to violations. Zelenskyy said Ukraine had proposed an Easter pause and would reciprocate. The article does not give calendar dates for the truce. It reports that broader peace talks remain stalled and that a similar short pause last year drew accusations of violations from both sides.

evidence.title: Trump Renews Threat of Attacks on Iran’s Bridges and Power Plants - The New York Times
evidence.text: Ukraine and Russia appeared close to a 32-hour, theatre-wide ceasefire beginning Saturday afternoon for Orthodox Easter. It could be their first official ceasefire across the war theatre since Russia’s February 2022 full-scale invasion. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine had repeatedly offered an Easter pause and was ready to reciprocate; Russian President Vladimir Putin acquiesced, and the Kremlin said it had ordered hostilities to stop “in all directions.” The Kremlin also said its troops should be ready to respond to provocations or attacks. The pause had not yet begun, and the article does not establish whether it would hold or extend beyond Easter. Earlier truces were described as unofficial, localized, or limited in scope.

evidence.title: Iran delegates arrive in Islamabad for talks with U.S., as ceasefire terms remain in dispute - NPR
evidence.text: Putin announced a 32-hour ceasefire for Orthodox Easter, from the following afternoon through midnight Sunday. Zelensky said Ukraine would observe it, and Ukrainian officials urged Russia not to resume strikes afterward and to restart peace talks. The Kremlin called the Easter truce a temporary humanitarian measure and said it wanted a permanent peace deal, not a ceasefire; Ukraine described that position as a delaying tactic. Similar truces have seen violations. Russia says it would end hostilities if Ukraine ceded the roughly 6,000 square kilometres of Donbas it has not conquered, a condition Zelensky rejects. Several rounds of US-led talks have failed to narrow the differences, and the Kremlin said an envoy’s US visit did not signal their resumption.

evidence.title: Russia’s Putin announces Orthodox Easter ceasefire, Ukraine’s Zelensky agrees - The Straits Times
evidence.text: Putin ordered Russian troops to cease fire “in all directions” from 16:00 local time (13:00 GMT) on Saturday, 11 April, through Orthodox Easter Sunday. Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to take “symmetrical steps” and urged Russia not to resume strikes afterward. Putin’s spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, ruled out an extension, saying the ceasefire was only temporary and “exclusively humanitarian.” The article does not establish that the truce took effect or held. Kyiv wants a full, stable ceasefire before peace negotiations, while Moscow insists on agreeing a peace deal first; US-mediated talks were on hold. The article also reports Ukrainian allegations of hundreds of violations during a previous Russian-declared ceasefire.

evidence.title: Who can claim victory if Iran ceasefire holds? An early winner is China - The Guardian
evidence.text: Putin announced a 32-hour ceasefire for Orthodox Easter, ordering Russian forces to stop hostilities from 4pm Saturday through Sunday. The Kremlin said it expected Ukraine to follow suit, but there was no immediate reaction from Kyiv. Earlier that week, Zelenskyy had proposed a holiday pause in attacks on each side’s energy infrastructure through US mediators. A 30-hour ceasefire declared by Putin the previous Easter ended with each side accusing the other of violations. Russia has effectively rejected a separate 30-day unconditional truce proposed by the US and Ukraine; US-led talks have made no progress on key issues, and the armies remain in combat.

evidence.title: Iran Update Special Report, April 10, 2026 | ISW - Institute for the Study of War
evidence.source: Institute for the Study of War
evidence.text: On April 9, 2026, Russian President Vladimir Putin announced a 32-hour ceasefire for Orthodox Easter, from 4 p.m. on April 11 through the end of April 12. The Kremlin said Russian forces were ordered to stop military action in all directions during that period, while remaining ready to respond to alleged provocations or attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Ukraine had proposed an Easter ceasefire and was ready for reciprocal steps. A similar 30-hour ceasefire in 2025 led each side to accuse the other of violations. The article says broader US-led peace talks remained deadlocked over Russian demands for territorial and political concessions that Zelensky rejected.

evidence.title: Strikes, Summits and the Possibility of Boots on the Ground in Iran: The Week That Shaped Two Wars. The Big Five, 5 April Edition - Futura Doctrina | Mick Ryan
evidence.text: On April 3, 2026, the Kremlin said Vladimir Putin and Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan discussed Ukraine, and Putin thanked Erdogan for his continued readiness to facilitate negotiations. The article reports no Russia–Ukraine ceasefire agreement, timetable, or commitment to a ceasefire by May 31. The leaders’ separate call for an immediate ceasefire concerned the Persian Gulf, not Ukraine.

evidence.title: Pakistan says it will host U.S.-Iran talks soon as Iran warns against U.S. ground operations - CBS News
evidence.text: Zelenskyy said he was concerned that Washington would provide Ukraine security guarantees only after a comprehensive peace agreement, not after a ceasefire. Kyiv claims Russia refuses to end the war unless it takes all of the Donbas. Russian forces hold most of the region but not a heavily fortified strip; Zelenskyy said the U.S. has not directly pressed Ukraine to withdraw from it. He also disputed Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s characterization of his account of the talks. Fighting continued: Ukrainian authorities reported that Russia launched more than 270 drones overnight, killing at least five people.

evidence.title: Trump says Iran is ready to negotiate a ceasefire but he's not ready to make a deal - NBC News
evidence.text: In a Saturday interview, President Donald Trump said he was trying to make peace between Russia and Ukraine. He claimed Russian President Vladimir Putin was willing to make a deal but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy did not want one: “Tell Zelenskyy to make a deal because Putin’s willing to make a deal.” Trump added that Zelenskyy was “far more difficult to make a deal with.” These are Trump’s assessments; the article reports no ceasefire agreement or timetable. Trump also said his temporary easing of sanctions on Russian oil, imposed after Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, would end when the current oil crisis was over.

market.question: Fed Rate Hike by September 2026 Meeting?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if the upper bound of the target federal funds rate is increased at any point between December 16, 2025 and the completion of the listed Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting (inclusive of any rate hike announced as a result of the listed meeting). Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

If the listed meeting does not take place within 7 calendar days (ET) of its scheduled end date, 11:59 PM ET, and no qualifying rate hike has been announced, this market will resolve to "No".

Emergency rate hikes will qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be the official website of the Federal Reserve (https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm), however a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

evidence.title: Four Fed bank boards wanted rate hike, minutes show - Reuters
evidence.text: Ahead of the July 28–29 Federal Reserve policy meeting, directors at four of the Fed’s 12 regional banks—Dallas, Cleveland, Minneapolis and Kansas City—recommended raising the primary credit (emergency lending) rate by 0.25 percentage points. Policymakers instead voted 9–3 to maintain the benchmark interest rate. The presidents of the Cleveland, Dallas and Minneapolis Feds dissented from that decision; Kansas City Fed President Jeff Schmid had no policy vote this year. The article says the primary credit rate generally tracks the top of the benchmark rate’s target range, which has stood at 3.5%–3.75% since December. The recommendations indicate support for tighter policy within parts of the Fed system, but regional bank directors do not set the benchmark rate, and the article reports no decision to raise it by the September 2026 meeting.

evidence.title: US data buoys dollar as Fed hike expectations nudged higher - Reuters
evidence.text: Minutes of the Fed Board’s July 20 and July 29 discount-rate meetings show that directors at the Cleveland, Minneapolis, Kansas City, and Dallas Reserve Banks sought a 25-basis-point increase in the primary credit rate, from 3.75% to 4%. The other eight regional banks favored no change. The Board of Governors unanimously declined the requests at both meetings, keeping the primary credit rate at 3.75%, consistent with the FOMC’s decision to hold its federal funds target range at 3.50%–3.75%. For the upcoming September 16 meeting, CME FedWatch data put the probability of no change at 65.6% and a 25-basis-point hike at 34.4%, down from 41.4% in previous weeks. The article does not specify the year of that September meeting.

evidence.title: What to watch for in the next Fed minutes - marketplace.org
evidence.text: As of August 19, financial markets viewed the Fed’s next policy-rate move as much more likely to be a hike than a cut. Three Fed officials had indicated they favored a quarter-percentage-point increase at the July policy meeting. The article says the Fed’s preferred inflation measure had remained above its 2% target for more than five years, and Chairman Kevin Warsh had emphasized returning inflation to target. These facts support the possibility of a hike, but the article does not say one was approved or specify whether the next move would occur by the September 2026 meeting.

evidence.title: Fed officials saw need for rate hike if inflation doesn't cool, minutes show - CNBC
evidence.text: Minutes of the Fed’s July 28–29 meeting showed that many policymakers thought higher rates could be necessary if inflation did not improve. Three of the 12 voting Federal Open Market Committee members dissented from the decision to hold rates steady, favoring an immediate 25-basis-point hike. Most officials preferred to wait for more economic data before the September meeting. Inflation data since July had been generally positive, but the Fed’s preferred gauge remained above its 2% target.

evidence.title: Fed Minutes Show Many Officials Said Rate Hikes May Be Needed - Bloomberg
evidence.text: At its July 28–29 meeting, the FOMC held rates at 3.50%–3.75%, though three voting members dissented in favor of a quarter-point hike. The minutes said many participants thought tightening would likely be needed if inflation did not decline, and some questioned whether financial conditions were restrictive enough to return inflation to 2%. The article reports softer subsequent data: CPI fell 0.4% in June and rose 0.1% in July, while July payrolls fell by 23,000. According to CME Group’s FedWatch tool, markets then expected the Fed to hold rates at its September and October meetings, with a hike expected in December. The article cautions that these forecasts change often.

evidence.title: Watch Fed Minutes Show Many Officials Wanted Rate Hike in July - Bloomberg
evidence.text: Minutes from the Fed’s July meeting showed that most participants supported holding rates steady and wanted more data before the next meeting, but several favored a hike because they saw broad-based price pressures. Three voting members—Cleveland Fed president Beth Hammack, Dallas Fed president Lorie Logan, and Minneapolis Fed president Neel Kashkari—dissented, preferring a quarter-percentage-point increase. Many participants said tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline. Since the meeting, July consumer-price data showed inflation cooling for a second consecutive month, while wholesale-price data were mixed.

evidence.title: Fed minutes show many officials said rate hikes may be needed - Moneycontrol.com
evidence.text: At its July 28–29 meeting, the Fed kept its benchmark rate at 3.50%–3.75%. Three policymakers dissented, calling for a 25-basis-point hike. The minutes said many participants thought tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline toward the Fed’s 2% target. The article says the Fed was expected to hold rates at its September 15–16 meeting, while investors were pricing in possible hikes beginning at the October 27–28 meeting. Officials remained divided on further hikes and more cautious about labor-market risks after data showed slightly easing inflation and unexpected job cuts in July.

evidence.title: Fed Minutes Show ‘Many’ Officials Prefer Hiking Rates If Inflation Doesn’t Decline - Barron's
evidence.text: At its July 28–29 meeting, the FOMC voted 9–3 to keep the federal funds rate at 3.5%–3.75%. The dissenters—Cleveland Fed President Beth M. Hammack, Minneapolis Fed President Neel Kashkari, and Dallas Fed President Lorie K. Logan—each preferred a quarter-point increase; no Board of Governors member dissented. The minutes said tightening would likely be necessary if inflation did not decline, and some officials questioned whether financial conditions were tight enough to return inflation to 2%. Inflation remained elevated: total PCE was 4.1% in May and core PCE was 3.4%. Since the July decision, however, July payrolls fell and core inflation came in subdued, prompting market pricing for a September rate increase to pull back.

evidence.title: An alarmed bond market gets the Trump administration to act again - PBS
evidence.text: Minutes from the Fed’s July 28–29 meeting said the majority favored holding rates steady, but several participants favored an increase. Many judged that higher rates would likely be needed if inflation did not fall further, and some questioned whether financial conditions were restrictive enough to return inflation to the 2% target. Almost all participants supported retaining the FOMC’s commitment to deliver price stability. The staff inflation forecast was similar to June’s, while its broader economic outlook was a “touch weaker.” The article reports no decision to raise rates at that meeting or by September 2026.

evidence.title: Fed Likely Hiking Interest Rates Unless Inflation Comes Down, Minutes Show - Forbes
evidence.text: At its July meeting, the Fed voted 9–3 to hold rates at 3.5%–3.75%; it was the first time since 2016 that three FOMC officials dissented in the same direction on a policy change. Minutes showed several officials supported higher rates because they saw broad-based price pressures and believed current policy was not taming inflation. A few argued that a July hike could avert steeper tightening later. Inflation has exceeded the Fed’s 2% target for five years. Most officials expected it to ease in the latter half of the year, but many warned it could remain elevated, with risks skewed upward. Chair Kevin Warsh prioritized price stability but did not say after the meeting whether achieving it would require higher rates. The article reports growing support for a hike, not a decision to raise rates by September.

evidence.title: US treasury doubles debt buyback to steady bond market amid inflation fears | US economy - The Guardian
evidence.text: Minutes from the Fed’s July meeting showed a majority of voting members favored keeping rates unchanged, while three wanted an increase. The current range was 3.5%–3.75%. Many participants said tightening would likely be needed if inflation did not fall toward the Fed’s 2% target; some questioned whether financial conditions were restrictive enough. Annual inflation was 3.4% in July, down from 4.2% in May. The article reports pressure from the White House to lower rates and says Fed chair Kevin Warsh had not indicated which direction the central bank would take. It reports no decision on a hike by the September 2026 meeting.

Former St. Louis Fed president Jim Bullard described the Fed as “on the sidelines,” while President Donald Trump reiterated his demand for lower rates. The article reports no Fed rate hike or decision for the September 2026 meeting.

evidence.text: As of August 21, 2026, traders estimated a 40% probability of a Federal Reserve rate hike in September, compared with 72% in December. Markets were awaiting Fed Chair Kevin Warsh’s speech at the Jackson Hole symposium amid uncertainty about future Fed policy.

evidence.title: Switching High-Yield Savings Accounts Earns $362 More Per Year: July Jobs Report Adds Urgency - Tech Times
evidence.text: The article says the FOMC was divided at its July meeting: three of its 12 voting members favored a rate hike. July CPI and August CPI are due before the meeting, but the August PCE report is due afterward.

evidence.text: The article says the Aug. 12 CPI report could determine whether the Fed raises rates at its September meeting. The unemployment rate was 4.1%, which the author says hawks could cite as evidence the labor market remains sound, while doves could point to weaker wages and payroll revisions against a September hike.

market.question: Will Tesla deliver 475000 or more vehicles in Q2 2026
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve according to Tesla's announced total vehicle deliveries for Q2 2026.

If Tesla does not publish Q2 2026 delivery figures by August 31, 2026, 11:59 PM ET, this market will resolve to the lowest bracket.

If the reported value falls exactly between two brackets, this market will resolve to the higher range bracket.

The resolution source will be https://ir.tesla.com/press.

evidence.title: Onvo L60 Refresh Launches Today: Nio 5nm Chip and LiDAR Reach the $29,000 Tier - Tech Times
evidence.text: Barclays forecasts Tesla will deliver roughly 418,000 vehicles in Q2 2026—57,000 below the 475,000 threshold, though above the Bloomberg consensus of about 397,000. Its estimate implies deliveries up about 17% from Q1 and 9% year over year. Barclays cited recovering European sales and China’s EV market: Tesla sold approximately 39,000 vehicles in Europe across April and May, and China retail sales reached 47,000 in May, up 23% year over year. It expects about 90,000 European deliveries and 105,000 U.S. deliveries for the quarter.

evidence.title: Tesla Shanghai Gigafactory posts 2026 monthly record with 85,982 May deliveries - GlobalChinaEV
evidence.text: CPCA data released June 2, 2026, show Tesla’s Shanghai Gigafactory delivered 85,982 vehicles in May, its highest monthly total of 2026. That was up 39.4% year over year and 8.18% from April’s 79,478, bringing April–May Shanghai deliveries to 165,460. The article says Shanghai accounts for more than half of Tesla’s global monthly deliveries, but these figures are Shanghai wholesale deliveries—including China sales and exports—not global deliveries. It provides neither June nor full Q2 global deliveries, so it does not establish whether Tesla will reach 475,000 vehicles in Q2.

evidence.title: Learn All Crypto Topics | Phemex Blog - Phemex
evidence.text: The article reports that Tesla’s new-car registrations across the EU 27 and UK fell 49% year over year in May 2026: 14,210 versus 27,840 in May 2025, according to European Automobile Manufacturers’ Association data released June 2. It attributes part of the decline to an understocked Model Y refresh transition, while estimating that underlying demand fell about 35%. It says China demand had stabilized and North American demand was holding, potential offsets to the European weakness. Tesla targeted a Q2 2026 Cybercab production start, but first deliveries to pilot fleets were targeted for July. The article gives no Q2 delivery forecast or worldwide delivery total, so it does not establish whether Tesla will reach 475,000 deliveries.

evidence.title: May 2026 EV Sales: EV share its 1 in 3, BEV at 22% - zecar
evidence.text: In May 2026, Tesla delivered 6,433 Model Y and Model 3 vehicles in Australia—its best-ever monthly result there—and was the country’s top BEV brand. The Model Y accounted for 5,605 deliveries and was Australia’s best-selling vehicle that month; the Model 3 accounted for 828. The article says Tesla’s record May came amid surging EV interest linked to a fuel crisis. These Australian figures are relevant to Tesla’s Q2 momentum, but the article does not report Tesla’s worldwide quarterly deliveries or establish whether they will reach 475,000.

evidence.title: VFACTS May 2026: Tesla Model Y tops the charts as EV sales surge in Australia's new-vehicle market - CarExpert
evidence.text: In Australia in May 2026, Tesla delivered 6,433 vehicles, up 65.1% year over year, ranking sixth among brands. Its Model Y accounted for 5,605 deliveries and was Australia’s best-selling vehicle that month; the Model 3 accounted for the other 828. The supporting brand comparison lists Toyota at 16,342 deliveries (down 30.7%), BYD at 8,211 (up 154.6%), Ford at 7,195 (down 15.0%), Hyundai at 7,007 (up 4.5%), and Kia at 6,761 (down 2.1%). These are May figures for Australia, not Tesla’s worldwide Q2 deliveries, so they do not establish whether Tesla will reach 475,000 vehicles for the quarter.

evidence.title: Tesla China records strongest wholesale month of 2026 in May - driveteslacanada.ca
evidence.text: CPCA data cited in the article put Tesla China’s May 2026 wholesale sales from Giga Shanghai at 85,982 vehicles, its highest monthly total of the year. That was up 39.4% from May 2025 and 8.2% from April 2026, when wholesale sales were 79,478. Through May, Tesla China recorded 378,858 wholesale sales in 2026, versus 292,875 in the same period of 2025. Wholesale figures include vehicles sold in China and exported abroad; the article does not provide Tesla’s global Q2 deliveries or June results, so these figures alone do not establish whether Tesla will reach 475,000 deliveries in Q2.

evidence.title: Q2 Tesla deliveries tracking to a beat, Barclays says - Yahoo Finance UK
evidence.text: VFACTS, EVC and manufacturer data cited in the article show 12,324 Tesla Model Y sales in Australia from January through May 2026, ranking it first among premium mid-size electric SUVs. The Zeekr 7X ranked second with 3,664 sales and was the fifth-best-selling BEV overall in Australia. These are Australian Model Y sales, not Tesla’s global Q2 deliveries; the article provides no Q2 delivery forecast or figure with which to assess the 475,000-vehicle threshold.

evidence.title: BYD Exported More Vehicles In April Than Tesla Sold Worldwide* - CleanTechnica
evidence.text: Tesla does not publish monthly sales figures, so its April 2026 total is an estimate: José Pontes puts it at 96,100. The article reports Tesla’s global Q1 2026 sales at 358,023 and says Q2 sales could be higher. It also notes that Tesla typically delivers far fewer vehicles in the first month of a quarter than in the last, so the April estimate alone does not establish whether Q2 deliveries will reach 475,000.

evidence.title: EV Sales Hit Record High in April 2026 Despite Overall Market Downturn - zecar
evidence.text: In Australia, Tesla Model Y recorded 822 deliveries in April 2026, down 70.8% from 2,818 in March, and ranked 34th overall. The article says Tesla typically delivers most vehicles near quarter-end, so a low April—the first month of Q2—is not unusual; it expects deliveries to recover in June. These figures cover one model in Australia, not Tesla’s worldwide Q2 deliveries, so they do not establish whether Tesla will reach 475,000 vehicles.

evidence.title: Tesla Shares Close at $404.11 Down 1.43% on May 19, 2026 Amid Model Y Price Hike - International Business Times Australia
evidence.text: Tesla reported 358,023 vehicle deliveries in Q1 2026, missing some analyst estimates but growing year over year. Delivering at least 475,000 in Q2 would require 116,977 more vehicles than in Q1, an increase of about 33%. The article notes near-term automotive demand softness, high financing rates, intensified competition from BYD, and the expiration of the $7,500 U.S. EV tax credit at the end of 2025. Tesla raised U.S. prices on higher-end Model Y variants by $500–$1,000 and discontinued Model S and Model X production in Q2 2026. It gives no Q2 delivery forecast.

evidence.title: Elon Musk Hails Tesla Model Y Dominance in California Q1 2026 Sales as It Crushes Rivals - International Business Times Australia
evidence.text: Tesla’s Model Y led California new-vehicle sales in Q1 2026 with 22,907 registrations, 54% more than the second-place Toyota Camry’s 14,905, according to figures posted by Tesla Owners Silicon Valley. The article describes this as a positive signal heading into Q2, but also notes softening demand in some segments and increased competition. It provides no Q2 2026 delivery figure or forecast for Tesla’s total deliveries, so the California registration result alone does not establish whether Tesla will reach 475,000 deliveries.

market.question: Israel x Hezbollah permanent peace deal by May 31, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if Israel and Hezbollah agree to a permanent peace deal by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A permanent peace deal refers to any agreement which explicitly indicates that military hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah have ended or will permanently cease, or uses equivalent language clearly signaling a lasting end to military hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. Agreements that are explicitly temporary or which do not include a definitive agreement to end military hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah on a lasting basis (e.g. a temporary extension of the 10-day ceasefire agreement announced on April 16, 2026), will not qualify.

A qualifying agreement will be considered to have been established if either of the following conditions are met:

- Israel and Hezbollah each sign or formally adopt a written agreement (e.g. a treaty or multi-point agreement) which meets the above criteria.

- Both Israel and Hezbollah provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The inclusion of Israel and Hezbollah in a qualifying peace deal between multiple parties will qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the government of Israel and Hezbollah; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

Lebanon’s Health Ministry said Israeli strikes nevertheless killed four people in southern Lebanon. The article reports no diplomatic meeting between Israel and Hezbollah or plans for one by May 31, 2026.

evidence.title: US and Iran in indirect talks to extend two-week ceasefire - theguardian.com
evidence.text: The article says Israel has held talks with the Lebanese government in Washington, portraying them as a “historic opportunity” to end the Iranian-allied Hezbollah militia’s grip on Lebanon. It does not report a diplomatic meeting between Israel and Hezbollah or give a date for one. Two Lebanese officials said a ceasefire with Israel could be announced “soon,” but provided no details. Israel’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he had not committed to a ceasefire and that Israeli forces were continuing to strike Hezbollah in Lebanon.

evidence.title: Israel and Hezbollah continue attacks after Israel-Lebanon talks in US - BBC
evidence.text: Israel and Lebanon held direct, high-level talks in Washington on Tuesday, mediated by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Israeli ambassador Yechiel Leiter and Lebanese ambassador Nada Moawad met; the article describes this as the countries’ first such contact in three decades. No ceasefire was announced. Hezbollah was not identified as a participant and strongly rejected the negotiations. On Wednesday, Hezbollah MP Hassan Fadlallah warned that Lebanon’s internal rift could widen over the government’s decision to negotiate with Israel and urged authorities to reconsider. He said Hezbollah wanted a comprehensive ceasefire rather than a return to the near-daily Israeli strikes and assassinations seen after the November 2024 ceasefire deal.

evidence.title: Trump says Iran talks could resume in days as U.S. military blocks Iranian ports - NPR
evidence.text: The article reports that Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors met directly in Washington on a Tuesday, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, for the first such talks in more than 30 years. They agreed to continue negotiations aimed at peace between Israel and Hezbollah after nearly seven weeks of fighting in Lebanon. Hezbollah, an Iran-backed militant group that also holds seats in Lebanon’s parliament, did not support the talks and called on the Lebanese government to cancel them. Fighting continued the next day. Lebanon wanted a ceasefire, but Israel said it would not agree until Hezbollah disarmed. The reported meeting was between Israel and Lebanon, not a direct Israel–Hezbollah meeting; the article gives no explicit calendar date for it.

evidence.title: US-Iran talks: What’s the latest on mediation efforts? - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: On April 14, 2026, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio hosted Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter and Lebanese Ambassador Nada Hamadeh Moawad for direct talks in Washington. The Lebanese government, led by President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, had called for negotiations with Israel despite Hezbollah’s objections. Israel said the talks would focus on disarming Hezbollah and ruled out discussing a ceasefire; Lebanese officials said only Moawad was authorised to discuss one. The article reports an Israel–Lebanon diplomatic meeting before May 31, 2026, but does not report Hezbollah participating in a meeting with Israel.

evidence.title: Israel and Lebanon agree to start peace negotiations after rare talks in D.C. - NPR
evidence.text: Israel and Lebanon held direct diplomatic talks in Washington on a Tuesday after six weeks of fighting between Israel and Hezbollah. The meeting involved the Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors to the U.S. and U.S. officials—not Hezbollah representatives. Israeli Ambassador Yechiel Leiter called the talks a victory simply because they occurred despite Hezbollah urging Lebanon not to participate. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem said in a televised speech on Monday that the negotiations were futile and lacked internal Lebanese consensus. The State Department said Israel and Lebanon agreed to launch direct negotiations at a mutually agreed time and venue; Leiter said the next talks would be in Washington in a few weeks. The article reports no planned diplomatic meeting between Israel and Hezbollah by May 31, 2026.

evidence.title: War: We’ll not abide by agreements from Lebanon-Israel talks – Hezbollah - Daily Post Nigeria
evidence.text: The article reports that Israel and Lebanon were set to meet at ambassador level on Tuesday in Washington, with U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio expected to host. On Monday, Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem urged the Lebanese government to cancel the meeting, called the talks pointless, and said Hezbollah would continue confronting Israeli attacks on Lebanon. The article describes a planned Israel–Lebanon meeting, not an Israel–Hezbollah meeting, and does not confirm that it took place.

evidence.title: Israel, Lebanon to meet for tough talks in Washington - euractiv.com
evidence.text: The article reports that the Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors held US-brokered, direct talks on a Tuesday in Washington, DC—the first such bilateral engagement since 1993. Lebanon sought a ceasefire, while Israel sought Hezbollah’s disarmament. This was an Israel–Lebanon meeting, not a meeting with Hezbollah: no Hezbollah representative is listed among the participants. Hezbollah urged the Lebanese government to withdraw, called the talks “futile,” and said it would not abide by any agreement reached in Washington. The article does not report an Israel–Hezbollah diplomatic meeting or give a calendar date for the Washington talks.

evidence.title: Israel, Lebanon launch historic direct talks in Washington - www.israelhayom.com
evidence.text: The article says Israeli and Lebanese representatives are scheduled to meet in Washington “today” for US-mediated talks on the war in Lebanon. Secretary of State Marco Rubio will mediate a meeting including the Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors to Washington and the US ambassador to Beirut. A State Department official calls these the first open, direct, high-level Israeli–Lebanese diplomatic talks since 1993. The article does not say Hezbollah will attend: its leader, Naim Qassem, called for the talks to be scrapped. The meeting is reported as scheduled, not as having taken place.

evidence.title: Iran war: What is happening on day 46 of the US-Iran conflict? - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: Lebanon’s Culture Minister Ghassan Salame told Al Jazeera that Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors were set to meet in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday to discuss “a pause in military activity if not a cease-fire.” Hezbollah chief Naim Qassem reportedly urged Lebanon to cancel the meeting, calling the talks pointless. The article describes a planned Lebanon–Israel meeting, not a meeting with Hezbollah, and does not confirm that it took place. The proposed talks came amid Israeli attacks on Lebanon that the article says had killed more than 2,000 people since March 2.

evidence.title: Israel, Lebanon meet for historic peace talks in Washington as fighting continues - washingtontimes.com
evidence.text: As of April 14, 2026, Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors were scheduled to hold talks that Tuesday in Washington, DC, aimed at halting the war despite ongoing fighting. Hezbollah was not described as a participant: its leader, Naim Qassem, urged Lebanon on Monday to cancel the meeting and reiterated Hezbollah’s opposition to direct engagement with Israel. The article reports a planned Israel–Lebanon meeting, not an Israel–Hezbollah meeting.

evidence.title: Lebanon-Israel Talks: Defining Zones of Possible Agreement - The Washington Institute
evidence.text: The article reports anticipated face-to-face discussions in Washington between the ambassadors of Lebanon and Israel, not representatives of Israel and Hezbollah. Wafiq Safa, a prominent member of Hezbollah’s political council, spoke on the eve of those discussions and said Hezbollah opposed the negotiations and would not adhere to any resulting agreement. Hezbollah leader Naim Kassem also urged Lebanon to withdraw. The article gives no date for the anticipated meeting and does not report a planned Israel–Hezbollah diplomatic meeting by May 31, 2026.

evidence.title: US-Israel-Iran War Highlights: Iran seeks compensation from Gulf states - The Times of India
evidence.text: The article reports that Israeli and Lebanese envoys held direct talks in Washington on a Tuesday, hosted by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio—the countries’ first direct negotiations since 1983. Israel demanded that Lebanon disarm Hezbollah and ruled out discussing a ceasefire. Hezbollah opposed the talks and was not represented. A senior Hezbollah official, Wafiq Safa, said the group would not abide by any agreements reached there. The reported meeting was between Israel and Lebanon, not Israel and Hezbollah.

evidence.title: The U.S. military says it will blockade Iranian ports as Iran peace talks collapse - NPR
evidence.text: Lebanon says the Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors to Washington will hold their first direct meeting on Tuesday at the State Department to discuss a ceasefire and a date for starting negotiations. The article does not say the meeting has occurred or that Hezbollah will participate. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said his goal in talks is to disarm Hezbollah and reach a peace agreement with Lebanon. Fighting was continuing: Israel said it struck more than 200 Hezbollah targets over the weekend, while Hezbollah said it continued attacks on Israel and Israeli troops in Lebanon.

evidence.title: US and Iran fail to reach a deal after marathon talks in Pakistan - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: The article says Lebanon and Israel will hold direct talks in Washington starting Tuesday, seeking to end Israel’s conflict with Hezbollah, an Iran-backed militant group in Lebanon. It reports a planned meeting, not one that has already occurred, and gives no calendar date for Tuesday. Lebanon’s government has made a truce a prerequisite for talks and plans to demand an Israeli withdrawal, the release of Lebanese prisoners, and the return of more than one million displaced Lebanese. Hezbollah supporters and other critics have protested the decision to negotiate. Vice President JD Vance said Lebanon was not part of the ceasefire deal with Iran, though Israel had offered to restrain its actions in Lebanon to help that deal continue.

evidence.title: What to Know About the U.S.-Iran Cease-Fire Talks - The New York Times
evidence.text: Netanyahu said Israel is seeking a deal with Lebanon. Reports said Yechiel Leiter, Israel’s ambassador to the US, had spoken with the Lebanese envoy in Washington, DC, for the first time; the article does not say whether they met in person or give a date for the contact. Leiter said Israel would not accept a ceasefire with Hezbollah. Israel has continued its offensive against Hezbollah in Lebanon and rejected Iran’s claim that a broader ceasefire covered Lebanon.

evidence.title: U.S., Iran prepare for peace talks with a gulf separating the two sides - The Washington Post
evidence.text: Israel’s ambassador to the US, Yechiel Leiter, said on Saturday that the US, Israel and Lebanon had held a preparatory phone meeting and that Israel had agreed to begin formal peace negotiations with Lebanon the following Tuesday under US State Department auspices. Direct talks between the Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors were due to take place in Washington. Leiter said Israel refused to discuss a ceasefire with Hezbollah, which he said continued to attack Israel and was the main obstacle to peace between the two countries. The article distinguishes the planned Israel–Lebanon talks from talks with Hezbollah: it reports no planned direct Israel–Hezbollah diplomatic meeting. It also says Hezbollah is part of Lebanon’s government, the two sides have fought since early March, and Hezbollah supporters protested the negotiations.

evidence.title: Iran, two US Navy ships cross Hormuz. Talks continue in Islamabad - Il Sole 24 ORE
evidence.text: Israeli and Lebanese ambassadors held discussions on Friday to arrange a meeting between Israeli and Lebanese officials at the US Department of State the following Tuesday. Israel’s US ambassador, Yechiel Leiter, said Israel had agreed to begin formal peace negotiations with Lebanon, but ruled out discussing a ceasefire with Hezbollah, which he said continued to attack Israel and was the main obstacle to peace. Hezbollah-affiliated Lebanese lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said the group rejected direct Lebanon–Israel negotiations. The planned meeting is between Israel and Lebanese officials, not Israel and Hezbollah.

evidence.title: Trump cautions Iran against charging tolls to go through Strait of Hormuz as fragile ceasefire holds - CBS News
evidence.text: On April 11, 2026, protesters in Beirut displayed portraits of the late Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah at a demonstration against direct negotiations between Israel and Lebanon. The article does not report a meeting between Israeli and Hezbollah representatives, or a date for one. It also reports that Israel said it struck about 200 Hezbollah targets in Lebanon in the preceding 24 hours, while the issue of Israeli attacks in Lebanon arose in separate US–Iran talks in Pakistan.

evidence.title: Trump downplays talks for ceasefire deal with Iran, claiming military victory. 'It doesn’t matter' - Fortune
evidence.text: Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Friday that a first meeting would be held Tuesday at the U.S. State Department to discuss a ceasefire and launch U.S.-mediated Lebanon–Israel negotiations. He said it followed a call between the Lebanese and Israeli ambassadors in Washington, joined by the U.S. ambassador to Beirut. The article does not say Hezbollah would participate: an adviser to Iran’s supreme leader warned against sidelining the group. Lebanese Prime Minister Nawaf Salam postponed a planned Washington trip, and the article says it was unclear what that meant for Tuesday’s talks. The meeting is reported as planned, not completed, and the article gives no calendar date for Tuesday.

evidence.title: Pakistan sets modest goal for US-Iran summit: A deal to keep talks going - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Thursday that Israel was ready to begin direct negotiations with Lebanon “as soon as possible,” focused on disarming Hezbollah and reaching a peace agreement. The announcement followed US pressure: President Donald Trump said he had asked Netanyahu to “low-key it” on Lebanon. Netanyahu also said there was no ceasefire in Lebanon and that Israel would keep striking Hezbollah even as talks proceed. The article reports a willingness to negotiate with Lebanon, not a scheduled or completed diplomatic meeting between Israel and Hezbollah.

evidence.title: Explainer: Israel and Lebanon are holding talks. What do we know? - Reuters
evidence.text: As of April 10, 2026, Lebanese and Israeli representatives were expected to meet the following week at the U.S. State Department in Washington for U.S.-mediated talks aimed at de-escalating fighting between Israel and Hezbollah, a State Department official told CBS News. The article reports an expected meeting, not one that had already taken place.

evidence.title: Why Lebanon struggles to neutralize Hezbollah - The Jerusalem Post
evidence.text: The article discusses possible direct talks between Israel and the Lebanese government, not a diplomatic meeting between Israel and Hezbollah. On March 9, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun proposed a total ceasefire, Hezbollah’s disarmament, and Lebanese-Israeli talks under international auspices, conditional on Israeli strikes in Lebanon stopping. A March 13 report said he had also proposed a one-month truce through the US ambassador, but the article says that proposal went nowhere. Israel has not signaled readiness for political talks with Beirut while hostilities continue. The writer argues that, if Lebanese-Israeli talks were arranged, Hezbollah would attempt to disrupt them; such talks could instead seek to end Hezbollah’s attacks on Israel. The article reports no proposed Israel-Hezbollah meeting.

market.question: Gaza flotilla enters Israeli waters by May 31?
market.resolution_criteria:
A flotilla organized by the Global Sumud Flotilla, among others, set sail from Spain on April 15, 2026 to deliver aid to Gaza (see: https://apnews.com/article/global-sumud-flotilla-gaza-aid-spain-israel-94b09412fdcb1a0fd6a6e0c981479539). 

This market will resolve to “Yes” if any vessel which is part of this flotilla enters Israel’s territorial sea by May 31, 2026 (ET). Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

For the purposes of this market, Israel’s territorial sea includes the territorial waters off the coast of Gaza that are controlled by Israel.

The primary resolution source will be a consensus of credible reporting.

evidence.title: Gaza Flotilla Interception Tests Humanitarian Claims Under Fragile Ceasefire Framework - The Media Line
evidence.text: Global Sumud Flotilla representative Hannah Smith said the Gaza-bound flotilla had 56 vessels before Israeli forces intercepted 21 on Thursday and left one, the Tam Tam, sinking; its occupants were rescued. She said 34 vessels were then in Crete, Greece. The article places the interception in international waters near Crete, more than 600 nautical miles from Gaza—not in Israeli waters. Smith said the group was regrouping and had no immediate plan to depart for Gaza. The article gives no calendar date for the interception or a plan to enter Israeli waters by May 31.

evidence.title: Türkiye criticizes Greece over silence on Israel's attack on Gaza-bound flotilla - Türkiye Today
evidence.text: The Global Sumud Flotilla’s 2026 Spring Mission left Barcelona for Gaza on April 12 and set out again from Sicily on April 26 with 345 activists from 39 countries. In the early hours of April 29, Israeli forces intercepted its vessels in international waters off Crete—about 80 nautical miles west of the island and 600 nautical miles from Gaza. Turkish Ministry of National Defense sources described the operation as an unlawful assault; the article says 175 activists were detained, 31 injured, and vessels damaged so they were unseaworthy. Most detainees were released to Crete on May 1. The article does not report the flotilla entering Israeli waters.

evidence.title: Flotilla activists describe 40 hours of ill-treatment by Israel after seizure - Türkiye Today
evidence.text: AFP reported that Israeli forces intercepted a Gaza-bound flotilla of more than 50 vessels early Thursday in international waters off Greece. Organizers said the interception was more than 1,000 kilometers from Gaza. Israel said two activists were brought to Israel for questioning, but the article does not say the vessels entered Israeli waters. It gives no calendar date for that Thursday or evidence of entry by May 31.

evidence.title: Activists flown to Greece after Israel intercepts Gaza-bound flotilla - Daily Sabah
evidence.text: British activist Sijaad Hussain said the Global Sumud Flotilla was carrying humanitarian aid toward Gaza when Israel attacked it in international waters, “far before Crete.” Another activist also said the boats were in international waters when an Israeli warship approached. The article describes an Israeli interception, not the flotilla entering Israeli waters. It gives no May 31 date, so it does not establish whether the flotilla entered Israeli waters by then.

evidence.title: ‘Apartheid without borders,’ says UN special rapporteur on Israel’s interception of Gaza-bound aid flotilla - Middle East Monitor
evidence.text: The article does not establish that the flotilla entered Israeli waters by May 31. It says Israeli forces intercepted some Global Sumud Flotilla boats earlier that week while they were off Greece near Crete. A source said 22 boats had been intercepted and 47 others were still sailing off southern Crete, with plans to continue toward Gaza. The article gives no date tying those events to May 31 and does not say the boats reached Israeli waters.

evidence.title: Gaza aid flotilla vessels taken to Crete after Israeli interception - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: The group’s tracker reported that Israel had intercepted 22 Global Sumud Flotilla boats, while 47 were still sailing. Organisers said the interceptions occurred on Wednesday in international waters near Greece, as the boats headed for Gaza. A source said on Friday that the remaining boats were off southern Crete and planned to anchor there before continuing toward Gaza. The article does not say any boat entered Israeli waters or establish that one would do so by May 31.

evidence.title: Israel frees all but two activists in Greece after seizing Gaza aid flotilla - Saudi Gazette
evidence.text: On May 1, 2026, Amnesty International said Israeli forces had boarded Global Sumud Flotilla vessels in international waters near Greece. It said around 175 activists were detained and being transported to Israel. The flotilla was attempting to deliver aid to Gaza, but the article does not say its vessels entered Israeli waters.

evidence.title: Israel stops Gaza-bound aid flotilla in international waters - dw.com
evidence.text: Pro-Palestinian activists said Israeli forces intercepted 22 boats carrying aid for Gaza in international waters near Crete. The Global Sumud Flotilla said the interception occurred more than 965 km (600 miles) from Gaza; its data showed most of the remaining 36 boats near Crete’s south coast. The flotilla had set sail two weeks earlier, with 58 vessels joining from Spain, France and Italy to challenge Israel’s naval blockade of Gaza. Israel confirmed taking early action in international waters to prevent a breach of the blockade. The article does not report that any flotilla boat entered Israeli waters or establish whether one would do so by May 31.

evidence.title: Israel Intercepts Aid Flotilla Heading to Breach Naval Blockade of Gaza - The New York Times
evidence.text: The article reports that Israeli military boats seized 15 flotilla ships near Crete, hundreds of miles from Gaza, according to organizer Global Sumud Flotilla. Israel’s Foreign Ministry said more than 20 aid ships carrying 175 activists were stopped in international waters near Greece while heading toward Gaza. Israel’s UN envoy said the flotilla was stopped before reaching Israel’s area. The article gives no May 31 date or evidence that the ships entered Israeli waters.

evidence.title: The Global Sumud Flotilla Sets Sail to Gaza Once Again - Knock LA
evidence.text: About 40 Global Sumud Flotilla vessels left Barcelona, Spain, the previous week. Australians Juliet Lamont, a Northern Rivers documentary filmmaker; Zack Schofield, a Rising Tide organiser; and Ethan Floyd, a University of Sydney law student, were set to join the convoy from eastern Sicily on Sunday. Boats from Greece and Turkey were expected to join in the coming days, bringing the flotilla to about 100 vessels and 1,000 participants. The article gives no expected date for reaching Israeli waters. It says Israel intercepted about 50 vessels from the flotilla’s previous mission in international waters and has intercepted all Gaza-bound flotillas since 2010.

evidence.title: Gaza aid flotilla activists taken to Crete after Israeli interception - Reuters
evidence.text: The article says Israeli forces seized ships in the Global Sumud Flotilla on Thursday and that participants were transferred to Greece. The flotilla sought to break the Israeli blockade of Gaza. Greece said the seizure occurred near its waters and was not coordinated with Athens. The article does not say the flotilla entered Israeli waters or give a date establishing that it did so by May 31.

evidence.text: The article says Israeli forces finished intercepting the last of more than 50 Global Sumud Flotilla boats on a Tuesday evening while they were sailing toward Gaza in international waters. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel had the right to prevent the flotilla from entering its territorial waters. The article does not give a calendar date for that Tuesday or report that the boats entered Israeli waters by May 31.

evidence.text: In mid-May, more than 50 vessels departed Marmaris, Turkey, on a mission to reach Gaza. Rising Tide organiser Zack Schofield sailed on the Marilyn, which the article says was among the first vessels intercepted on May 18, about 250 nautical miles from Gaza. The article describes the flotilla’s interceptions as occurring in international waters and says Israel has intercepted all Gaza-bound flotillas since 2010. It does not report that a vessel entered Israeli waters by May 31.

evidence.text: The article reports that Israeli forces intercepted the Global Sumud Flotilla while it was sailing from Marmaris, Turkey, toward Gaza. The flotilla, described as 50 boats carrying more than 400 activists from 44 countries, had departed four days earlier. The Global Sumud Flotilla said Israeli naval warships encircled it in international waters, approximately 250 nautical miles from Gaza’s coast. A family statement dated May 20, 2026, says one detained participant was in Israeli custody. The article does not report that the flotilla entered Israeli waters; it places the interception in international waters.

evidence.text: The flotilla’s website tracker placed the boats stopped by Israeli forces about 90–100 miles from Gaza’s coastline. Flotilla officials said Israeli forces had seized 31 vessels near Cyprus on Monday, May 19, more than 250 nautical miles from Gaza. market.question: Israel x Iran permanent peace deal by July 31, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if Israel and Iran agree to a permanent peace deal by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A permanent peace deal refers to any agreement which explicitly indicates that military hostilities between Israel and Iran have ended or will permanently cease, or uses equivalent language clearly signaling a lasting end to military hostilities between Israel and Iran. Agreements that are explicitly temporary or which do not include a definitive agreement to end military hostilities between Israel and Iran on a lasting basis (e.g. a temporary extension of a previously announced ceasefire agreement), will not qualify.

A qualifying agreement will be considered to have been established if either of the following conditions are met:

- Israel and Iran each sign or formally adopt a written agreement (e.g. a treaty or multi-point agreement) which meets the above criteria.

- Both Israel and Iran provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The inclusion of Israel and Iran in a qualifying peace deal between multiple parties will qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the governments of Israel and Iran; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

President Trump said he believed the U.S.–Iran ceasefire was over, though he did not rule out further talks to end the war permanently. The article says renewed US-Iran attacks undermined a shaky ceasefire and diminished hopes of turning a June 17 memorandum of understanding into a permanent peace deal. Iran reported attacks on US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait after US strikes on Iranian targets; both sides accused the other of breaching the ceasefire. An Iranian negotiator also cited Israeli attacks against Lebanon. The article discusses a prospective US-Iran peace deal, not a separate Israel-Iran agreement, and reports no permanent deal.

market.question: Israel x Iran permanent peace deal by July 31, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if Israel and Iran agree to a permanent peace deal by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A permanent peace deal refers to any agreement which explicitly indicates that military hostilities between Israel and Iran have ended or will permanently cease, or uses equivalent language clearly signaling a lasting end to military hostilities between Israel and Iran. Agreements that are explicitly temporary or which do not include a definitive agreement to end military hostilities between Israel and Iran on a lasting basis (e.g. a temporary extension of a previously announced ceasefire agreement), will not qualify.

A qualifying agreement will be considered to have been established if either of the following conditions are met:

- Israel and Iran each sign or formally adopt a written agreement (e.g. a treaty or multi-point agreement) which meets the above criteria.

- Both Israel and Iran provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The inclusion of Israel and Iran in a qualifying peace deal between multiple parties will qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the governments of Israel and Iran; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

This market will resolve to “Yes” if Israel and Iran agree to a permanent peace deal by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A permanent peace deal refers to any agreement which explicitly indicates that military hostilities between Israel and Iran have ended or will permanently cease, or uses equivalent language clearly signaling a lasting end to military hostilities between Israel and Iran. Agreements that are explicitly temporary or which do not include a definitive agreement to end military hostilities between Israel and Iran on a lasting basis (e.g. a temporary extension of a previously announced ceasefire agreement), will not qualify.

A qualifying agreement will be considered to have been established if either of the following conditions are met:

- Israel and Iran each sign or formally adopt a written agreement (e.g. a treaty or multi-point agreement) which meets the above criteria.

- Both Israel and Iran provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The inclusion of Israel and Iran in a qualifying peace deal between multiple parties will qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the governments of Israel and Iran; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.
