The MOU declares an immediate, permanent end to military operations by the U.S., Iran and their allies on all fronts, including Lebanon, but says a final deal would confirm that termination. Nuclear issues, sanctions relief and other terms remain to be negotiated. Israel is not named as a signatory, and the article does not report a signed Israel–Iran peace deal or give a date establishing whether a final deal would be reached by July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: Day 129 of US-Israel War on Iran: ‘We Have No Peace With the US, Won’t Recognise Israel’, Says Iran - TheWire.in
evidence.text: The article reports that Iran’s slain Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was to be buried on July 9 after a two-day public farewell. His son and successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, did not appear at the funeral prayers because of fears of an Israeli assassination attempt. The article’s title says Iran “won’t recognise Israel.” It reports no Israel–Iran peace agreement or negotiations.

evidence.title: Cease-Fire Deal Appears Within Reach, Officials Say - The New York Times
evidence.text: Trump said the US had reached a memorandum of understanding with Iran to end the war launched by the US and Israel more than 100 days earlier; Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf is believed to have signed for Iran. Pakistan’s prime minister said both sides declared an immediate and permanent end to military operations. But the article explicitly says **Israel is not a party** to the deal, nor are Lebanon or Hezbollah. Iran’s published terms call for a permanent cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon, while US officials said Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon was not a condition and Israel retained the right to defend itself against Hezbollah. Israel and Hezbollah continued exchanging strikes despite a Lebanon ceasefire in place since April 16 and renewed in June; Israel also struck alleged Hezbollah targets after the new deal was announced. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israeli forces would remain in security zones in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza indefinitely. The MOU envisages 60 days of negotiations toward a final US–Iran agreement, rather than itself establishing a permanent Israel–Iran peace deal.

evidence.title: US, Iran to sign a ‘peace deal’ on Friday: What we know - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: The article says the US and Iran have reached an understanding on a peace deal and plan to sign a formal document in Geneva on June 19, 2026. Details of the proposed 14-point agreement are not yet known. Crucially for an Israel–Iran deal by July 31, Israel has made clear it is not a party to the US–Iran agreement. The article says it is unclear whether the agreement will address Iran’s proxies, including Hezbollah, Hamas and the Houthis. Israeli Defence Minister Katz said Israel intends to keep the IDF in security zones in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza indefinitely. The writer argues that the US–Iran deal could ease hostilities but doubts it would bring permanent regional peace.

evidence.title: Will Israel use Lebanon to derail US-Iran peace process? - Anadolu Ajansı
evidence.text: The article says the U.S. and Iran signed an interim memorandum of understanding on Wednesday and agreed to at least 60 more days of negotiations; a substantive final peace deal has not been reached. The MOU says the U.S., Iran and their allies in the current war declare an immediate and permanent end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, and that a final deal will confirm the permanent termination of the war on all fronts. The article notes that neither Israel nor Hezbollah is named in that provision. It says Israel has signaled it is not on board, has said it will not withdraw its forces from Lebanon, and has continued bombing targets there during the cease-fire. The article also says major issues, including Iran’s nuclear program, remain unresolved and that the 60-day negotiating period can be extended.

evidence.title: US and Iran agree to 'immediate' end of military operations in memorandum of understanding - France 24
evidence.text: Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Sunday that both sides had declared an “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon.” The article identifies the agreement as a preliminary US–Iran memorandum mediated by Pakistan, not an Israel–Iran peace deal. Mediators were to meet ahead of a Friday signing in Switzerland, with further negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme and US sanctions planned for the following 60 days. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said operations would stop permanently on Monday night, including in Lebanon. But Israel’s defence minister said Monday that Israeli forces would remain “indefinitely” in areas captured in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza, while Iran’s foreign minister called for a complete halt to Israeli attacks on Lebanon. The article does not report a signed permanent peace deal between Israel and Iran.

evidence.title: No lasting peace without resolving the Palestinian cause: Sisi sends firm message to Israel - Egypt Independent
evidence.text: The article reports that Iran and the US signed an initial deal last month to halt hostilities, allowing commercial ships to transit the Strait of Hormuz free of charge for 60 days. Negotiations on a permanent settlement are ongoing, but the US says Iran cannot charge transit tolls or fees under a final agreement. Iran’s ambassador to China, Abdolreza Rahmani Fazli, says Iran will charge “service fees,” with special considerations for China and other friendly countries. The article says the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in late February, but reports no permanent Israel–Iran peace deal or agreement to reach one by July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: Iran says the deal to end the war with the U.S. requires Israel to withdraw from Lebanon - PBS
evidence.text: As of June 16, 2026, the U.S. and Iran had agreed to a memorandum of understanding to extend their ceasefire and pursue further talks, not a permanent Israel–Iran peace deal. Vice President JD Vance called the roughly page-and-a-half document “very general”; it leaves major issues for a 60-day negotiation window, which extends beyond July 31. Israel’s presence in Lebanon remains a major obstacle. Iran insists that any agreement ending the conflict include an end to the fighting there, while a spokesperson for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel would continue defending itself against security threats. A senior U.S. official said Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon is not a condition of the memorandum and that Israel could respond if Hezbollah attacks Israeli positions or towns.

evidence.title: Iran updates: Netanyahu refrains from criticizing Iran deal - DW.com
evidence.text: Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a US–Iran deal on Sunday and said both sides had declared an “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts,” including Lebanon. Trump said Monday that the pact was “all signed”; US officials said Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf had signed it electronically. The pact extends a ceasefire for 60 days while the sides negotiate details of a final agreement, with an official signing ceremony planned in Geneva later that week. The article does not report a final, permanent Israel–Iran peace agreement or Israeli participation in the pact. Israeli politicians objected: Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel would strike Iran “with full force” if attacked over events in Lebanon, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir said Trump’s agreement did not bind Israel. The article says occasional fire had continued between Iran and Israel and the US since their April 8 ceasefire.

evidence.title: Iran, US agree to halt war and reopen Hormuz, sending oil prices tumbling - The Express Tribune
evidence.text: Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said it finalized the text of a US–Iran memorandum on June 14 and claimed that, under the agreements reached, war and military operations “on all fronts, including Lebanon” would end immediately and permanently that night. It said the memorandum would be signed on June 19 in Switzerland. The text has not been officially published by either government, and the article describes it as a framework for further negotiations, not a final settlement. A reported 60-day process would address unresolved nuclear issues and broader sanctions relief, but Iran says final talks will begin only after the US meets commitments on frozen funds, oil sanctions and the naval blockade. The reported agreement is between Iran and the US; the article does not report an Israel–Iran peace deal.

evidence.title: US-Iran Deal Raises Hopes for Regional Peace Despite Israeli Pushback - Morocco World News
evidence.text: The article reports that the United States and Iran agreed to an “immediate and permanent” end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, with a signing scheduled for June 19 in Switzerland. Pakistan’s prime minister announced the halt, and Washington and Tehran confirmed the deal. Iran’s deputy foreign minister said the two countries would hold talks within two months toward a “final agreement”; the agreement’s details remained unclear. The article does not report Israel agreeing to or signing a permanent peace deal with Iran. Trump said an Israeli airstrike on Hezbollah in Beirut’s suburbs had delayed the signing and said he had angrily confronted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Tehran had threatened retaliation, and the article says an earlier Israeli strike near Beirut had prompted Iranian missiles and Israeli counterstrikes despite a ceasefire that had largely held since April. Iran has insisted that any agreement to halt the war include Lebanon.

evidence.title: U.S. and Iran Reach Framework for Peace - The New York Times
evidence.text: Iran and the US agreed to a memorandum of understanding after more than 100 days of war that began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said on Monday that the deal would end war and military operations “immediately and permanently” on all fronts, including Lebanon, as of that night, and immediately end the naval blockade against Iran. Pakistan’s prime minister likewise said the parties had agreed to a permanent termination of military operations on all fronts. The US-Iran memorandum was scheduled for signing in Geneva on June 19. Iran said negotiations on a final agreement would follow only after US obligations were fulfilled. The article does not report an Israel-Iran peace agreement or identify Israel as a party to the memorandum.

evidence.title: Trump announces peace deal with Iran, opening of Hormuz Strait - WorldCargo News
evidence.text: The article reports that the United States and Iran agreed to a memorandum of understanding calling for an “immediate and permanent” end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon. Mediator Pakistan announced it on Sunday; Washington and Tehran confirmed it, with a signing ceremony scheduled for June 19 in Switzerland. Iran’s deputy foreign minister said the countries would hold talks within two months to seek a “final agreement,” and the article says the memorandum’s details remained unclear. This is a US–Iran agreement, not a reported permanent peace deal between Israel and Iran. Israel’s strike against Iran-backed Hezbollah near Beirut had threatened to delay the agreement; an earlier Israeli strike there had prompted Iranian missiles and Israeli counterstrikes despite a ceasefire that had largely held since April. Iran had demanded that any agreement to halt the war include the conflict in Lebanon.

evidence.title: Here’s What to Know About U.S.-Iran Peace Talks - The New York Times
evidence.text: The article reports that the United States and Iran—not Israel and Iran—signed a 60-day memorandum of understanding on June 17, 2026. It formally halted hostilities, reopened the Strait of Hormuz and began 60 days of negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme. The memorandum seeks a permanent end to military operations involving both countries and their allies, including in Lebanon, but it is not a permanent Israel-Iran peace deal. Subsequent indirect U.S.-Iran talks in Doha showed no reported breakthrough toward a permanent agreement. Iran says any deal must include Lebanon’s safety from Israeli attacks; the article says Israel has continued attacking Lebanon. A separate U.S.-Israel-Lebanon framework links Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon to Hezbollah’s disarmament, but Hezbollah has rejected its conditions.

evidence.title: Vance vs. Rubio: Iran Edition - The Atlantic
evidence.text: On 17 June, the US and Iran signed a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding calling for an “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts.” The article does not report an Israel–Iran peace deal; it says talks on a deal to permanently end the war would continue. The ceasefire was under threat less than two weeks after it was agreed: an Iranian projectile hit a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz, the US struck targets in Iran, and Iran struck at US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain. Tehran says fighting in Lebanon must stop for a wider ceasefire deal to stick. The article separately reports a US-mediated framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon, not Israel and Iran.

evidence.title: Global shares ease as investors ponder U.S.-Iran peace talks; yen nears 40-year lows - bnnbloomberg.ca
evidence.text: The article reports an interim agreement aimed at ending the war in Iran, but says an escalation in fighting in Lebanon jeopardized its chances of becoming a lasting Middle East peace deal. Israel and Hezbollah agreed to a ceasefire in Lebanon on Friday, according to a U.S. official. U.S.-Iranian peace talks were called off after U.S. Vice President JD Vance withdrew from a planned Friday meeting with Iranian negotiators in Switzerland. The article does not report a permanent Israel-Iran peace deal or give a date for one.

evidence.title: A Look at the Text of the Agreement Between the United States and Iran - The New York Times
evidence.text: The article reports an interim U.S.–Iran accord, reached days before the renewed fighting, that calls for a permanent halt to military operations by the parties and their allies, including in Lebanon. It does not report an Israel–Iran peace deal or a final settlement. The article says the accord may have reduced the risk of direct U.S.–Iran confrontation but has not resolved conflicts involving Israel and the Iran-backed group Hezbollah. Fighting resumed after a brief lull: Israel confirmed four soldiers killed in Lebanon, and Lebanese authorities reported at least 18 people killed and 33 wounded in Israeli strikes on 11 towns. Israel and Hezbollah each accuse the other of violating the ceasefire, and the article says there is no agreed mechanism to enforce it or settle such disputes. Some Israeli ministers criticize the accord as insufficient for Israel’s security, while continued fighting could undermine negotiations before a final settlement begins. The article gives no date for an Israel–Iran permanent deal by July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: What’s in the US-Iran deal? 14 key provisions revealed - Gulf Business
evidence.text: The article describes a 14-point memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran, not an Israel–Iran peace deal. Its first clause calls for the “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon,” but neither Israel nor Hezbollah is a signatory, leaving implementation of a Lebanon ceasefire unclear. The article says Israel has repeatedly stated it will not withdraw from Lebanon; despite a 10-day Israel–Lebanon ceasefire announced on April 16 to allow talks on a more permanent agreement, Israeli attacks and advances continued. Iran has repeatedly made an end to Israeli operations in Lebanon a prerequisite for a broader peace deal. Neither side had released a physical copy of the US–Iran memorandum, and Iranian officials had not confirmed the US account of its text.

evidence.title: Jeffrey Sachs: US-Iran Deal Reached – Peace or Tactical Pause? (Transcript) - singjupost.com
evidence.text: The article says the U.S. and Iran are expected to sign a memorandum of understanding on Friday for an extended 60-day cease-fire and further negotiations. A senior U.S. official says either side can walk away until there is a binding final deal. The proposed MOU calls for ending military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, and for the U.S., Iran, and their allies in the current war not to initiate further attacks. It calls for a U.S.–Iran final deal within 60 days, extendable by mutual consent, addressing sanctions, Iran’s nuclear program, and a reconstruction plan of at least $300 billion. Israel is not named as a signatory, and the article does not report a permanent Israel–Iran peace deal or establish that one will be reached by July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: US and Iran agree deal to end war as Trump says Strait of Hormuz to reopen - BBC
evidence.text: Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a U.S.–Iran peace agreement, with a signing scheduled for 19 June in Switzerland. He said it would bring an immediate, permanent end to military actions, including in Lebanon, but the article also describes further negotiations during a proposed 60-day ceasefire and says Iranian officials had not confirmed the deal. It does not report Israel as a party to the agreement or confirm an Israel–Iran peace deal. U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran since late February had effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz and raised global energy prices; Trump said the strait would reopen and the U.S. naval blockade would be removed. An Israeli airstrike in Beirut targeting Iranian-backed Hezbollah had threatened the negotiations.

evidence.title: Can Washington force Israel to comply with a U.S.-Iranian deal it rejects? - CBC
evidence.text: The U.S. and Iran reached an initial memorandum of understanding on Sunday, ahead of a planned formal signing in Switzerland on Friday. It is intended to extend a ceasefire and help end the war, but its text had not been released, further negotiations were expected, and an analyst cautioned that it was a limited framework rather than a full settlement. Although Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran from an aligned position, Israel is not party to the U.S.–Iran deal. Netanyahu said he did not always share Trump’s views, did not yet know what the agreement would contain, and remained responsible for Israel’s security. He also said Israel’s campaign against Iran and its regional allies was not over. The article does not report an Israel–Iran permanent peace agreement.

evidence.title: US, Iran reach ‘peace deal’; signing set for Friday - The New Region
evidence.text: Trump announced a tentative US–Iran agreement, the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, aimed at ending Middle East hostilities and reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The article says it was expected to be signed on Friday in Switzerland, but its terms had not been released. Iran’s foreign minister said it could end hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon; a UN spokesman described it as providing for an immediate and permanent ceasefire and further negotiations. A 60-day period of talks on sanctions, Iran’s nuclear programme and regional security was expected after it took effect. The article does not report an Israel–Iran permanent peace deal. Israel was continuing military operations in Lebanon, and Iran called Israeli strikes on Beirut on June 14 a breach of an April 8 US–Iran ceasefire understanding.

evidence.title: Lebanon ceasefire, Hormuz reopening, sanctions relief: What the 14-point US-Iran peace deal contains - The Times of India
evidence.text: Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced that the US and Iran had reached a comprehensive peace agreement declaring an immediate, permanent end to military operations across all fronts, including Lebanon. He said a signing ceremony was scheduled for June 19 in Switzerland, with implementation talks beforehand. US President Donald Trump said the deal was complete. The article says the war began on February 28, when the US and Israel launched military action against Iran, prompting Iranian retaliation against American allies in the Gulf. It does not say Israel is a party to the agreement or that Israel and Iran have signed a permanent peace deal.

market.question: Israel x Iran permanent peace deal by July 31, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if Israel and Iran agree to a permanent peace deal by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A permanent peace deal refers to any agreement which explicitly indicates that military hostilities between Israel and Iran have ended or will permanently cease, or uses equivalent language clearly signaling a lasting end to military hostilities between Israel and Iran. Agreements that are explicitly temporary or which do not include a definitive agreement to end military hostilities between Israel and Iran on a lasting basis (e.g. a temporary extension of a previously announced ceasefire agreement), will not qualify.

A qualifying agreement will be considered to have been established if either of the following conditions are met:

- Israel and Iran each sign or formally adopt a written agreement (e.g. a treaty or multi-point agreement) which meets the above criteria.

- Both Israel and Iran provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The inclusion of Israel and Iran in a qualifying peace deal between multiple parties will qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the governments of Israel and Iran; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

evidence.title: US and Iran pause strikes for third night to make space for talks, US ambassador says - BBC
evidence.text: The article says a US-Israeli war with Iran began in February. Iran and the US signed a memorandum of understanding in June to halt military operations, reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and reach an agreement to end the war within 60 days. The article does not say Israel signed it. The ceasefire effectively unraveled after Iranian forces attacked tankers in the strait on 13 July; the US resumed airstrikes and a naval blockade, and Iran attacked US facilities. After 13 consecutive nights of US strikes, both sides paused attacks to allow talks, but the US ambassador said Trump was keeping all options on the table. Disputes over the strait remained a major obstacle to permanently ending the war.

evidence.title: Analysis: The Israel-Lebanon framework agreement explained - The Long War Journal
evidence.text: A mid-June interim deal aimed to permanently end the war and gave negotiators 60 days to reach a final accord addressing Iran’s disputed nuclear program and other issues. Almost halfway through that period, talks had stalled and exchanges of fire had cast doubt on the deal. The U.S. reimposed its blockade of Iranian ports after Iranian attacks on commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, while regional mediators were trying to restart U.S.–Iran negotiations. Israel’s fighting with Hezbollah in Lebanon had also threatened the interim deal; a separate Israel–Lebanon framework agreement had stalled in implementation. The article reports no permanent Israel–Iran peace deal and gives no final-accord deadline specifically tied to July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: Operationalizing the Trilateral Framework Agreement - Middle East Institute
evidence.text: The article says an interim U.S.–Iran memorandum, covering their allies in the war, was meant to end military operations on all fronts and reopen the Strait of Hormuz. It called for negotiations toward a permanent peace deal and an agreement on Iran’s nuclear program within 60 days. But the interim deal collapsed less than a month after signing: U.S. airstrikes on Iran and Iranian attacks in the region resumed, amid a dispute over passage through the strait. Negotiations were apparently paused, and the article says it is unclear whether they resumed or made progress. It places the 60-day deadline in mid-August—after July 31, 2026. The proposed final deal is between the U.S. and Iran; the article does not report a permanent Israel–Iran peace agreement.

evidence.title: US informs Israel of plans to intensify attacks on Iran - The Express Tribune
evidence.text: The article reports that the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17, agreeing to a 60-day ceasefire on all fronts, including Lebanon, while negotiating a lasting peace deal. This was a US–Iran arrangement, not a reported permanent Israel–Iran peace deal. Talks on issues including the Strait of Hormuz, sanctions and Iran’s nuclear programme were delayed as Israel continued attacks in southern Lebanon. The article says Israel continued attacks for the first few days after the MoU was signed, and Iran later accused the US of failing to stop them. After renewed US–Iran strikes in early July, Trump said he thought the MoU was “over,” though he allowed talks to continue; a US official said Washington remained committed to negotiations. Talks expected to resume around July 11 had become uncertain. No permanent peace deal is reported.

evidence.title: US waives Iran sanctions after talks; Lebanon fighting abates - Reuters
evidence.text: As of June 21, 2026, the US and Iran had signed an initial agreement to end their war and were holding talks on a final deal. The document calls for an “immediate and permanent” end to military operations on “all fronts,” including Lebanon, and says a final agreement will permanently “terminate” the conflict. The article says it is unclear how Israel will react; it does not say Israel signed the agreement. Israel has described its conflict with the Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon as separate, and deadly clashes continued despite a ceasefire. The US and Iran aim to reach a final deal within 60 days of signing the initial agreement, but may extend that period by mutual consent. Key issues, including Iran’s nuclear programme, remain unresolved.

evidence.title: Iran says it is closing Strait of Hormuz, testing fragile agreement with U.S. - The Washington Post
evidence.text: A U.S.–Iran interim memorandum signed on Wednesday calls for the “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon,” between the two countries and their allies. It says a *final deal* will confirm the permanent end of the war on all fronts, including Lebanon; the article does not say such a final deal has been reached or that Israel signed the memorandum. Israeli attacks in Lebanon continued after the signing. The article says more than 4,000 people have been killed there since Israel’s offensive began on March 2, and that the strikes prompted Iran to postpone U.S. talks planned for Friday in Switzerland. After further attacks despite another declared ceasefire, Iran announced it was closing the Strait of Hormuz again. Analysts describe the continuing Israel–Hezbollah conflict as a threat to the U.S.–Iran agreement; Israeli withdrawal and Hezbollah’s disarmament remain unresolved.

evidence.title: Lebanon emerges as the ultimate test of the U.S.-Iran memorandum - ArabAmericanNews
evidence.text: After weeks of talks mediated mainly by Pakistan, the U.S. and Iran signed an initial agreement to end their war and begin a 60-day negotiation, extendable by mutual consent, toward a final accord. The article says they agreed to end hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon, but also says even a permanent end to the war is partly contingent on a final accord. This is a U.S.–Iran agreement, not an Israel–Iran peace deal. Israel was kept outside the talks and away from the text; across Israel’s political spectrum, the agreement is viewed as a bad bargain. Iran’s effort to include Lebanon would constrain Israeli operations against Hezbollah, while Iran’s missile program and support for regional proxies were left out. Major nuclear and sanctions questions remain unresolved, and Iranian officials distrust the U.S. after American-Israeli attacks launched during earlier negotiations.

evidence.title: Lebanon says Israeli strikes kill 47 as Israel says four soldiers killed by Hezbollah - BBC
evidence.text:
The article says the US and Iran signed a deal aimed at ending the Middle East conflict. It calls for an end to hostilities on all fronts, respect for Lebanon’s territorial integrity and sovereignty, and provisions on Iran’s nuclear programme and sanctions relief. The US and Iran committed to pursuing a final settlement within 60 days, extendable by mutual agreement. The article does not say Israel and Iran signed a permanent peace deal.

Fighting continued after the deal was announced: Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah exchanged strikes, and Lebanon reported at least 47 people killed in Israeli air strikes. A US official later confirmed an immediate Israel–Hezbollah ceasefire, which the Israeli military also acknowledged. Israel had said it did not intend to withdraw from Lebanon and regarded its conflict with Hezbollah as separate from the war on Iran. US officials said withdrawal was not a condition of the ceasefire framework and Israel retained a right to self-defence. A scheduled round of direct talks on the US–Iran deal was delayed. These facts show a framework and a stated goal of a final settlement, not a completed permanent Israel–Iran peace agreement.

evidence.title: US releases official agreement with Iran. Read the 14-point text - CNN
evidence.text: NPR says it obtained a preliminary memorandum of understanding signed on a Wednesday by President Trump, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Pakistan’s prime minister; Pakistan mediated between the U.S. and Iran. The text says the U.S., Iran and their allies in the current war declare an immediate, permanent end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, and pledge not to initiate operations against one another. It calls for a final deal confirming that termination, to be negotiated within 60 days unless extended by mutual consent and endorsed by a binding U.N. Security Council resolution. Israel is not named as a signatory, and the article does not report a completed Israel–Iran peace deal. The agreement’s date field is incomplete, showing only ‘2026.’

evidence.title: Israel and Hezbollah agree to ceasefire after fighting postpones Iran-United States peace talks - News On AIR
evidence.text: The article reports that Iran and the U.S. signed a memorandum of understanding during the week of June 19, 2026, intended to end the Iran war, halt fighting in Lebanon, and begin 60 days of talks on wider issues, including Iran’s nuclear program. According to deal text read by a senior U.S. official—but not seen directly by CBS News—it calls for the “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon,” a commitment not to initiate war or military operations against each other, restraint from threats or force, and respect for Lebanon’s territorial integrity and sovereignty. The article does not report a separate Israel–Iran peace deal. The agreement’s durability was already in doubt: Israel continued strikes in southern Lebanon, where its military reported four soldiers killed and Lebanon’s state news agency reported at least 16 people killed in Israeli airstrikes. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israeli forces would not withdraw from southern Lebanon while Israel’s security needs required them to remain; Hezbollah said their continued presence would breach the agreement. Planned Iran–U.S. follow-up talks in Switzerland were postponed, with no new date announced.

evidence.title: 19 Big Questions About Trump’s (Now Real) Iran Deal - New York Magazine
evidence.text: The article says the US released a 14-point memorandum of understanding (MOU) with Iran to end the current war. Point 1 says the US, Iran and their allies in that war, by signing the MOU, declare an immediate and permanent end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, and pledge not to initiate war or use or threaten force against each other. It says a final deal will confirm that termination. The US and Iran commit to negotiating a final deal within 60 days, extendable by mutual consent, with endorsement by a binding UN Security Council resolution. Israel is not named in the quoted provision, and the article describes an MOU and a planned final deal—not a completed Israel–Iran peace deal.

evidence.title: Trump says ceasefire with Iran is 'over' as NATO summit wraps - NPR
evidence.text: An April truce and a June 14 US–Iran memorandum were intended to start at least 60 days of phased talks, ending in an agreement on Iran’s nuclear programme and a permanent end to hostilities, including a ceasefire in Lebanon. That timetable extends beyond July 31. Israel’s withdrawal from southern Lebanon is described as a key Iranian demand; Trump said he believed it could still happen. But renewed US–Iran strikes and attacks on commercial ships have put the ceasefire in jeopardy. Trump said he thought it was over and called talks a waste of time, though he later said he did not expect a long conflict. The article describes a proposed broader settlement, not an agreed Israel–Iran peace deal.

evidence.title: Iran, Israel voice caveats on deal ahead of expected signing ceremony - CBS News
evidence.text: The article says the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on Sunday declaring an immediate and permanent end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon. It says a final deal would confirm that permanent termination and require respect for Lebanon’s sovereignty, implying an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon. But the article distinguishes the signed MOU from a future final deal and reports Israeli objections: Defense Minister Katz said Israel would not leave its security zones, Prime Minister Netanyahu called it “Trump’s decision,” and Israel launched fresh attacks on Hezbollah targets on Wednesday. The article gives no calendar date for the signing or expected final deal.

evidence.title: What's in the deal between the US and Iran? - BBC
evidence.text: A White House official told the BBC that a US–Iran memorandum of understanding extending their ceasefire has been signed and is in effect; the White House says President Donald Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed it. Its first paragraph says the US, Iran and allies will declare an “immediate and permanent” end to military operations on “all fronts,” including Lebanon. It also says neither side will initiate or threaten military operations and calls for respect for Lebanon’s sovereignty. Iran has said continued Israeli operations in Lebanon would violate the understanding, while the article says Israel’s reaction to this provision is unclear. The memorandum calls for a final deal that would permanently end the conflict, but US–Iran negotiations for that deal are only beginning, with a 60-day target that can be extended. The article does not report a signed Israel–Iran permanent peace deal.

evidence.title: Read the Full Text of the 14-Point Agreement Between the U.S. and Iran - Time Magazine
evidence.text: Presidents Trump and Masoud Pezeshkian signed a U.S.–Iran memorandum of understanding on Wednesday, opening a 60-day period of direct negotiations on a final agreement to end the war; talks were expected to begin Friday, and the deadline can be extended by mutual consent. The MOU declares an immediate, permanent end to military operations by the U.S., Iran and their allies on all fronts, including Lebanon, but says a final deal would confirm that termination. Nuclear issues, sanctions relief and other terms remain to be negotiated. Israel is not named as a signatory, and the article does not report a signed Israel–Iran peace deal or give a date establishing whether a final deal would be reached by July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: US launches new strikes against Iran in retaliation for attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz - EL PAÍS English
evidence.text: The article reports that the U.S. and Iran traded attacks overnight Wednesday, their second escalation since signing an interim deal in mid-June. Iran had attacked three commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday; the U.S. said it struck Iranian targets in retaliation, and Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said it responded with missiles and drones against Kuwait and Bahrain. President Trump said he believed the U.S.–Iran ceasefire was over, though he did not rule out further talks to end the war permanently. The article describes no permanent peace deal between Israel and Iran; its reported interim agreement was between the U.S. and Iran.

evidence.title: Trump Says Interim Accord to End Iran War Is ‘Over,’ Warns of New US Strikes - The Daily Signal
evidence.text: On July 8, US President Donald Trump said he considered the interim agreement to end the war with Iran “over” and did not want to deal with Tehran. The article says renewed US-Iran attacks undermined a shaky ceasefire and diminished hopes of turning a June 17 memorandum of understanding into a permanent peace deal. It says the war began with US-Israeli airstrikes on Iran on February 28. Iran reported attacks on US military sites in Bahrain and Kuwait after US strikes on Iranian targets; both sides accused the other of breaching the ceasefire. An Iranian negotiator also cited Israeli attacks against Lebanon. The article discusses a prospective US-Iran peace deal, not a separate Israel-Iran agreement, and reports no permanent deal.

evidence.title: Cease-Fire Deal Appears Within Reach, Officials Say - The New York Times
evidence.text: Trump said the US had reached a memorandum of understanding with Iran to end the war launched by the US and Israel more than 100 days earlier; Iranian parliamentary speaker Mohammad Baqer Qalibaf is believed to have signed for Iran. Pakistan’s prime minister said both sides declared an immediate and permanent end to military operations. But the article explicitly says **Israel is not a party** to the deal, nor are Lebanon or Hezbollah. Iran’s published terms call for a permanent cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon, while US officials said Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon was not a condition and Israel retained the right to defend itself against Hezbollah. Israel and Hezbollah continued exchanging strikes despite a Lebanon ceasefire in place since April 16 and renewed in June; Israel also struck alleged Hezbollah targets after the new deal was announced. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israeli forces would remain in security zones in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza indefinitely. The MOU envisages 60 days of negotiations toward a final US–Iran agreement, rather than itself establishing a permanent Israel–Iran peace deal.

evidence.title: US, Iran to sign a ‘peace deal’ on Friday: What we know - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: The article says the US and Iran have reached an understanding on a peace deal and plan to sign a formal document in Geneva on June 19, 2026. Details of the proposed 14-point agreement are not yet known. Crucially for an Israel–Iran deal by July 31, Israel has made clear it is not a party to the US–Iran agreement. The article says it is unclear whether the agreement will address Iran’s proxies, including Hezbollah, Hamas and the Houthis. Israeli Defence Minister Katz said Israel intends to keep the IDF in security zones in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza indefinitely. The writer argues that the US–Iran deal could ease hostilities but doubts it would bring permanent regional peace.

evidence.title: Trump says interim accord to end war is ‘over’ after Iranian strikes - The Business Times
evidence.text: The article describes a June interim agreement between the US and Iran, not an Israel–Iran peace deal. It called for an “immediate and permanent” halt to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, for 60 days. On July 8, 2026, President Donald Trump said the interim accord was “over” as US strikes on Iran resumed, though the article says negotiations still appeared to be ongoing. It reports no permanent Israel–Iran agreement.

evidence.title: Will Israel use Lebanon to derail US-Iran peace process? - Anadolu Ajansı
evidence.text: The article says the U.S. and Iran signed an interim memorandum of understanding on Wednesday and agreed to at least 60 more days of negotiations; a substantive final peace deal has not been reached. The MOU says the U.S., Iran and their allies in the current war declare an immediate and permanent end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, and that a final deal will confirm the permanent termination of the war on all fronts. The article notes that neither Israel nor Hezbollah is named in that provision. It says Israel has signaled it is not on board, has said it will not withdraw its forces from Lebanon, and has continued bombing targets there during the cease-fire. The article also says major issues, including Iran’s nuclear program, remain unresolved and that the 60-day negotiating period can be extended.

evidence.title: US and Iran agree to 'immediate' end of military operations in memorandum of understanding - France 24
evidence.text: Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said Sunday that both sides had declared an “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon.” The article identifies the agreement as a preliminary US–Iran memorandum mediated by Pakistan, not an Israel–Iran peace deal. Mediators were to meet ahead of a Friday signing in Switzerland, with further negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme and US sanctions planned for the following 60 days. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said operations would stop permanently on Monday night, including in Lebanon. But Israel’s defence minister said Monday that Israeli forces would remain “indefinitely” in areas captured in Lebanon, Syria and Gaza, while Iran’s foreign minister called for a complete halt to Israeli attacks on Lebanon. The article does not report a signed permanent peace deal between Israel and Iran.

evidence.title: Iran says the deal to end the war with the U.S. requires Israel to withdraw from Lebanon - PBS
evidence.text: As of June 16, 2026, the U.S. and Iran had agreed to a memorandum of understanding to extend their ceasefire and pursue further talks, not a permanent Israel–Iran peace deal. Vice President JD Vance called the roughly page-and-a-half document “very general”; it leaves major issues for a 60-day negotiation window, which extends beyond July 31. Israel’s presence in Lebanon remains a major obstacle. Iran insists that any agreement ending the conflict include an end to the fighting there, while a spokesperson for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel would continue defending itself against security threats. A senior U.S. official said Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon is not a condition of the memorandum and that Israel could respond if Hezbollah attacks Israeli positions or towns.

evidence.title: Iran updates: Netanyahu refrains from criticizing Iran deal - DW.com
evidence.text: Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a US–Iran deal on Sunday and said both sides had declared an “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts,” including Lebanon. Trump said Monday that the pact was “all signed”; US officials said Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf had signed it electronically. The pact extends a ceasefire for 60 days while the sides negotiate details of a final agreement, with an official signing ceremony planned in Geneva later that week. The article does not report a final, permanent Israel–Iran peace agreement or Israeli participation in the pact. Israeli politicians objected: Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel would strike Iran “with full force” if attacked over events in Lebanon, and National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir said Trump’s agreement did not bind Israel. The article says occasional fire had continued between Iran and Israel and the US since their April 8 ceasefire.

evidence.title: Iran, US agree to halt war and reopen Hormuz, sending oil prices tumbling - The Express Tribune
evidence.text: Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said it finalized the text of a US–Iran memorandum on June 14 and claimed that, under the agreements reached, war and military operations “on all fronts, including Lebanon” would end immediately and permanently that night. It said the memorandum would be signed on June 19 in Switzerland. The text has not been officially published by either government, and the article describes it as a framework for further negotiations, not a final settlement. A reported 60-day process would address unresolved nuclear issues and broader sanctions relief, but Iran says final talks will begin only after the US meets commitments on frozen funds, oil sanctions and the naval blockade. The reported agreement is between Iran and the US; the article does not report an Israel–Iran peace deal.

evidence.title: US-Iran Deal Raises Hopes for Regional Peace Despite Israeli Pushback - Morocco World News
evidence.text: The article reports that the United States and Iran agreed to an “immediate and permanent” end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, with a signing scheduled for June 19 in Switzerland. Pakistan’s prime minister announced the halt, and Washington and Tehran confirmed the deal. Iran’s deputy foreign minister said the two countries would hold talks within two months toward a “final agreement”; the agreement’s details remained unclear. The article does not report Israel agreeing to or signing a permanent peace deal with Iran. Trump said an Israeli airstrike on Hezbollah in Beirut’s suburbs had delayed the signing and said he had angrily confronted Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. Tehran had threatened retaliation, and the article says an earlier Israeli strike near Beirut had prompted Iranian missiles and Israeli counterstrikes despite a ceasefire that had largely held since April. Iran has insisted that any agreement to halt the war include Lebanon.

evidence.title: U.S. and Iran Reach Framework for Peace - The New York Times
evidence.text: Iran and the US agreed to a memorandum of understanding after more than 100 days of war that began with US and Israeli attacks on Iran on February 28. Iran’s Supreme National Security Council said on Monday that the deal would end war and military operations “immediately and permanently” on all fronts, including Lebanon, as of that night, and immediately end the naval blockade against Iran. Pakistan’s prime minister likewise said the parties had agreed to a permanent termination of military operations on all fronts. The US-Iran memorandum was scheduled for signing in Geneva on June 19. Iran said negotiations on a final agreement would follow only after US obligations were fulfilled. The article does not report an Israel-Iran peace agreement or identify Israel as a party to the memorandum.

evidence.title: Trump announces peace deal with Iran, opening of Hormuz Strait - WorldCargo News
evidence.text: The article reports that the United States and Iran agreed to a memorandum of understanding calling for an “immediate and permanent” end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon. Mediator Pakistan announced it on Sunday; Washington and Tehran confirmed it, with a signing ceremony scheduled for June 19 in Switzerland. Iran’s deputy foreign minister said the countries would hold talks within two months to seek a “final agreement,” and the article says the memorandum’s details remained unclear. This is a US–Iran agreement, not a reported permanent peace deal between Israel and Iran. Israel’s strike against Iran-backed Hezbollah near Beirut had threatened to delay the agreement; an earlier Israeli strike there had prompted Iranian missiles and Israeli counterstrikes despite a ceasefire that had largely held since April. Iran had demanded that any agreement to halt the war include the conflict in Lebanon.

evidence.title: Day 129 of US-Israel War on Iran: ‘We Have No Peace With the US, Won’t Recognise Israel’, Says Iran - TheWire.in
evidence.text: The article reports that Iran’s slain Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was to be buried on July 9 after a two-day public farewell. His son and successor, Mojtaba Khamenei, did not appear at the funeral prayers because of fears of an Israeli assassination attempt. The article’s title says Iran “won’t recognise Israel.” It reports no Israel–Iran peace agreement or negotiations.

evidence.title: No lasting peace without resolving the Palestinian cause: Sisi sends firm message to Israel - Egypt Independent
evidence.text: The article reports that Iran and the US signed an initial deal last month to halt hostilities, allowing commercial ships to transit the Strait of Hormuz free of charge for 60 days. Negotiations on a permanent settlement are ongoing, but the US says Iran cannot charge transit tolls or fees under a final agreement. Iran’s ambassador to China, Abdolreza Rahmani Fazli, says Iran will charge “service fees,” with special considerations for China and other friendly countries. The article says the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in late February, but reports no permanent Israel–Iran peace deal or agreement to reach one by July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: Here’s What to Know About U.S.-Iran Peace Talks - The New York Times
evidence.text: The article reports that the United States and Iran—not Israel and Iran—signed a 60-day memorandum of understanding on June 17, 2026. It formally halted hostilities, reopened the Strait of Hormuz and began 60 days of negotiations over Iran’s nuclear programme. The memorandum seeks a permanent end to military operations involving both countries and their allies, including in Lebanon, but it is not a permanent Israel-Iran peace deal. Subsequent indirect U.S.-Iran talks in Doha showed no reported breakthrough toward a permanent agreement. Iran says any deal must include Lebanon’s safety from Israeli attacks; the article says Israel has continued attacking Lebanon. A separate U.S.-Israel-Lebanon framework links Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon to Hezbollah’s disarmament, but Hezbollah has rejected its conditions.

evidence.title: Vance vs. Rubio: Iran Edition - The Atlantic
evidence.text: On 17 June, the US and Iran signed a 14-point Memorandum of Understanding calling for an “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts.” The article does not report an Israel–Iran peace deal; it says talks on a deal to permanently end the war would continue. The ceasefire was under threat less than two weeks after it was agreed: an Iranian projectile hit a cargo ship in the Strait of Hormuz, the US struck targets in Iran, and Iran struck at US bases in Kuwait and Bahrain. Tehran says fighting in Lebanon must stop for a wider ceasefire deal to stick. The article separately reports a US-mediated framework agreement between Israel and Lebanon, not Israel and Iran.

evidence.title: Global shares ease as investors ponder U.S.-Iran peace talks; yen nears 40-year lows - bnnbloomberg.ca
evidence.text: The article reports an interim agreement aimed at ending the war in Iran, but says an escalation in fighting in Lebanon jeopardized its chances of becoming a lasting Middle East peace deal. Israel and Hezbollah agreed to a ceasefire in Lebanon on Friday, according to a U.S. official. U.S.-Iranian peace talks were called off after U.S. Vice President JD Vance withdrew from a planned Friday meeting with Iranian negotiators in Switzerland. The article does not report a permanent Israel-Iran peace deal or give a date for one.

evidence.title: A Look at the Text of the Agreement Between the United States and Iran - The New York Times
evidence.text: The article reports an interim U.S.–Iran accord, reached days before the renewed fighting, that calls for a permanent halt to military operations by the parties and their allies, including in Lebanon. It does not report an Israel–Iran peace deal or a final settlement. The article says the accord may have reduced the risk of direct U.S.–Iran confrontation but has not resolved conflicts involving Israel and the Iran-backed group Hezbollah. Fighting resumed after a brief lull: Israel confirmed four soldiers killed in Lebanon, and Lebanese authorities reported at least 18 people killed and 33 wounded in Israeli strikes on 11 towns. Israel and Hezbollah each accuse the other of violating the ceasefire, and the article says there is no agreed mechanism to enforce it or settle such disputes. Some Israeli ministers criticize the accord as insufficient for Israel’s security, while continued fighting could undermine negotiations before a final settlement begins. The article gives no date for an Israel–Iran permanent deal by July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: What’s in the US-Iran deal? 14 key provisions revealed - Gulf Business
evidence.text: The article describes a 14-point memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran, not an Israel–Iran peace deal. Its first clause calls for the “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon,” but neither Israel nor Hezbollah is a signatory, leaving implementation of a Lebanon ceasefire unclear. The article says Israel has repeatedly stated it will not withdraw from Lebanon; despite a 10-day Israel–Lebanon ceasefire announced on April 16 to allow talks on a more permanent agreement, Israeli attacks and advances continued. Iran has repeatedly made an end to Israeli operations in Lebanon a prerequisite for a broader peace deal. Neither side had released a physical copy of the US–Iran memorandum, and Iranian officials had not confirmed the US account of its text.

evidence.title: Jeffrey Sachs: US-Iran Deal Reached – Peace or Tactical Pause? (Transcript) - singjupost.com

A senior U.S. official says either side can walk away until there is a binding final deal. The proposed MOU calls for ending military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, and for the U.S., Iran, and their allies in the current war not to initiate further attacks. It calls for a U.S.–Iran final deal within 60 days, extendable by mutual consent, addressing sanctions, Iran’s nuclear program, and a reconstruction plan of at least $300 billion. Israel is not named as a signatory, and the article does not report a permanent Israel–Iran peace deal or establish that one will be reached by July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: US and Iran agree deal to end war as Trump says Strait of Hormuz to reopen - BBC
evidence.text: Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a U.S.–Iran peace agreement, with a signing scheduled for 19 June in Switzerland. He said it would bring an immediate, permanent end to military actions, including in Lebanon, but the article also describes further negotiations during a proposed 60-day ceasefire and says Iranian officials had not confirmed the deal. It does not report Israel as a party to the agreement or confirm an Israel–Iran peace deal. U.S. and Israeli strikes against Iran since late February had effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz and raised global energy prices; Trump said the strait would reopen and the U.S. naval blockade would be removed. An Israeli airstrike in Beirut targeting Iranian-backed Hezbollah had threatened the negotiations.

evidence.title: Can Washington force Israel to comply with a U.S.-Iranian deal it rejects? - CBC
evidence.text: The U.S. and Iran reached an initial memorandum of understanding on Sunday, ahead of a planned formal signing in Switzerland on Friday. It is intended to extend a ceasefire and help end the war, but its text had not been released, further negotiations were expected, and an analyst cautioned that it was a limited framework rather than a full settlement. Although Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and U.S. President Donald Trump launched the war against Iran from an aligned position, Israel is not party to the U.S.–Iran deal. Netanyahu said he did not always share Trump’s views, did not yet know what the agreement would contain, and remained responsible for Israel’s security. He also said Israel’s campaign against Iran and its regional allies was not over. The article does not report an Israel–Iran permanent peace agreement.

evidence.title: US, Iran reach ‘peace deal’; signing set for Friday - The New Region
evidence.text: Trump announced a tentative US–Iran agreement, the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding, aimed at ending Middle East hostilities and reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The article says it was expected to be signed on Friday in Switzerland, but its terms had not been released. Iran’s foreign minister said it could end hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon; a UN spokesman described it as providing for an immediate and permanent ceasefire and further negotiations. A 60-day period of talks on sanctions, Iran’s nuclear programme and regional security was expected after it took effect. The article does not report an Israel–Iran permanent peace deal. Israel was continuing military operations in Lebanon, and Iran called Israeli strikes on Beirut on June 14 a breach of an April 8 US–Iran ceasefire understanding.

evidence.title: Lebanon ceasefire, Hormuz reopening, sanctions relief: What the 14-point US-Iran peace deal contains - The Times of India

He said a signing ceremony was scheduled for June 19 in Switzerland, with implementation talks beforehand. US President Donald Trump said the deal was complete. The article says the war began on February 28, when the US and Israel launched military action against Iran, prompting Iranian retaliation against American allies in the Gulf. It does not say Israel is a party to the agreement or that Israel and Iran have signed a permanent peace deal.

market.question: US x Iran permanent peace deal by December 31, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if Iran and the United states agree to a permanent peace deal by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”. 

A permanent peace deal refers to any agreement which explicitly indicates that military hostilities between the United States and Iran have ended or will permanently cease, or uses equivalent language clearly signaling a lasting end to military hostilities between the United States and Iran. Agreements that are explicitly temporary or which do not include a definitive agreement to end military hostilities between the US and Iran on a lasting basis (e.g. a temporary extension of the two-week ceasefire agreement announced on April 7, 2026), will not qualify.

A qualifying agreement will be considered to have been established if either of the following conditions are met:

- The United States and Iran each sign or formally adopt a written agreement (e.g. a treaty or multi-point agreement) which meets the above criteria.

- Both the governments of the United States and Iran provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the governments of the United States and Iran; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

evidence.title: UAE joins Saudi Arabia, Qatar in urging Trump not to restart Iran war - straitstimes.com
evidence.text: The US and Iran agreed to a truce on April 8 and are exchanging messages through Pakistan about a possible peace deal, but both say they are prepared to resume hostilities if talks fail. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio reported “slight progress,” and Iranian media indicated movement toward an agreement. Pakistan’s army chief was expected to visit Iran as talks continued. The UAE, Saudi Arabia and Qatar have urged President Trump to give diplomacy a chance rather than restart military action. Obstacles remain: the Gulf states differ over the terms of an agreement, and the UAE says any deal must address Iran’s nuclear programme, ballistic missiles, drones and affiliated groups. A senior UAE adviser put the chance of an agreement at “50-50.” The article reports no permanent peace deal.

evidence.title: Trump says Iran attack on ‘hold’: What we know about latest negotiations - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: The article says U.S. attacks on Iranian targets began on February 28, 2026, and that hostilities continued despite official statements that they had ended. President Trump said in March, “We’ve won”; on May 2 he told Congress the hostilities had terminated; and Secretary of State Marco Rubio said three days later that Operation Epic Fury was over. By contrast, a State Department legal adviser described it on April 21 as the latest round of an ongoing armed conflict. CENTCOM reported Iranian attacks on ships protected by the U.S., a May 6 U.S. strike disabling an Iranian-flagged tanker, and a May 7 exchange in which Iranian forces attacked three U.S. warships and U.S. forces struck Iranian military facilities. U.S. aircraft disabled two more Iranian-flagged vessels the following day. Trump said the ceasefire remained in place, while the article says the continuing exchanges and U.S. blockade mean the conflict continues regardless of officials’ statements. It reports no permanent peace deal.

evidence.title: US-Iran diplomacy picks up: What’s the latest? - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: A permanent U.S.–Iran peace deal had not been reached. A cease-fire took effect on April 8 but appeared shaky after President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s counterproposal to a U.S. framework for longer-lasting peace. On Monday, Iran submitted a revised 14-point proposal to Pakistani mediators, according to Iranian state-linked media; it was unclear whether it resolved differences over Iran’s nuclear program and the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state media said Iran sought U.S. sanctions relief, continued control of the Strait, and an end to Israeli hostilities in Lebanon. The U.S. reportedly wanted major nuclear concessions, including Iran’s enriched uranium stockpile. Trump said he cancelled strikes planned for Tuesday because serious negotiations were under way, but warned that a large-scale assault could proceed if no acceptable deal was reached.

evidence.title: UAE spooked? Fearing Gulf chaos, Abu Dhabi joins Saudis, Qatar in urging Trump against fresh Iran war - The Times of India
evidence.text: The article says the US and Israel attacked Iran in late February and that, as of 22 May, the war was entering its third month. It reports no peace agreement; references to a lasting deal or the conflict ending are hypothetical. Rising gasoline prices and inflation have angered US drivers and, according to the article, contributed to a historic backlash against Donald Trump in the polls. National gasoline averaged $4.55 on 22 May, about $1.50 above its prewar level. Trump said prices would fall rapidly when the war ends, but energy experts said damaged infrastructure, disrupted supply chains and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz could delay a return to prewar prices even if peace were declared immediately.

evidence.title: Trump says he does not need China's help to end Iran war, Tehran tightens grip on Hormuz - Reuters
evidence.text: As of May 13, 2026, Reuters reported that more than a month after a tenuous US-Iran ceasefire took effect, the two sides had made no progress toward an agreement to end hostilities. The US was demanding an end to Iran’s nuclear programme and its chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz. Iran was demanding compensation for war damage, an end to the US blockade, and an end to the war on all fronts, including Lebanon. President Donald Trump dismissed Iran’s positions as “garbage” on May 11. Although Trump was expected to discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping that week, he said on May 12 that he did not think he needed China’s help to end it.

evidence.title: Trump warns Iran 'will be laughing no longer' amid talks over peace proposal - The New Indian Express
evidence.text:
President Donald Trump rejected Iran’s response to the latest U.S. peace proposal and said Monday that the cease-fire was on “massive life support.” He called Tehran’s response weak and “unacceptable,” though he did not publicly identify the provisions he rejected. According to Iran’s Tasnim news agency, Tehran sought a permanent end to the war on all fronts, compensation for war damage, an end to the U.S. naval blockade, sanctions relief, permission for Iranian oil sales, and continued control of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran’s Foreign Ministry defended its proposal and said it had been sent through Pakistani intermediaries.

A U.S. framework reportedly offered last week would end fighting and begin 30 days of negotiations toward a comprehensive agreement focused on Iran’s nuclear program. Nuclear material and facilities remain a central dispute: Trump said Iranian officials had indicated they would hand over nuclear material, while Iran has said it will protect its nuclear and missile capabilities. The article describes the fighting as paused but negotiations as deadlocked, with renewed hostilities possible. Iran also wants assurance it will not be attacked after a deal and has tied regional security, including attacks in Lebanon, to its demands.

evidence.title: Iran refuses to address nuclear program in latest peace deal response to US - New York Post
evidence.text: The United States and Iran had not agreed on a peace proposal as of May 10. President Donald Trump called Iran’s response to his framework “totally unacceptable.” Iranian state media said the response sought compensation for war damages and emphasized Iranian sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz. The U.S. proposal would pause fighting and reopen the strait for a month while the sides negotiated a permanent peace plan; the article says it had not gained traction with Iranian negotiators. Earlier peace talks in Islamabad on April 12 also ended without agreement. A fragile, month-old ceasefire was holding despite recent naval clashes and continued restrictions on strait traffic. After the May 10 failure to agree, oil prices jumped about $3 a barrel: Brent rose $3.18 to $104.47, and U.S. West Texas Intermediate rose $3.09 to $98.51.

evidence.title: Donald Trump says Iran has one week to respond to US deal - The Jerusalem Post
evidence.text:
Iran says it is reviewing a US proposal to end the war but has not formally responded. The sides exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, though neither has declared the ceasefire in place since April 8 over. Trump warned of stronger military action if Iran did not quickly agree to a deal.

The reported 14-point US plan would require Iran to forgo nuclear weapons, stop uranium enrichment for at least 12 years and surrender an estimated 440kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent. In return, the US would gradually lift sanctions, release billions in frozen Iranian assets and withdraw its naval blockade; both sides would reopen the Strait within 30 days of signing. Iran’s own recent 14-point proposal sought a permanent end to the war rather than an extended truce, with issues resolved within 30 days, guarantees against future attacks, sanctions relief and an end to hostilities including in Lebanon. Iranian officials call several US demands unrealistic, and a reporter described a ‘huge gap’ between the sides. Reporting from Tehran says Iran currently wants to negotiate an end to the war on all fronts, with nuclear talks only in a second phase after security guarantees and sanctions relief.

evidence.title: Trump says Iran's government is in a "state of collapse," but analysts see evolution, not fractures - CBS News
evidence.text: Pakistani officials said the US and Iran were close to a basic interim agreement, possibly as early as the coming weekend, to halt the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz while negotiations continue. Officials said the gaps between Tehran and Washington made a broader settlement impossible for now, though a one-page temporary arrangement to prevent renewed conflict and secure shipping passage should be obtainable. Weeks of efforts toward a permanent end to hostilities had made little progress. Pakistan, the principal mediator, wants a permanent end to the war announced, with other issues resolved in later direct talks. Under the latest US proposal, a first phase would end the war and reopen the strait; a second would address Iran’s nuclear programme over the following 30 days. At earlier talks, Iran proposed a three-to-five-year enrichment moratorium versus the US demand for 20–25 years; mediators thought roughly 10 years might be possible. Iran also opposed the US demand to hand over its stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium, and experts said Tehran could not accept Trump’s demand to export its highly enriched uranium to the US. Senior Iranian officials had recently rejected concessions, although Pakistani officials remained optimistic about an agreement.

evidence.title: Iran War Updates: Tehran and U.S. Offer Conflicting Messages on State of Negotiations - The New York Times
evidence.text: Axios reported that a proposed one-page, 14-point memorandum is the closest the U.S. and Iran have come to an agreement since the war began on February 28, but no agreement has been finalized. It reportedly calls for an end to hostilities followed by 30 days of negotiations; several key terms would depend on a later comprehensive agreement. Reported terms include lifting both countries’ Strait of Hormuz blockades in exchange for U.S. sanctions relief and a 15-year Iranian moratorium on uranium enrichment. Iran would also transfer its highly enriched uranium stockpile abroad. Pakistan’s foreign minister said the aim was a “permanent end” to the conflict. Trump said Iran had one week to respond, while an Iranian spokesperson said the proposal was being evaluated. Axios also quoted an Iranian official calling it “more of a wishlist than a reality.”

evidence.title: US-Iran talks: Will Trump accept Tehran’s 14-point deal as talks stall? - Gulf News
evidence.text: Iran has sent a 14-point proposal to the United States via Pakistan. It calls for a permanent end to the war within 30 days, guarantees against future US or Israeli attacks, withdrawal of US forces from around Iran, sanctions relief, release of billions of dollars in frozen assets, compensation for war damage, an end to hostilities including in Lebanon, and a new framework for Strait of Hormuz shipping. Tehran wants those steps agreed before substantive nuclear talks; Washington instead demands nuclear limits and verifiable guarantees first. Since an April 8 ceasefire following US-Israeli strikes, the sides have exchanged proposals without a breakthrough. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on Iran’s offer and warned that strikes could resume. The article describes continuing maritime tensions and a US naval blockade, but says neither side appears ready to abandon talks.

evidence.title: Tehran condemns Trump's ‘brazen’ remarks about seizure of Iranian vessels - chinadailyhk
evidence.text:
Iran has submitted a new 14-point proposal to the United States through mediator Pakistan, seeking a permanent end to the war rather than an extension of the ceasefire that began April 8. Iran wants the issues resolved within 30 days. Reported terms include guarantees against future attacks, withdrawal of US forces from around Iran, sanctions relief and release of frozen assets, war reparations, an end to hostilities including in Lebanon, a new Strait of Hormuz mechanism, and recognition of Iran’s right to enrich uranium. The proposal responds to a US-backed nine-point plan focused primarily on a two-month ceasefire.

Trump said he was reviewing the proposal but was unsure a deal was possible; he later said it was difficult to imagine the terms being acceptable. No peace deal has been reached. Major obstacles include disagreement over uranium enrichment and Iran’s nuclear capability, control of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the US blockade of Iranian ports, and Iranian mistrust of the US. One analyst said neither side was likely to abandon negotiations immediately.

evidence.title: US, Iran said closing in on framework for permanent deal, as Trump renews bomb threats - The Times of Israel
evidence.text: The only round of direct US-Iran talks since the war began took place in Islamabad in early April. Those talks ended without an agreement to turn the ceasefire into a wider peace deal.
