market.question: US x Iran permanent peace deal by December 31, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if Iran and the United states agree to a permanent peace deal by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”. 

A permanent peace deal refers to any agreement which explicitly indicates that military hostilities between the United States and Iran have ended or will permanently cease, or uses equivalent language clearly signaling a lasting end to military hostilities between the United States and Iran. Agreements that are explicitly temporary or which do not include a definitive agreement to end military hostilities between the US and Iran on a lasting basis (e.g. a temporary extension of the two-week ceasefire agreement announced on April 7, 2026), will not qualify.

A qualifying agreement will be considered to have been established if either of the following conditions are met:

- The United States and Iran each sign or formally adopt a written agreement (e.g. a treaty or multi-point agreement) which meets the above criteria.

- Both the governments of the United States and Iran provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the governments of the United States and Iran; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

evidence.title: Live updates: House passes resolution to halt military action in Iran in rebuke of Trump - The Washington Post
evidence.text: Trump said on Tuesday that U.S.-Iran peace talks were ongoing despite renewed exchanges of fire and reports that they had stalled over Israeli strikes in Lebanon. He warned Tehran it was time, “one way or another,” to make a deal. In an interview recorded late Tuesday, he claimed Iran had agreed not to obtain a nuclear weapon and said Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei was involved in the talks. But Iran has not officially announced that it will abandon nuclear enrichment, and its Foreign Ministry spokesperson said Monday that no negotiations on the details of the nuclear issue had taken place. Although a cease-fire is in place, the article reports renewed U.S. and Iranian strikes, including attacks affecting Kuwait and Bahrain. It reports no completed peace deal or agreement that would make peace permanent.

evidence.title: There are supposed to be ceasefires across the Middle East, but the fighting is worsening - The Washington Post
evidence.text: As of June 3, 2026, the article says the U.S. and Iran were struggling even to agree on a memorandum that could lead to an indefinite ceasefire and further negotiations. Both had incentives to de-escalate after costly hostilities, but the author argues that turning a memorandum into lasting peace is unlikely. Iranian leaders suspect the U.S. seeks regime change and could use talks as cover for attacks, as they believe happened in June 2025 and February 2026; U.S. policymakers suspect Iran would use talks to preserve its nuclear option and rebuild missile capabilities. Opponents in Washington cite perceived weaknesses in the 2015 nuclear deal, while Iranian hardliners, including in the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, may reject compromises. The article also warns that Israeli military or covert actions could derail diplomacy. It predicts Tehran is unlikely to abandon its nuclear-weapons option and concludes that lasting peace would require changes in both governments’ attitudes for which it sees no near-term signs.

evidence.title: US-Iran talks appear stalled as Trump claims otherwise - DW.com
evidence.text: In its June 2 roundup, DW reports that Lebanon is a key obstacle to a final agreement ending the US war against Iran: Tehran is demanding a permanent ceasefire there. Iranian regime-affiliated agencies Fars and Tasnim reported that US-Iran talks had stopped amid continued fighting in Lebanon, citing a mediator who said Iran had not communicated with the US that Tuesday after demanding a Lebanon ceasefire for negotiations to continue. President Donald Trump disputed the reports, saying conversations were ongoing. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US wanted Israel-Lebanon talks to proceed separately from negotiations with Iran, which Tehran resisted. Rubio also said Iran had agreed to discuss previously excluded nuclear issues, but cautioned that this did not guarantee an acceptable deal.

evidence.title: U.S. House votes to curb Trump's war powers in strongest rebuke yet - CBC
evidence.text: Trump has repeatedly said Washington and Tehran are close to a permanent deal and that negotiations are progressing; he also described talks as continuing at a “rapid pace.” The article says no formal agreement has been reached. A US-Iran truce took effect on 8 April but has not ended the fighting: the US said it struck Iranian military sites over the weekend, and Tehran said it targeted a US base in Kuwait in response. Iran insists any agreement must include peace in Lebanon, where fighting has continued. Iran’s Tasnim news agency reported that Tehran could suspend indirect negotiations with the US over Israeli military actions there.

evidence.title: Iran: War has devastated life for millions of refugees and displaced - nrc.no
evidence.text: As of June 2, 2026, a U.S.–Iran ceasefire was in place, but peace talks appeared to be stalling. Iran said Monday that Israel’s invasion of Lebanon violated the ceasefire and that it was halting peace talks with the U.S. Iran’s Tasnim news outlet also reported that direct talks were being suspended. On Tuesday, Mohammad Jafar Assadi, deputy head of Iran’s central military command, said renewed hostilities with the U.S. were inevitable unless Iran surrendered—something he said it would never do. President Trump offered a different account Monday, saying talks with Iran were continuing “at a rapid pace,” though he provided no details. He also said the U.S. would maintain its blockade of Iranian ports and vessels.

evidence.title: Middle East: Israel captures key fortress amid Lebanon push - DW.com
evidence.text: US and Iranian mediators are discussing a draft memorandum that The New York Times reports is closer to approval by both sides, but several key terms remain unresolved and President Donald Trump has not approved it. It would provide a framework for later negotiations on Iran’s nuclear programme, US sanctions, regional security and a formal end to hostilities. Talks follow a US military campaign launched on February 28; sporadic US-Iranian exchanges of fire continue despite a fragile ceasefire. Major obstacles include reopening the Strait of Hormuz and lifting the US blockade, access to Iranian assets frozen abroad, and nuclear terms. A proposed international reconstruction and investment fund of up to $300 billion is also under discussion, conditional on a permanent agreement. Negotiators remain uncertain who in Iran has final authority to approve a deal.

evidence.title: Iran war: US to lift naval blockade of ports, Trump says - DW.com
evidence.text: As of Friday, May 29, the US and Iran were officially observing a truce announced on April 7, despite occasional fighting, but had not reached a permanent peace deal. Sources cited by Iran’s semi-official Fars news agency said Iranian leaders had not made a definite decision on a memorandum of understanding with the US, although it was in the final stages of ratification. President Donald Trump left a roughly two-hour meeting with advisers without announcing his promised final determination; the White House said he would accept only a deal meeting his red lines, including that Iran never possess a nuclear weapon. The sides’ reported terms remained disputed: Fars-cited sources rejected Trump’s claims about toll-free passage through the Strait of Hormuz and joint destruction of Iran’s enriched uranium, and said Iran demanded release of $12 billion in frozen funds before the next negotiating phase. Iran’s Foreign Ministry said a final agreement depended on the US ending what it called excessive, shifting and contradictory demands. The article says Washington had repeatedly suggested a more permanent deal was near but had presented no concrete result.

Trump said prices would fall rapidly when the war ends, but energy experts said damaged infrastructure, disrupted supply chains and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz could delay a return to prewar prices even if peace were declared immediately.

evidence.title: Donald Trump says Iran has one week to respond to US deal - The Jerusalem Post
evidence.text:
Iran says it is reviewing a US proposal to end the war but has not formally responded. The sides exchanged fire in the Strait of Hormuz on Thursday, though neither has declared the ceasefire in place since April 8 over. Trump warned of stronger military action if Iran did not quickly agree to a deal.

The reported 14-point US plan would require Iran to forgo nuclear weapons, stop uranium enrichment for at least 12 years and surrender an estimated 440kg of uranium enriched to 60 percent. In return, the US would gradually lift sanctions, release billions in frozen Iranian assets and withdraw its naval blockade; both sides would reopen the Strait within 30 days of signing. Iran’s own recent 14-point proposal sought a permanent end to the war rather than an extended truce, with issues resolved within 30 days, guarantees against future attacks, sanctions relief and an end to hostilities including in Lebanon. Iranian officials call several US demands unrealistic, and a reporter described a ‘huge gap’ between the sides. Reporting from Tehran says Iran currently wants to negotiate an end to the war on all fronts, with nuclear talks only in a second phase after security guarantees and sanctions relief.

evidence.title: Trump says Iran's government is in a "state of collapse," but analysts see evolution, not fractures - CBS News
evidence.text: Pakistani officials said the US and Iran were close to a basic interim agreement, possibly as early as the coming weekend, to halt the war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz while negotiations continue. Pakistan, the principal mediator, wants a permanent end to the war announced, with other issues resolved in later direct talks. Under the latest US proposal, a first phase would end the war and reopen the strait; a second would address Iran’s nuclear programme over the following 30 days. At earlier talks, Iran proposed a three-to-five-year enrichment moratorium versus the US demand for 20–25 years; mediators thought roughly 10 years might be possible. Iran also opposed the US demand to hand over its stockpile of 60%-enriched uranium, and experts said Tehran could not accept Trump’s demand to export its highly enriched uranium to the US. Senior Iranian officials had recently rejected concessions, although Pakistani officials remained optimistic about an agreement.

evidence.title: Iran War Updates: Tehran and U.S. Offer Conflicting Messages on State of Negotiations - The New York Times

Reported terms include lifting both countries’ Strait of Hormuz blockades in exchange for U.S. sanctions relief and a 15-year Iranian moratorium on uranium enrichment. Iran would also transfer its highly enriched uranium stockpile abroad. Pakistan’s foreign minister said the aim was a “permanent end” to the conflict. Trump said Iran had one week to respond, while an Iranian spokesperson said the proposal was being evaluated. Axios also quoted an Iranian official calling it “more of a wishlist than a reality.”

Tehran wants those steps agreed before substantive nuclear talks; Washington instead demands nuclear limits and verifiable guarantees first. Since an April 8 ceasefire following US-Israeli strikes, the sides have exchanged proposals without a breakthrough. President Donald Trump has cast doubt on Iran’s offer and warned that strikes could resume. The article describes continuing maritime tensions and a US naval blockade, but says neither side appears ready to abandon talks.

evidence.title: Tehran condemns Trump's ‘brazen’ remarks about seizure of Iranian vessels - chinadailyhk
evidence.text:
Iran has submitted a new 14-point proposal to the United States through mediator Pakistan, seeking a permanent end to the war rather than an extension of the ceasefire that began April 8. Iran wants the issues resolved within 30 days. Reported terms include guarantees against future attacks, withdrawal of US forces from around Iran, sanctions relief and release of frozen assets, war reparations, an end to hostilities including in Lebanon, a new Strait of Hormuz mechanism, and recognition of Iran’s right to enrich uranium. The proposal responds to a US-backed nine-point plan focused primarily on a two-month ceasefire.

Trump said he was reviewing the proposal but was unsure a deal was possible; he later said it was difficult to imagine the terms being acceptable. No peace deal has been reached. Major obstacles include disagreement over uranium enrichment and Iran’s nuclear capability, control of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, the US blockade of Iranian ports, and Iranian mistrust of the US. One analyst said neither side was likely to abandon negotiations immediately.

evidence.title: What’s Iran’s 14-point proposal to end the war? And will Trump accept it? - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: As of May 4, 2026, no U.S.–Iran peace deal was in sight. Pakistan described its continuing mediation between the two countries. President Trump disparaged Iran’s latest proposal but said Sunday that negotiations were going “very well,” without giving details. A ceasefire was in place, yet the Strait of Hormuz remained a point of conflict: Iranian officials said U.S. interference there would violate the ceasefire, and Iran’s military threatened to attack U.S. forces entering the strait. The article reports an active diplomatic exchange, not an agreed permanent peace deal.

evidence.title: Iran war pushes oil prices to 4-year high as Hegseth faces off with senators - CBS News

They want to make a deal badly.” He said Secretary of State Marco Rubio was involved in the negotiations. Trump insisted Iran give up its enriched uranium and said the U.S. needed guarantees Iran would never have a nuclear weapon. Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, vowed Thursday to protect the country’s nuclear and missile capabilities. The U.S. blockade of Iranian ports continued during the ceasefire; Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian called it an extension of military operations and said its continuation was intolerable.

evidence.text: As of April 28, 2026, the U.S. and Iran remained at war but were discussing a possible path to ending it. White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said President Trump’s national security team had discussed the proposal, but declined to say the U.S. was considering it. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said any agreement must definitively prevent Iran from moving toward a nuclear weapon, calling that the core issue. Iranian defense ministry spokesman Reza Talaei-Nik said Tuesday that the U.S. could no longer ‘dictate’ policy to independent nations and must abandon what he called its ‘illegal and irrational demands.’ The article reports no peace agreement.

Trump also said cancelling the trip did not mean the war would resume. Araghchi left Pakistan without meeting US officials; the article reported no progress on a second round of talks and said Iranian media had linked Iran’s refusal to meet to the continuing US blockade of the Strait of Hormuz.

market.question: US x Iran permanent peace deal by December 31, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if Iran and the United states agree to a permanent peace deal by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”. 

A permanent peace deal refers to any agreement which explicitly indicates that military hostilities between the United States and Iran have ended or will permanently cease, or uses equivalent language clearly signaling a lasting end to military hostilities between the United States and Iran. Agreements that are explicitly temporary or which do not include a definitive agreement to end military hostilities between the US and Iran on a lasting basis (e.g. a temporary extension of the two-week ceasefire agreement announced on April 7, 2026), will not qualify.

A qualifying agreement will be considered to have been established if either of the following conditions are met:

- The United States and Iran each sign or formally adopt a written agreement (e.g. a treaty or multi-point agreement) which meets the above criteria.

- Both the governments of the United States and Iran provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the governments of the United States and Iran; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

market.question: Will Sofia host Eurovision 2027?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve according to the city announced to host Eurovision 2027.

This market will resolve immediately based on the official announcement for which city will host Eurovision 2027, regardless of whether that decision is later changed or the city hosts the event.

If no decision is announced by December 31, 2026, 11:59PM ET, this market will resolve to "Other".

The resolution source for this market will be information from Eurovision, including https://www.eurovision.com/, or a consensus of credible reporting.

evidence.title: Sofia or Burgas will host Eurovision 2027 - bnrnews.bg
evidence.text: As of 14 July 2026, Sofia and Burgas had advanced to the final evaluation phase of the selection process for the Eurovision Song Contest 2027 host city. Varna and Plovdiv had been eliminated. The first stage assessed proposed venues against European Broadcasting Union technical requirements and contest production standards. The Bulgarian host city was expected to be announced in July; the article does not confirm whether Sofia will be chosen.

evidence.title: Eurovision 2027: The Host City Race Enters Its Final Stage - eurovisionfun.com
evidence.text: The EBU announced that Sofia, Bulgaria’s capital, and the seaside city of Burgas are the two finalists to host Eurovision 2027. Plovdiv and Varna were on an earlier shortlist but did not advance. The article does not name a host city or identify which arena Sofia proposed, so Sofia remains a contender, not a confirmed host.

evidence.title: Sofia and Burgas Advance in Eurovision 2027 Host City Race as Varna and Plovdiv Drop Out - Novinite.com
evidence.text: On July 13, Bulgarian National Television said Sofia and the seaside city of Bourgas had been shortlisted to host Eurovision 2027. Varna and Plovdiv were eliminated after an assessment of proposed venues against technical and infrastructure criteria. The evaluation was still underway, with the host city due to be named by July 31. Sofia remains a candidate, but the article does not say it has been chosen.

evidence.title: 🇧🇬 Sofia or Burgas to Host Eurovision 2027 - Eurovoix
evidence.text: Bulgarian National Television says Sofia and Burgas are the two finalists to host Eurovision 2027, ahead of Varna and Plovdiv. Sofia proposes Arena 8888 and cites its hotel capacity, public transport and international airport; Burgas proposes Arena Burgas. The bids were assessed on venue infrastructure, accessibility, transport, accommodation and organisational readiness. The host city has not yet been chosen: a selection is expected by 30 July, though the announcement may come later.

evidence.title: Eurovision 2027: Which venues is Sofia proposing for the EuroVillage and EuroClub? - eurovisionfun.com
evidence.text: Sofia is one of four cities that have expressed interest in hosting Eurovision 2027, alongside Burgas, Plovdiv and Varna. The article says a shortlist of two cities is expected before the final decision, with the host city expected to be revealed by July 31. It does not say Sofia has been selected.

evidence.title: Eurovision 2027: Official timeline unveiled – All the key dates you need to know - eurovisionfun.com
evidence.text: Bulgaria is set to host Eurovision 2027, but Sofia has not been selected as the host city. Under a government action plan approved July 1, the host city is to be named by July 31. Sofia, Plovdiv, Varna and Bourgas are bidding, and two cities are expected to be shortlisted before the final decision.

market.question: Will the United States send warships through the Strait of Hormuz by June 30, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if a national government, its military, or a broad consensus of credible reporting confirms that the listed country's warships transited through the Strait of Hormuz between market creation and June 30, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A "warship transit" is defined as a military vessel passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Military cargo or support vessels will be considered “warships”; however, commercial or civilian vessels will not qualify.

For the purposes of this market, only transits through the Strait of Hormuz will be considered, defined as passage through the narrowest portion of the waterway between Iran and Oman. Operations solely in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, or Arabian Sea without passage through this narrowest section will not qualify.

Official confirmation by a national government or its military that its vessels transited through the Strait of Hormuz during the specified timeframe will resolve this market immediately. An overwhelming consensus of credible reporting confirming that such a transit occurred during the specified timeframe will also suffice.

Qualifying confirmations include statements such as official announcements that a country has deployed naval vessels to transit or escort shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Confirmations referring only to naval presence in the broader region, including the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, or Arabian Sea, without confirmed transit through the Strait itself, as well as aerial operations, cyber operations, or actions by proxies or third parties, will not alone qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information by the respective national governments or their militaries; however, an overwhelming consensus of credible reporting will also suffice.

market.question: Will the United States send warships through the Strait of Hormuz by June 30, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if a national government, its military, or a broad consensus of credible reporting confirms that the listed country's warships transited through the Strait of Hormuz between market creation and June 30, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A "warship transit" is defined as a military vessel passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Military cargo or support vessels will be considered “warships”; however, commercial or civilian vessels will not qualify.

For the purposes of this market, only transits through the Strait of Hormuz will be considered, defined as passage through the narrowest portion of the waterway between Iran and Oman. Operations solely in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, or Arabian Sea without passage through this narrowest section will not qualify.

Official confirmation by a national government or its military that its vessels transited through the Strait of Hormuz during the specified timeframe will resolve this market immediately. An overwhelming consensus of credible reporting confirming that such a transit occurred during the specified timeframe will also suffice.

Qualifying confirmations include statements such as official announcements that a country has deployed naval vessels to transit or escort shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Confirmations referring only to naval presence in the broader region, including the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, or Arabian Sea, without confirmed transit through the Strait itself, as well as aerial operations, cyber operations, or actions by proxies or third parties, will not alone qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information by the respective national governments or their militaries; however, an overwhelming consensus of credible reporting will also suffice.

market.question: Will the United States send warships through the Strait of Hormuz by June 30, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if a national government, its military, or a broad consensus of credible reporting confirms that the listed country's warships transited through the Strait of Hormuz between market creation and June 30, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A "warship transit" is defined as a military vessel passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Military cargo or support vessels will be considered “warships”; however, commercial or civilian vessels will not qualify.

For the purposes of this market, only transits through the Strait of Hormuz will be considered, defined as passage through the narrowest portion of the waterway between Iran and Oman. Operations solely in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, or Arabian Sea without passage through this narrowest section will not qualify.

Official confirmation by a national government or its military that its vessels transited through the Strait of Hormuz during the specified timeframe will resolve this market immediately. An overwhelming consensus of credible reporting confirming that such a transit occurred during the specified timeframe will also suffice.

Qualifying confirmations include statements such as official announcements that a country has deployed naval vessels to transit or escort shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Confirmations referring only to naval presence in the broader region, including the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, or Arabian Sea, without confirmed transit through the Strait itself, as well as aerial operations, cyber operations, or actions by proxies or third parties, will not alone qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information by the respective national governments or their militaries; however, an overwhelming consensus of credible reporting will also suffice.

market.question: Will the United States send warships through the Strait of Hormuz by June 30, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if a national government, its military, or a broad consensus of credible reporting confirms that the listed country's warships transited through the Strait of Hormuz between market creation and June 30, 2026, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A "warship transit" is defined as a military vessel passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Military cargo or support vessels will be considered “warships”; however, commercial or civilian vessels will not qualify.

For the purposes of this market, only transits through the Strait of Hormuz will be considered, defined as passage through the narrowest portion of the waterway between Iran and Oman. Operations solely in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, or Arabian Sea without passage through this narrowest section will not qualify.

Official confirmation by a national government or its military that its vessels transited through the Strait of Hormuz during the specified timeframe will resolve this market immediately. An overwhelming consensus of credible reporting confirming that such a transit occurred during the specified timeframe will also suffice.

Qualifying confirmations include statements such as official announcements that a country has deployed naval vessels to transit or escort shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.

Confirmations referring only to naval presence in the broader region, including the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, or Arabian Sea, without confirmed transit through the Strait itself, as well as aerial operations, cyber operations, or actions by proxies or third parties, will not alone qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information by the respective national governments or their militaries; however, an overwhelming consensus of credible reporting will also suffice.

If the specified individual is detained, effectively removed from the specified position, or otherwise permanently prevented from fulfilling the duties of the specified position within this market’s timeframe, it will qualify for a “Yes” resolution.

market.question: Next Mythos-Class Model released by August 31, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
On June 9, 2026, Anthropic released the Mythos-class model Claude Fable 5.

This market will resolve to "Yes" if Anthropic releases the next Mythos-class model and makes it available to the general public by the listed date (ET). Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No."

Any model whose official name includes “Mythos,” or that Anthropic officially describes as a “Mythos-class” model or similar, will qualify for this market’s resolution.

For this market to resolve to "Yes," the qualifying model (as defined above) must be launched and publicly accessible, including via open beta or open rolling waitlist signups. A closed beta or any form of private access will not suffice. The release must be clearly defined and publicly announced by Anthropic as being accessible to the general public.

If a qualifying model is made publicly accessible and labeled with the relevant version name within the company’s official website, this will qualify as “publicly announced”. Labeling errors, placeholder text, or version names displayed on the website that do not correspond to a model that is actually accessible to the general public under the rules will not qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from Anthropic; however,  a consensus of credible reporting will also be used.

evidence.title: Anthropic's Mythos 5 AI attempted GitHub supply chain attack in UK test - BetaNews
evidence.text: Anthropic launched Claude Fable 5 on June 9, 2026, with safeguards for cybersecurity, biology, chemistry, and distillation attempts. Its August 7 announcement was an update to Fable 5’s biology safeguards, not a new model release. Anthropic said Mythos-class models can outperform experts on some complex biological tasks and provide operational support on others, potentially giving malicious actors significant help. Fable 5’s system card rated its biological capabilities “CB-1” but not “CB-2,” while calling the latter judgment less clear than for previous models. The article does not announce a next Mythos-class model or give a release date for one.

The inclusion of Israel and Hezbollah in a qualifying peace deal between multiple parties will qualify.

- Both Israel and Hezbollah provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The inclusion of Israel and Hezbollah in a qualifying peace deal between multiple parties will qualify.

evidence.title: Iran warns Israel of decisive response over Lebanon attacks - Crypto Briefing

market.question: Israel x Hezbollah permanent peace deal by July 31, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to “Yes” if Israel and Hezbollah agree to a permanent peace deal by the specified date, 11:59 PM ET. Otherwise, this market will resolve to “No”.

A permanent peace deal refers to any agreement which explicitly indicates that military hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah have ended or will permanently cease, or uses equivalent language clearly signaling a lasting end to military hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah. Agreements that are explicitly temporary or which do not include a definitive agreement to end military hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah on a lasting basis (e.g. a temporary extension of the 10-day ceasefire agreement announced on April 16, 2026), will not qualify.

A qualifying agreement will be considered to have been established if either of the following conditions are met:

- Israel and Hezbollah each sign or formally adopt a written agreement (e.g. a treaty or multi-point agreement) which meets the above criteria.

- Both Israel and Hezbollah provide clear public confirmation that a qualifying agreement has been definitively established. Negotiations, statements of progress, or other statements which do not constitute a definitive announcement that a qualifying agreement has been reached will not count.

The inclusion of Israel and Hezbollah in a qualifying peace deal between multiple parties will qualify.

The primary resolution source for this market will be official information from the government of Israel and Hezbollah; however, a consensus of credible reporting may also be used.

evidence.title: Lebanon, Israel to hold next talks in Italy on Aug 4, Lebanese official says - The Straits Times
evidence.text: As of July 22, 2026, Israel and Lebanon had held more than three months of direct talks aimed at permanently ending hostilities after a March 2 war between Israel and Hezbollah. A June ceasefire was in force, and the first Israeli withdrawal under the plan had occurred, but Israel still occupied a roughly 10km-deep buffer zone and said it would remain while Hezbollah was armed. Hezbollah rejected the Lebanese government’s direct talks with Israel and refused to disarm fully. Lebanon’s president said Israeli withdrawal could remove Hezbollah’s stated justification for remaining armed, and that disarmament could follow. The next round of talks was scheduled for August 4—after the July 31 deadline; the article reports no permanent peace deal with Hezbollah.

evidence.title: 'I would speak to Hezbollah': Trump tells Lebanon's president as peace talks advance - WPDE

This is a call for talks, not a report that an agreement has been reached. The article concerns Israel–Lebanon negotiations, not direct Israel–Hezbollah peace talks. It describes Hezbollah as an Iran-guided and -funded armed group outside Lebanese state control and says Hezbollah initiated wars on October 8, 2023, and in March 2026. The authors argue that Lebanon must reclaim a state monopoly on force to secure peace across its southern border. The article gives no deadline for an agreement.

evidence.title: Why Lebanon’s Trilateral Framework Is a Recipe for Disaster - The National Interest

It does not report a permanent agreement between Israel and Hezbollah. U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio called the framework “the beginning of the beginning” and warned that much work remained. Implementation was uneven: Israel said it would retain troops in some parts of southern Lebanon until Hezbollah is disarmed, and Israeli forces remained in part of one pilot-zone village. Lebanon has pledged to disarm non-state groups, including Hezbollah, but the article does not say that disarmament has occurred.

evidence.title: Trump says U.S. will win Iran war "one way or the other" as Tehran holds funeral for supreme leader - CBS News

The parties stated an intention to end the conflict and establish peaceful relations, but the article describes a framework and continuing negotiations, not a completed permanent peace deal.

evidence.title: Lebanon's Aoun calls for sustained US support after peace deal - Dawn

Days later, following talks in Washington, Lebanon and Israel agreed to a US-backed framework intended to pave the way for a permanent end to hostilities. Hezbollah, which entered the wider war with rocket fire at Israel on March 2, rejected the framework. It calls for Hezbollah’s disarmament, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, and Lebanese army deployment there, beginning in two pilot areas; it sets no withdrawal timeline. The truce remains fragile: Israel has continued intermittent strikes, both sides accuse each other of ceasefire violations, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israel’s military would remain as long as necessary. Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said Israel’s presence prevents the Lebanese army’s deployment and obstructs the foundations of lasting peace. The article therefore describes a proposed path to peace, not a permanent deal accepted by Hezbollah.

evidence.title: US-Iran peace deal: Six things we learned from the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding - middleeasteye.net

evidence.title: What the Trump-Iran agreement says about Lebanon, Hormuz and uranium - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: The United States and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on Wednesday intended to end the Middle East war on all fronts, including Lebanon. It calls for an “immediate and permanent cessation of military operations” and guarantees Lebanon’s territorial integrity and sovereignty; a final agreement would affirm a “permanent end to the war on all fronts.” The article does not report an Israel-Hezbollah peace deal. On Thursday, Hezbollah parliamentary bloc head Mohammad Raad called for indirect negotiations and said Israel had 60 days to withdraw fully from Lebanon. The article says Israeli attacks continued and Israel insisted it would keep occupying parts of southern Lebanon.

evidence.title: U.S. intelligence warns Israel is likely to undermine Iran peace deal, officials say - The Washington Post
evidence.text: As of June 19, 2026, an interim U.S.–Iran deal required the United States, Iran and their allies to declare an immediate and permanent end to military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon. Israel, which was left out of the talks, said it was not party to the deal. The agreement gave the U.S. and Iran 60 days to reach a lasting accord or extend the interim deal; planned talks in Switzerland on June 19 were postponed after fighting flared in Lebanon. Lebanese officials reported 18 people killed in airstrikes, while Israel reported four soldiers killed in an incident in Lebanon. Hezbollah lawmaker Hassan Fadlallah said Iran had made further U.S. talks contingent on a comprehensive ceasefire and that Washington was responsible for ensuring Israel stopped its attacks. Lebanon’s president said the escalation would not hinder ceasefire efforts. The article reports no permanent Israel–Hezbollah peace deal.

evidence.title: Trump’s Iran Deal: What We Know So Far - Council on Foreign Relations
evidence.text: The article says a 14-point US–Iran memorandum calls for the “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon,” and pledges to respect Lebanon’s sovereignty. But Israel and Hezbollah, which are at war, are not signatories, leaving it unclear how a Lebanon ceasefire would be implemented. On April 16, Trump announced a 10-day Israel–Lebanon ceasefire after six weeks of Israel–Hezbollah fighting to allow talks on a more permanent security and peace agreement. The article says Israeli attacks and advances in Lebanon continued despite that ceasefire. Israel has repeatedly said it will not withdraw; Defence Minister Israel Katz said its military would remain in Lebanese security zones for an unlimited period. Iran has maintained that an end to Israeli operations in Lebanon is a prerequisite for a broader peace deal.

evidence.title: U.S. and Iran Sign Preliminary Deal, but Its Terms Remain Secret - nytimes.com
evidence.text: The article says a U.S.–Iran memorandum of understanding signed on Sunday calls for the immediate and permanent end of military operations on all fronts, including Lebanon, by the U.S., Iran and their allies. It says the agreement requires respect for Lebanon’s sovereignty, which the article interprets as requiring Israel to withdraw from southern Lebanon. The quoted provision says a *final deal* will confirm the permanent termination of the war, so the article does not establish that a final Israel–Hezbollah peace deal has been signed. It also reports Israeli opposition to withdrawing and fresh Israeli attacks on Hezbollah targets on Wednesday. The article gives no date for the final deal.

evidence.title: Trump Champions Peace Agreement, Threatens to Resume Bombing If Iran Doesn't Comply - Time Magazine
evidence.text: The proposed U.S.–Iran memorandum says that, by signing it, the two countries declare the “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon.” But the article describes a 60-day cease-fire intended to allow further negotiations, not a completed Israel–Hezbollah peace deal. It says fresh strikes between Israel and Hezbollah could derail a permanent truce. Iran insists that a permanent truce include an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ruled out an immediate withdrawal. Trump acknowledged a U.S.–Israel “dispute over Lebanon” and said the issue still needed work.

evidence.title: Is Lebanon included? Country hopeful for US-Iran ceasefire, despite doubts - aljazeera.com
evidence.text:
Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said the newly announced US–Iran deal called for the “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon.” Lebanese President Joseph Aoun welcomed the announcement but said the understandings still needed to become practical steps; Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri said the deal included a clause halting Israeli attacks across Lebanon. The article does not report a permanent peace deal between Israel and Hezbollah.

Whether fighting will stop remains uncertain. Reuters reported that Hezbollah had conducted no operations since the announcement as of Monday afternoon, but Lebanese state media reported an Israeli drone strike that killed a driver in southern Lebanon. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israel opposed withdrawing its army from Lebanon and would keep forces in security zones without a time limit. Earlier ceasefires also failed to end hostilities: under the November 2024 agreement, Israel did not fully withdraw and continued attacks; an April 16 ceasefire left fighting in southern Lebanon ongoing; and a June 3 Israel–Lebanon ceasefire had little effect, with Israeli attacks and Hezbollah rocket fire continuing.

evidence.title: Next round of Israel-Lebanon talks to be held in Rome - Armenpress
evidence.text: Lebanon and Israel signed a framework agreement last month intended to pave the way for a permanent end to hostilities; the article does not say they have reached a permanent peace deal. The agreement calls for Hezbollah’s disarmament, a gradual Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon and Lebanese army deployment there, starting in two pilot areas, but sets no withdrawal timeline. Hezbollah has strongly criticized it. A ceasefire has been in effect since June 21, yet both sides accuse the other of violations. Lebanese state media reported that an Israeli strike on Monday killed four people, including three women; Israel said it targeted four people it considered a threat. Lebanon’s president said Israel’s continued presence prevents army deployment, while Israel’s prime minister said its forces would remain as long as necessary to protect Israelis. The article’s title says the next round of Israel-Lebanon talks will be held in Rome.

evidence.title: Lebanese parliament speaker welcomes US-Iran deal, inclusion of Lebanon - The New Region
evidence.text: Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a U.S.–Iran deal, saying “both sides” had declared the “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon.” Iranian state television carried a similar claim. But the article describes the agreement as an initial memorandum, with signing expected Friday in Switzerland; Iran said it would not begin implementing it before then. It does not report a separate Israel–Hezbollah peace deal. Israel’s fighting with Hezbollah in Lebanon had nearly derailed negotiations, and Israel bombed Beirut’s southern suburbs Sunday. After the announcement, Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said Israel would not withdraw from land seized in Lebanon while the interim deal was pending and planned to remain there “indefinitely.” Iran had tied the interim deal to a halt in Israeli attacks on Hezbollah.

evidence.title: Iran says the deal to end the war with the U.S. requires Israel to withdraw from Lebanon - PBS
evidence.text: As of June 16, 2026, the article describes an ongoing Israel–Hezbollah war that erupted on March 2, with Israel pressing an offensive in southern Lebanon. Israel’s presence in Lebanon remains a major obstacle to ending the wider conflict. Iran insists that any agreement to end it must stop the fighting in Lebanon, while a spokesperson for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said Israel would continue to defend itself against security threats. A senior U.S. official said Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon is not required by the U.S.–Iran memorandum of understanding, which the official described as a ceasefire. The official said Israel could respond if Hezbollah attacked Israeli positions or towns. The upcoming 60-day U.S.–Iran talks are to prioritize nuclear issues; Iran has said its support for groups including Hezbollah is excluded from those talks. The article reports no permanent Israel–Hezbollah peace deal.

evidence.title: US and Iran have reached ‘Peace Deal’ including Lebanon truce, Pakistani PM announces - The Times of Israel
evidence.text: Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif announced a US–Iran deal and said both sides had declared an “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon,” where Israel and Iran-backed Hezbollah have been fighting. Trump said the pact was signed, but the article describes it as extending a ceasefire for 60 days while details of a final agreement are negotiated; it does not report a permanent Israel–Hezbollah peace deal. Lebanon’s president welcomed the announcement, but Lebanon’s NNA reported a lethal Israeli drone strike on Monday after it. evidence.title: TIMELINE – How the US-Israel war with Iran unfolded over 108 days - The Express Tribune
evidence.text: The article describes a tentative US–Iran memorandum of understanding, not a permanent Israel–Hezbollah peace deal. Its terms had not been published, and accounts of what it says about Lebanon conflicted. Hezbollah had not officially commented. Lebanese parliament speaker Nabih Berri, a Hezbollah ally and intermediary with the US, thanked both sides for what he called “an essential and binding clause on halting the Israeli aggression on all of Lebanon.” Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said on Monday, June 15, that he hoped the deal would put a “definitive end” to the Israel–Hezbollah conflict. Iran’s foreign minister said Israeli attacks on Lebanon must stop under the deal. But Lebanon’s state news agency reported fresh Israeli attacks in southern Lebanon overnight, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Israeli forces would remain in southern Lebanon security zones for as long as necessary.

evidence.title: Iran updates: Netanyahu refrains from criticizing Iran deal - DW.com
evidence.text: The article reports a US–Iran peace deal announced by Pakistan and confirmed by Washington and Tehran, with a signing scheduled for June 19 in Switzerland. That bears on Israel–Hezbollah fighting, but the article does not report a permanent peace deal between Israel and Hezbollah. evidence.text: The article reports that Israeli forces continued to clash with Hezbollah fighters despite a US-brokered agreement between Israel and Lebanon intended to pave the way toward a lasting end to hostilities. The article describes an agreement aimed at ending hostilities, not a permanent peace deal.

evidence.text: The article says Israel and Lebanon have reached a 2026 framework agreement—their first agreement since the short-lived May 1983 peace treaty, and, in the writer’s view, potentially their most significant bilateral agreement since the 1949 Armistice Agreements. It reports no permanent peace deal or breakthrough in talks and gives no date for the reported seizure.

evidence.source: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
evidence.text: Iran’s published 14-point proposal calls for an immediate, permanent cessation of hostilities on all fronts, including Lebanon. US officials said the memorandum of understanding sought to include Iran’s regional proxies, but Israeli withdrawal from Lebanon was not a condition, and they reiterated Israel’s right to defend itself against Hezbollah. A temporary ceasefire in Lebanon has been in place since April 16 and was renewed in June, yet Israel–Hezbollah strikes have continued; Israel struck what it said were Hezbollah targets in southern Lebanon even after the latest deal was announced. Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said Israeli forces would remain in security zones in Lebanon indefinitely. The article identifies Israel’s actions in Lebanon as a major obstacle to regional peace and notes that Israel, Lebanon and Hezbollah are not parties to the deal.

evidence.title: Trump announces peace deal with Iran, ending hostilities - EWTN News
evidence.text: The article says southern Lebanon remains tense, with reports of Israeli strikes despite claims of a ceasefire. It describes these developments as part of ongoing Israel–Hezbollah tensions and says further escalation could affect the prospects for a peace deal. It reports no permanent Israel–Hezbollah agreement or date for one.

evidence.title: Iran warns Israel of decisive response over Lebanon attacks - Crypto Briefing
evidence.text: The article describes a proposed more permanent U.S.–Iran ceasefire, not an Israel–Hezbollah peace deal. Trump has publicly criticized Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu for continuing to strike Hezbollah, while Iran insists that any ceasefire accord with the U.S. protect Hezbollah from Israeli attacks. Fighting nevertheless continued: Israel said it struck near Beirut in response to Hezbollah attacks on northern Israel, prompting an Iranian threat to strike Israel. In an earlier exchange that week, Iran fired missiles at Israel. Netanyahu said Israel’s struggle was “not over” and that it would remain in security zones in Lebanon as long as necessary. Defense Minister Israel Katz likewise opposed withdrawing Israeli forces from Lebanon despite pressure. Israeli political opposition to concessions was also evident: National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir said Trump’s agreement would not bind Israel and demanded Hezbollah’s dismantling and no withdrawal from captured territory. These unresolved security and political disputes weigh against a permanent Israel–Hezbollah deal, though the article does not say whether one will be reached by July 31, 2026.

evidence.title: Can Washington force Israel to comply with a U.S.-Iranian deal it rejects? - CBC
evidence.text: The article reports a U.S.–Iran peace deal slated for signing on June 19, 2026, but does not report a permanent peace deal between Israel and Hezbollah. Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif said both sides had declared an “immediate and permanent termination of military operations on all fronts, including in Lebanon.” The article says a clause suspending military hostilities in Lebanon is likely to appear in the memorandum, though the deal’s details remain unclear and Trump did not mention Lebanon when confirming the deal on Truth Social. An exchange of words, handshake, direct conversation, or other clear personal interaction between the named individuals will qualify as a meeting. Merely standing in proximity, making eye contact, or being present in the same room or event without direct interaction will not qualify.

A meeting is defined as any encounter where both Zelenskyy and Putin are present and interact with each other in person.

The resolution source will be a consensus of credible reporting.

evidence.text: As of August 24, 2026, the article reports no planned meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy said Ukraine desperately wants peace but is “not ready to capitulate.” He said he believed Moscow would not end its invasion even if Kyiv ceded more territory in eastern Ukraine, a condition Putin has set for ending the conflict. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said negotiations should begin from the line of contact and that Ukraine should not give up territory Russia could not win on the battlefield. The article gives no indication that a Putin–Zelenskyy meeting will occur by August 31.

The article does not report that Putin has agreed to talks or that a Putin–Zelenskyy meeting is scheduled by August 31, 2026.

evidence.title: Putin rejected Black Sea shipping truce offer, Zelenskyy says - Türkiye Today

Zelenskyy said Russia rejected Ukraine’s proposed truce on attacks against ships carrying agricultural commodities through the Black Sea, seeking assurances against strikes on Russian energy infrastructure in return. Putin acknowledged economic damage from Ukrainian drone attacks, including strikes on oil refineries deep inside Russia, and said he had rejected Kyiv’s ceasefire proposals as “unacceptable” and, in some cases, “exotic,” without explaining why. He said Russia remained open to peace dialogue only on the basis of “the realities on the ground.” Zelenskyy said Kyiv was willing to discuss an energy ceasefire on reciprocal terms, as well as agricultural or broader ceasefires.

evidence.title: Zelenskyy says Putin rejected Black Sea shipping truce offer - The Spokesman-Review
evidence.text: The article reports no planned meeting between Putin and Zelenskyy. Zelenskyy said Russia rejected Ukraine’s proposal to stop attacks on ships carrying agricultural goods through the Black Sea because Moscow wanted guarantees against strikes on its energy infrastructure. On Saturday, Putin acknowledged economic damage from Ukrainian drone attacks, including strikes on oil refineries deep inside Russia, but said he had rejected Kyiv’s ceasefire proposals as “unacceptable” and, in some cases, “exotic,” without elaborating. Putin said he remained open to peace dialogue only “on the basis of the realities on the ground.” Zelenskyy said Kyiv was willing to discuss a reciprocal energy ceasefire or a full ceasefire on equal terms.

market.question: Will the next diplomatic US-Iran meeting be in another Middle East/North Africa country by September 30, 2026?
market.resolution_criteria:
On June 22, the first round of U.S.-Iran diplomatic talks in Switzerland concluded, with mediators reporting progress toward a roadmap for a final deal and follow-on technical talks expected to continue (see: https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2026/6/22/us-iran-agree-on-roadmap-towards-final-deal-in-switzerland-talks).

This market will resolve according to the country in which the next formal senior-level round of peace talks between representatives of the United States and Iran begins by September 30, 2026, 11:59 PM ET.

A qualifying round must be a deliberate in-person diplomatic meeting or negotiating round concerning US-Iran relations, involving senior representatives of both the United States and Iran who are acting in an official capacity and are authorized to conduct or materially direct diplomacy on behalf of their governments.

Indirect in-person diplomacy through designated mediators, facilitators, or interlocutors will qualify, provided senior representatives of both the United States and Iran are participating in the same formal diplomatic process with the knowledge and authorization of their respective governments. The representatives need not be in the same room at the same time.

Follow-on technical talks from the June 22 Switzerland round will not qualify by themselves. Technical, staff-level, working-group, implementation, monitoring, preparatory, or deconfliction meetings will not qualify unless they occur as part of a new formally convened senior-level U.S.-Iran peace-talks round.

Brief greetings, chance encounters, photo opportunities, ceremonial appearances, or talks not deliberately aimed at diplomacy or negotiation will not count.

The meeting must be in-person (including indirect in-person meetings) and must be publicly acknowledged by either government or reported by a consensus of credible media. Remote meetings, phone calls, or other meetings where the relevant parties are not present will not count.

If a qualifying round occurs in more than one country, resolution will be based on the country where the first qualifying senior-level diplomatic session begins.

If the next qualifying round begins in any country in the Middle East or North Africa other than the listed options, this market will resolve to “Other - Middle East/North Africa.”

If the next qualifying round begins in any country in Europe other than the listed options, this market will resolve to “Other - Europe.”

For purposes of this market, countries’ regions will be determined based on the U.S. State Department’s regional classifications in the “Countries and Areas List” (https://www.state.gov/countries-and-areas-list). Any country classified as part of “Europe and Eurasia” will be considered to be in Europe. Any country classified as part of “Near East (Middle East and North Africa)” will be considered to be in the Middle East/North Africa.

If the next qualifying round begins in any unlisted country that is not classified in either specified region, this market will resolve to “Other.”

If no qualifying round begins by September 30, 2026, 11:59 PM ET, this market will resolve to “No Meeting by September 30.”

The resolution sources for this market will be official information from the governments of the United States and Iran, and a consensus of credible reporting.

evidence.title: Trump warns of economic consequences for any country supporting Iran - SABC News
evidence.text: Earlier in August, Trump said US-Iran talks were underway, but Iranian officials denied that a formal meeting had been scheduled. Trump has also described the contacts as “semi-negotiating,” a characterization Tehran disputes. The article says messages can pass through intermediaries, including Oman, Pakistan and Qatar, without a formal US-Iran meeting; Pakistan and Qatar have been involved in mediation efforts. Iran separately said on August 9 that its shipping agreement with Oman was in its “final stages,” but that is not described as a US-Iran meeting. The article identifies no confirmed date or location for the next formal US-Iran meeting.

evidence.title: Iran’s Nuclear Program and State of War - Jerusalem Studio 1035 - TV7 Israel News
evidence.text: Iran denied that any US-Iran negotiations were under way, contradicting President Donald Trump’s statement on Sunday that talks would begin Monday afternoon. Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said Iran had no plans to host US officials or send negotiators abroad; he said all Iranian negotiators were in Iran except Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi, who was on a religious pilgrimage in Iraq. A senior Iranian source told Reuters that no talks were scheduled and Araqchi would be unavailable until at least the end of the week. Tehran said its only ongoing discussions were with Oman, exclusively about shipping through the Strait of Hormuz—not a US-Iran meeting. The article says Iran has rejected direct US negotiations since a US-backed memorandum of understanding collapsed in early July. It identifies no planned location for a next US-Iran meeting.

evidence.title: Trump says new Iran negotiations starting: What we know - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: Trump said on Sunday that new US-Iran negotiations would begin Monday, but gave no location or participants. Reporting from Doha on Monday, Al Jazeera’s Osama Bin Javaid said an unnamed source had suggested mediators were ready to fly to Tehran for an indirect negotiation session. He said Pakistani and Qatari emissaries might help arrange it, though specific details were unknown. Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said Iran would not host a delegation or visit another country “during these days”; the article says it was unclear whether that ruled out indirect talks through mediators. Iran was separately talking with Oman about reopening the Strait of Hormuz. The article therefore identifies Tehran as a possible site for an indirect session, but does not establish where or whether the next diplomatic US-Iran meeting will occur.

evidence.title: Trump Warns of Fresh Strikes on Iran if Nuclear Talks Fail - IranWire
evidence.text: Iran called for a diplomatic solution after U.S. President Donald Trump rejected its Hormuz proposal. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Tehran was awaiting a definitive U.S. response through mediators. The article does not report an agreed next U.S.-Iran meeting, its location, or whether it would occur by September 30, 2026.

evidence.title: Why has the US halted its bombing of Iran? - Al Jazeera
evidence.text: US and Iranian strikes have paused, and US Ambassador Mike Waltz said the pause gives ongoing talks space. Iran’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei told Austrian broadcaster ORF on Sunday that mediators are exchanging messages between Iran and the US, while saying Iran had previously been “betrayed” despite its diplomatic efforts. Qatar, Egypt and Pakistan have worked with other regional mediators on a new ceasefire and recently proposed a 10-day pause in fighting. An earlier ceasefire was brokered in Islamabad, and the US and Iran signed a memorandum of understanding on June 17 while peace talks were under way. Iran is also discussing a Strait of Hormuz reopening proposal with Oman. The article reports diplomatic activity but gives no confirmed date or location for a next US-Iran meeting.

evidence.title: Give Peace A Chance? U.S. Reaching a Strategic Dead End against Iran - The Soufan Center
evidence.text: As of late July 2026, a regional official involved in mediation said both the U.S. and Iran wanted to return to their June interim ceasefire deal. A compromise under negotiation would let Iran manage vessel transit through the Strait of Hormuz with fewer restrictions on ships. Iran said it had held several rounds of technical talks with Oman about the strait in Tehran over the weekend; Oman's delegation left Saturday, but Iran said the talks were continuing. President Trump also said the U.S. was negotiating with Iran. The article does not announce a date or location for a next U.S.-Iran meeting, or say it will take place in another Middle East or North Africa country by September 30, 2026.

evidence.title: The U.S. and Iran pause attacks on each other for a 2nd day as Tehran talks with Oman over Hormuz - Fortune
evidence.text: A regional official involved in mediation said diplomacy was underway and that the pause in U.S. and Iranian strikes was a “positive signal” for de-escalation. The official said both countries wanted to return to an interim ceasefire deal signed in mid-June, with mediators negotiating a compromise over Iran’s management of vessel transit through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran separately said it was continuing talks with Oman about safe passage through the strait. The article reports no scheduled next U.S.–Iran diplomatic meeting, host country, or meeting date.

evidence.title: Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi heads to Tehran for talks amid Iran-US mediation efforts - The Express Tribune

market.question: Will the next diplomatic US-Iran meeting be in another Middle East/North Africa country by September 30, 2026?

This market will resolve according to the country in which the next formal senior-level round of peace talks between representatives of the United States and Iran begins by September 30, 2026, 11:59 PM ET.

A qualifying round must be a deliberate in-person diplomatic meeting or negotiating round concerning US-Iran relations, involving senior representatives of both the United States and Iran who are acting in an official capacity and are authorized to conduct or materially direct diplomacy on behalf of their governments.

Indirect in-person diplomacy through designated mediators, facilitators, or interlocutors will qualify, provided senior representatives of both the United States and Iran are participating in the same formal diplomatic process with the knowledge and authorization of their respective governments. The representatives need not be in the same room at the same time.

Follow-on technical talks from the June 22 Switzerland round will not qualify by themselves. Technical, staff-level, working-group, implementation, monitoring, preparatory, or deconfliction meetings will not qualify unless they occur as part of a new formally convened senior-level U.S.-Iran peace-talks round.

Brief greetings, chance encounters, photo opportunities, ceremonial appearances, or talks not deliberately aimed at diplomacy or negotiation will not count.

The meeting must be in-person (including indirect in-person meetings) and must be publicly acknowledged by either government or reported by a consensus of credible media. Remote meetings, phone calls, or other meetings where the relevant parties are not present will not count.

If a qualifying round occurs in more than one country, resolution will be based on the country where the first qualifying senior-level diplomatic session begins.

Any country classified as part of “Near East (Middle East and North Africa)” will be considered to be in the Middle East/North Africa.

The resolution source will be official information from the Bank of England, including the statement or release from its September 2026 Monetary Policy Committee meeting, scheduled for September 17 2026, as listed on the official Bank of England calendar (https://www.bankofengland.co.uk/monetary-policy/upcoming-mpc-dates). This market may resolve as soon as the statement or release of the Bank of England's September 2026 Monetary Policy Committee meeting with relevant data is issued.

If the specified rate is defined by an upper and lower bound, the relevant change will be the change to the upper bound.

If the specified rate is changed to a level not expressed in the displayed options, the change will be rounded according to the following guidelines. Increases or decreases of less than 25 bps will be rounded to 25 bps (e.g. an increase or decrease of 10 bps would be considered to be an increase or decrease of 25 bps). Increases or decreases of greater than 25 bps will be rounded to the nearest 25 bps and will be rounded away from 0 in cases of equidistance (e.g., an increase or decrease of 37.5 bps would be considered to be an increase or decrease of 50 bps). Displayed options of “Increase” or “Decrease” will include policy rate increases or decreases of any size.

If the specified meeting is postponed to a date and time before the start of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve based on the outcome of that postponed meeting. If the specified meeting is cancelled, or postponed such that no decision is announced by the start of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve to the “No Change” bracket. Emergency changes to the specified rate not resulting from the specified meeting will not be considered.

evidence.title: Nationwide customers hit with new charges from tomorrow as change confirmed - Liverpool Echo
evidence.text: A Reuters survey conducted September 4–8 found that all 65 economists expected the Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee to leave its 3.75% base rate unchanged at its September 17 meeting. Fifty-seven expected no change through year-end; the other eight expected a rise to 4% by then. These are forecasts, not a reported meeting decision.

evidence.title: Bank of England to hold rates, show patience with war-driven inflation: Reuters poll - Reuters
evidence.text: The article’s title says a Reuters poll expects the Bank of England to hold rates. The article text, however, offers mixed signals ahead of the Monetary Policy Committee’s September 17 meeting. Nationwide said it would raise selected fixed and tracker mortgage rates by up to 0.20% from the following day. Adam Stiles of Helix Financial Partners said the tracker-rate increase was “rather telling” about Nationwide’s outlook for the meeting and expected rates to remain high until volatility eased. Jack Tutton of SJ Mortgages said the increase might reflect either tracker demand or Nationwide forecasting a base-rate rise. The article does not state the year of the September 17 meeting or report its outcome.

evidence.title: US Fed leaves federal funds rate unchanged: How can a status quo impact the Indian stock market? - Livemint
evidence.text: The Bank of England held its Base Rate at 3.75% after the Monetary Policy Committee’s July meeting, leaving borrowing costs unchanged. The rate had been at 3.75% since a reduction in December 2025. The article says the next MPC meeting is in September, when policymakers will consider new inflation, labour-market and growth data. Inflation had eased to 2.6% in June, but uncertainty over energy prices and geopolitical tensions had tempered expectations of an imminent cut. The article does not report a September decision, so the July hold does not establish whether rates will be unchanged after the September 2026 meeting.

evidence.title: RECAP: How the Bank of England reached its latest decision - mpamag.com
evidence.text: The article reports that the Bank of England’s MPC held Bank Rate at 3.75% at its latest decision, by a 6–3 vote. Megan Greene, Catherine Mann and Huw Pill voted to raise it immediately to 4%; dissent had grown from two members at the June meeting. The minutes described upside inflation risks from energy prices, although CPI had fallen to 2.6% and there was little evidence yet of second-round effects. Members who voted to hold said rates could move in either direction. The article says the next scheduled decision is in September 2026; it does not report the outcome of that meeting.

evidence.title: POLL Bank of England to hold rates for remainder of year despite inflation risks - reuters.com
evidence.text: The Bank of England has held its Bank Rate at 3.75% so far this year, but financial markets predict a rise this year, possibly as early as its September meeting, with rates reaching as high as 4.25% by late 2027. The article also says a majority of the nine-member Monetary Policy Committee are wary of raising rates because higher borrowing costs could weaken the UK economy without much affecting global oil prices. A September hold is therefore possible, but the market prediction weighs against it.

evidence.title: Expect A STATUS QUO Policy - LinkedIn
evidence.text: The article reports that the Bank of England kept interest rates at 3.75%, with its Monetary Policy Committee voting 6–3 to hold. Governor Andrew Bailey said holding Bank Rate was appropriate because global conditions looked more uncertain and inflationary, while domestic conditions were more benign for inflation. The article says the BoE had held rates since December 2025, following four cuts. It does not identify this as the September 2026 meeting or say what the BoE will decide then.

evidence.text: The article says the Bank of England held interest rates at the decision it describes. Portfolio manager James Lynch said there was “a high bar” for a rate increase. The article does not give a date for that rate decision or state what the BOE will decide at a September 2026 meeting; its reference to September concerns an updated outlook for quantitative tightening.

evidence.title: VIEW Bank of England leaves rates steady, more officials back a hike - reuters.com
evidence.text: The Bank of England’s Monetary Policy Committee voted 6–3 to leave its base rate unchanged at 3.75% amid volatility from the Middle East conflict. Catherine Mann, Megan Greene and Huw Pill voted to raise it to 4%. Governor Andrew Bailey said the Bank was not edging toward a rate hike, though the committee said it was ready to act if inflation pressures became entrenched. Markets had priced in a greater than 90% chance of a hold at this meeting, but investors expected a rise to 4% before year-end. The article does not explicitly identify this as the September 2026 meeting.

The BoE’s majority favoured waiting despite inflation risks from higher energy prices and the U.S.–Iran conflict.

evidence.text: The Bank of England is expected to hold its 3.75% base rate at this week’s meeting, but the next Monetary Policy Committee meeting is in mid-September 2026. market.question: Will the Bank of Russia make no change to the key rate after the September Meeting?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve according to the change in the key rate resulting from the Bank of Russia’s September meeting, relative to the level it was prior to this meeting.

The resolution source for this market is information released by the Bank of Russia after its September 11, 2026 meeting as listed on the official Bank of Russia calendar: https://www.cbr.ru/eng/dkp/cal_mp/#t13

This market may resolve as soon as the Bank of Russia’s press release for their September 11, 2026 meeting with relevant data is issued. If no decision on the key rate is issued by the end date of the next scheduled meeting, this market will resolve to the "No change" bracket.

evidence.title: ECB Holds Rates Steady As Oil Risks Loom. Traders Are Betting On A September Hike - International Business Times
evidence.text: The Bank of Russia cut its key rate to 14% from 14.25%, surprising most analysts in a Reuters poll who had expected it to hold. The bank lowered its economic growth forecast to 0–1% from 0.5–1.5%, while raising its 2026 inflation forecast to 6–7% from 4.5–5.5%. Annual inflation rose to 6% in June from 5.3% a month earlier, and household inflation expectations rose in July to their highest level since March 2022. The article reports no decision or stated plan for the September meeting.

evidence.title: BOE on Alert for Signs of Persistent Inflation as It Holds Rates - WSJ
evidence.text: The article says the Bank of Russia cut its key rate by 25 basis points to 14.00% on 24 July, its ninth consecutive cut from a peak of 21%. It provides no forecast or other evidence about whether the rate will remain unchanged after the September meeting.

evidence.title: Russians withdraw 2.4T rubles in cash, sparking liquidity concerns - Crypto Briefing
evidence.text: The article says the Bank of Russia’s data and statements suggest a pause in rate cuts, but its specific forecast concerns the July 24 meeting, not the September meeting. June’s seasonally adjusted annual inflation rate rose from 2% to 10.6%. Although the bank described the fuel-driven jump as largely one-off, its analysts warned that higher fuel costs were spreading to other prices. Deputy Governor Alexei Zabotkin said the bank could not ignore fuel prices and inflation expectations. The article says a 25-basis-point cut in July was possible, but a pause was much more likely. It makes no explicit prediction about the rate decision after September’s meeting.

market.question: Will the iPhone 18 Pro cost at least $1200?
market.resolution_criteria:
This market will resolve to "Yes" if the standard edition of the iPhone 18 Pro launches at the listed price or more. Otherwise, this market will resolve to "No".

This market will resolve based on the pre-tax launch price in USD of the standard edition of the iPhone 18 Pro as listed on the official Apple Store website or Apple’s retail pricing in the United States on the first official day of its release.

If the price differs between configurations (e.g., base storage vs. higher storage), this market will resolve according to the lower price of the version that includes the full standard iPhone 18 Pro model with no additional features, accessories, or services (e.g., base storage capacity only).

If the iPhone 18 Pro is not released by March 31, 2027, 11:59 PM ET, this market will resolve to "No".

The primary resolution source for this market will be the official Apple Store (online or retail pricing), however a consensus of credible reporting will also be used.

evidence.title: Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max Release Date India vs USA Pre-orders - RS Web Solutions
evidence.text: Bloomberg sources say Apple executives are considering a $100 (about £80) increase to the starting price of the next Pro-grade iPhone. The article says this would be roughly a 7% year-on-year rise for the iPhone 18 Pro lineup, driven by higher component costs and supply-chain pressure. Apple has not confirmed an iPhone price increase, and the article does not give a US starting price from which to determine whether the iPhone 18 Pro would cost at least $1,200.

evidence.title: iPhone 18: Rumors and Release Date - MacRumors
evidence.text: Apple has not confirmed iPhone 18 pricing. GF Securities analyst Jeff Pu predicts that the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max could each cost $250–$300 more than their predecessors, citing higher chip and memory costs and AI-related pressure on chip supplies. The article calculates a possible US starting price of $1,449–$1,499 for the Pro Max, but gives no US starting-price estimate for the iPhone 18 Pro. Pu’s forecast supports a price increase for the Pro, but the article does not establish whether it will cost at least $1,200. Apple is expected to confirm pricing at its September unveiling.

evidence.title: The iPhone 17's Current Price Might Look Like A Great Deal Soon - bgr.com
evidence.text: The article does not report a confirmed iPhone 18 Pro price. It says Apple is expected to unveil the Pro models in September 2026 and that Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman considers a price increase for new iPhones inevitable after Mac and iPad prices rose about 23% on average. Some sources suggest the Pro models could cost Apple nearly 40% more to produce, while Samsung and Google have each raised premium-phone prices by $100. If Apple follows that $100 trend, the article estimates the iPhone 18 Pro could start at $1,199, up from $1,099 for the iPhone 17 Pro—$1 below the question’s $1,200 threshold. It also raises the possibility that Apple could increase the base Pro model’s storage to 512GB to charge more.

evidence.title: Apple iPhone price increase ‘inevitable’: report - VnExpress International
evidence.text: The article does not report an announced iPhone 18 Pro price. It says Samsung and Google recently raised smartphone prices by about $100; a similar Apple increase would put the iPhone 18 Pro at $1,199—about 9% above the 17 Pro’s $1,099 starting price, but $1 below $1,200. In an Aug. 23 report, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman called an iPhone price increase “inevitable” because of memory and silicon shortages, and said even a $100 increase would leave Apple absorbing some added costs. The article says Apple could raise prices further, but gives no specific higher price.
